title: Ravens sign G Michael Jordan after Vega Ioane injury
summary: The Ravens have responded to the Seahawks’ trade for Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson by adding some offensive line reinforcements of their own. Well, that might be an exaggeration. Baltimore did sign Michael Jordan to their practice squad, but the move should obviously not be taken in the context of Seattle’s blockbuster trade. Instead, it […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - SEPTEMBER 15: Guard Mike Jordan #60 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on the field before the NFL game between Houston Texans and Tampa Bay Buccaneers on September 15, 2025, at NRG Stadium in Houston, TX. (Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Ravens have responded to the Seahawks’ trade for Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson by adding some offensive line reinforcements of their own. Well, that might be an exaggeration. Baltimore did sign Michael Jordan to their practice squad, but the move should obviously not be taken in the context of Seattle’s blockbuster trade. Instead, it should be seen as a reaction to Tuesday’s news that first-round pick Vega Ioane will miss time with a sprained MCL. The Ravens have already been dealing with a slew of offensive line injuries; now, either Andrew Vorhees or Emery Jones will re-enter the starting lineup at right guard. The other will back up both guard spots with backup center Kyle Hergel available in a pinch. The Ravens have Chuma Edoga on their practice squad as additional guard depth, but he only has one game day elevation remaining and may not be worth an active roster spot. Bringing Jordan in now allows him to learn the offense and stay prepared in case he is needed as depth in the coming weeks. Jordan, 28, was originally a Bengals fourth-round pick in 2019. He started 19 games over his first two seasons – due in part to Cincinnati’s offensive line injuries – but was out of the game day picture entering 2021. Jordan was waived in September and later picked up by the Panthers, who badly needed O-line help and installed him as their starting left guard to close out the season. He served as a backup the following year before 11 starts for the Patriots in 2024 and nine for the Buccaneers last year, again as a result of his teammates’ injuries. The 6-foot-6, 315-pound guard has never graded out as a starting-caliber offensive lineman, according to Pro Football Focus , but he has demonstrated some improvements in pass protection. His 60.4 and 71.1 pass-blocking grades in 2024 and 2025 were career-bests, as was his identical 96.8 pass blocking efficiency in each year. He does not profile as an instant upgrade to the starting lineup, but his experience ensures Baltimore has a relatively experienced player to fill in at guard if needed. In a corresponding move, the Ravens released running back Jonathan Ward from their practice squad. He has spent time in Baltimore in each of the last two seasons but has not appeared in a game. The team now has three running backs on their active roster and none on their practice squad, suggesting that rookie Adam Randall is close to returning from injured reserve. He was sidelined with a foot injury to start the year and became eligible to return in Week 5. The Ravens offense is desperate to improve in short-yardage situations, and the 6-foot-3, 240-pound running back could be part of the solution. He ran hard in the preseason and averaged 3.71 yards after contact ( via PFF ). Keep an eye out for reports on Wednesday morning about his potential presence on the practice field.

title: Ravens rookie guard Vega Ioane to miss time with MCL sprain
summary: The Baltimore Ravens are down yet another offensive lineman. Rookie guard Vega Ioane is expected to “miss a little time” after suffering an MCL injury in Week 7 against the Cincinnati Bengals. Ioane, 22, went down late in the first quarter of Sunday’s loss and did not return. He was replaced by third-year lineman Emery […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - OCTOBER 18: Olaivavega Ioane #71 of the Baltimore Ravens takes the field prior to a game against the Cleveland Browns at Huntington Bank Field on October 18, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens are down yet another offensive lineman. Rookie guard Vega Ioane is expected to “miss a little time” after suffering an MCL injury in Week 7 against the Cincinnati Bengals. Ioane, 22, went down late in the first quarter of Sunday’s loss and did not return. He was replaced by third-year lineman Emery Jones, who has played a majority of the Ravens’ right guard snaps over their last four games. Jones entered the regular season as Baltimore’s No. 3 guard, but injuries have pressed him into a significant role. Jovaughn Gwyn and Ethan Pocic went down in Week 3, moving Ioane to center and inserting Andrew Vorhees at right guard. Vorhees injured his foot in the same game, giving Jones his first snaps of the season. Vorhees attempted to play through his foot issue in Week 4, but had to be replaced by Jones mid-game. The 2024 third-round pick started in Weeks 5 and 6 before newly-acquired center Cam Jurgens was able to enter the starting lineup and move Ioane back to his natural position. If Vorhees’ foot is healed, the Ravens could put him back at right guard. He did get the first crack at the job after Ioane moved to center. But the team might know what they have in Vorhees, who struggled mightily as a starter in 2025. Jones has not been great this year, ranking among the league’s bottom 15 guards in sack rate, pass block efficiency, pass block grade, and run block grade, per Pro Football Focus (min. 150 snaps) . But that is still a relatively small sample size, and he still might be the better option to hold down the fort until Ioane gets back. Ioane, meanwhile, will look to get back on the field as quickly as possible. The No. 14 overall pick impressed at center despite his lack of experience at the position and was primed to build on his even-better play at guard after the Jurgens trade. There was even some chatter of Offensive Rookie of the Year consideration, which could pick back up with a short absence and a strong return. It’s worth noting that Ioane was dealing with an ankle issue heading into Sunday’s game, so the time off should help that injury heal, too. #Ravens first-round guard Vega Ioane, one of the NFL’s best rookies this season, suffered an MCL sprain against the #Bengals , sources tell me and @MikeGarafolo . It’s considered to be a short-term injury, though he will miss a little time. pic.twitter.com/fSkoHvg4mn — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) October 27, 2026

title: Ravens discussion: should Eric DeCosta have traded for Quenton Nelson?
summary: The Ravens made a blockbuster trade for offensive line a few weeks ago, but they may have been outdone by the Seahawks on Tuesday. Eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson is heading from Indianapolis to Seattle in exchange for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick, per The Ringer’s Tom Pelissero. Baltimore’s offensive […]
full_text: Quenton Nelson Indianapolis Colts offensive guard Quenton Nelson (56) walks off the field following their game at Lucas Oil Stadium on Sept. 9, 2018. The Indianapolis Colts lost to the Cincinnati Bengals 34-23.Indianapolis Colts Play The Cincinnati Bengals In Their 2018 Season Opener | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Ravens made a blockbuster trade for offensive line a few weeks ago, but they may have been outdone by the Seahawks on Tuesday. Eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson is heading from Indianapolis to Seattle in exchange for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick, per The Ringer’s Tom Pelissero . Baltimore’s offensive line issues have been glaring (again) this year, and rookie guard Vega Ioane is now set to miss time with a sprained MCL. Nelson would certainly upgrade the unit, potentially at right guard initially before taking over for John Simpson at left guard after Ioane’s return. But after sending a 2028 second-rounder to the Eagles for Cam Jurgens a few weeks ago, does trading even more draft capital make sense considering the Ravens’ current and future salary cap picture? Here are Baltimore Beatdown’s thoughts Nikhil Mehta I have always loved Quenton Nelson, so in my heart of hearts, I would have loved to make this trade. But, partially because I am expecting my colleagues to be all for it, I’ll play devil’s advocate. Seattle’s 2027 third and 2028 fifth are valued somewhere in the second-round range – higher or lower depending on how you value the Day 3 pick. But the Seahawks can absorb all of the roughly $10 million Nelson is owed over the remainder of the season. The Ravens cannot, which would force them to restructure current contracts and/or ask the Colts to eat some of Nelson’s salary. The former exacerbates an already-untenable 2027 cap situation; the latter would drive the trade price up, likely requiring a second-round pick and potentially a Day 3 kicker to complete the deal. Nelson is also on an expiring deal, and like it or not, Baltimore has $5.5 million in guaranteed money committed to John Simpson next year. Nelson is definitely an upgrade this year, but can Baltimore get a long-term deal done? If not, second-round value is a high price for a half-season rental, especially considering the sobering reality that the 2026 Ravens may not be a Super Bowl-caliber team. They may need another year to remake their roster under Jesse Minter’s new coaching staff to reach their full potential. The upshot of a rental, though, is worth mentioning. Nelson decidedly pushes Baltimore closer to championship contention, and if he walks in free agency, the Ravens should be in line for at least a fourth-, if not a third-round compensatory pick in 2028. Eric DeCosta absolutely could have gotten this done. But I see why he didn’t. Dustin Cox Yes, I believe the Ravens should have traded for Nelson. Nelson has been one of the best offensive linemen in the NFL for his career and should still have several high-end seasons left in him. With Baltimore’s offensive line woes and difficulty developing guards in recent years, Eric DeCosta could have solved both guard spots for the foreseeable future with Nelson and Vega Ioane. I understand wanting to hold on to draft capitol after sending a 2028 second-rounder out the door for Cam Jurgens already, but players of Nelson’s caliber are extremely hard to come by, especially for this price. Nelson will demand a top-of-the-market deal after this season, but he is a player worth paying for if you are serious about fixing your offensive line. I was out on the idea when I expected Nelson to net a second or even first-round pick, but I believe this is a missed opportunity to protect Lamar Jackson. Stephen Bopst Yes – obviously there is a contractual component that made the Cam Jurgens trade attractive for Baltimore, but in retrospect, it’s looking like a fairly significant overpay relative to what the Seahawks gave up for Nelson. A trade for Nelson would’ve fortified the Ravens offensive line for years to come and given Eric DeCosta the flexibility to address other areas of need on the team. Unfortunately, I think it was more of a contractual issue for Baltimore. They only have ~$2M in cap space and Nelson is due $10M this year. That’s what happens when you pay Marlon Humphrey and Roquan Smith big money! It wouldn’t surprise me if a future trade involves off-loading one of them to create more flexibility. Zach Canter I’ve been clamoring for the Ravens to grab Quenton Nelson for a while now. He was my biggest trade target at this deadline to turn this team into a contender. Reinforce the offensive line, go all in on protecting Lamar Jackson and running the ball, be an elite offense to win playoff games. The price only costing a 3rd and 5th makes this sting even more. That being said, I think there’s a multitude of reasons the Ravens probably didn’t do this trade. They might have been worried about not reaching a long term extension with Nelson and didn’t want that price on a rental. They also just might not think this is the year to go all in. The more feasible reason are likely cap cost and priorities. Nelson is due $10M and tbe Ravens only have $2.1M in cap space. While they could have been doing with restructures, extensions, or paying a higher draft capital to get Indy to eat cost, I think there’s Ravens could be saving that cap space for the defense. They might be targeting a different Colt in DeForest Buckner or Chargers edge rusher Khalil Mack to bolster their 4-man pass rush since their coverage unit is so iffy. The Ravens might be ok with John Simpson being the weakest link on offensive line. While I know fans will hate it and I would have loved Nelson, provided Ioane comes back, this is not a bad line, especially in pass protection. Jurgens looked good in his debut against Dexter Lawerence, the tackles are steady, and Ioane has been a OROTY-level blocker. They can survive and score 30 points a game with Lamar Jackson, Zay Flowers and that line. They might not survive if defensive improvements don’t happen. Now, it’s your turn! Should Eric DeCosta have pulled the trigger on a trade for Quenton Nelson, or was he right to stand pat after moving a second-rounder for Cam Jurgens? Let us know in the comment section below!

title: Winners and losers from Ravens’ Week 7 loss to the Bengals
summary: The Ravens dropped to 4-3 with their second loss in a row to a divisional opponent in Week 7. There is plenty of blame to share after Baltimore was outscored 35-0 in the second half by the Bengals, but still a few positive performances to highlight. Let’s get into the winners and losers from Sunday’s […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - OCTOBER 25: Zay Flowers #4 of the Baltimore Ravens carries the ball after a reception for a touchdown against the Cincinnati Bengals during the first quarter at M&T Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Ravens dropped to 4-3 with their second loss in a row to a divisional opponent in Week 7. There is plenty of blame to share after Baltimore was outscored 35-0 in the second half by the Bengals, but still a few positive performances to highlight. Let’s get into the winners and losers from Sunday’s game: Winners Zay Flowers: Flowers’ monster season continued on Sunday as the Bengals seemingly had no answers for stopping the Ravens’ top receiver. Flowers’ first catch of the day went for a 48-yard touchdown on a screen pass on the opening drive. He added another 89 yards on seven more catches throughout the rest of the game, finishing the day with eight receptions for 137 yards and a touchdown. Flowers’ production should only increase once Lamar Jackson is back under center. K’Von Wallace: Wallace played 17 snaps on Sunday with Jaylinn Hawkins out with a knee injury. While his day was not perfect, the veteran safety made enough plays to stand out. Wallace ended Cincinnati’s second drive of the game with a pressure on Joe Burrow that forced an incompletion on second down and a tackle on Chase Brown short of the sticks on third down. Wallace then forced a fumble on a kickoff return, but the Bengals were able to retain possession of the ball. Wallace could make the decision to go back to Hawkins a difficult one if he can continue to make plays in his absence. Cam Jurgens: Jurgens made his debut for Baltimore in Week 7 and appeared to provide a stable presence at center after much turnover at the position to this point. According to PFF, Jurgens allowed just one pressure against Cincinnati. Vega Ioane unfortunately left the game early on with a knee injury after moving back to right guard, so the Ravens are still waiting to see their projected starting offensive line play together for any significant stretch of time. Travis Jones: Jones finished the game tied for the team lead in pressures with three, according to PFF. He has had a tackle for loss on a run play. Losers Tyler Huntley: Huntley came out of the gate hot against the Bengals, leading to a 13-0 lead heading into halftime. The second half was a completely different story for the backup quarterback as the offense struggled to move the ball, failing to score another point for the remainder of the game. Following a touchdown that put Cincinnati up 28-13 in the fourth quarter, Huntley threw an interception on the first play of Baltimore’s drive. The Bengals capitalized on Huntley’s error with another touchdown on a short field to go up 35-13 with just over six minutes remaining. For as admirable as Huntley is in a pinch, the Ravens desperately need their MVP quarterback back under center. Roger Rosengarten: Rosengarten was beaten cleanly by Boye Mafe for a sack on third down on Baltimore’s second drive of the game. He was later flagged for a false start on another third down. John Simpson: Simpson allowed a team-high four pressures while also being flagged for holding on a play where Huntley ran for seven yards to move the chains on third down. Derrick Henry: Through a combination of factors, the usually dominant Hall-of-Fame back has struggled in several games this season. Henry was held to just 45 yards and 17 carries against Cincinnati — a measly 2.6 yards per carry. Blocking has been an issue, as Henry has been hit near the line of scrimmage too often, but it is fair to wonder if age is finally becoming a factor for the 32-year-old workhorse. Over the past two games against divisional opponents, Henry has been held to 103 total rushing yards while being kept out of the end zone. Kyle Hamilton: It feels wrong to ever put Hamilton in this section, but his play on Sunday left a lot to be desired. Hamilton missed three tackles, including on a touchdown run where he had a chance to stop Samaje Perine in the backfield. He was also credited by PFF with giving up a touchdown to Tee Higgins, though it’s hard to know what his responsibility was on the play. Marlon Humphrey: Humphrey, one of the longest-tenured players on the team, has been a source of scrutiny over the years, due to both on- and off-field behavior. According to PFF, Humphrey allowed 60 yards on three receptions while missing two tackles. The veteran cornerback has now allowed the most receiving yards in the fourth quarter this season with 176, according to Next Gen Stats. Nate Wiggins: Wiggins struggled against the Bengals as well, allowing 80 yards and a touchdown on six catches while also being flagged for defensive holding, though the penalty was declined. Jesse Minter / Anthony Weaver: While a large portion of the blame deserves to fall on the players, as the trend of defensive meltdowns has now lasted through multiple defensive coordinators and two head coaches, Minter and Weaver still have to face criticism as well for their unit’s horrendous second-half performance on Sunday. Minter’s decision to go for it on fourth down from the 12-yard line while trailing 14-13 instead of going up 16-14 with a field goal has been questioned, but it ultimately proved to be the right decision, as his defense was unable to stop Cincinnati’s offense from scoring touchdowns on the following three drives. Declan Doyle: For all the good Doyle has done in his first season calling plays at the NFL level, he still has room to grow. The Ravens’ offense has been shut out in the second half of the past two games after strong starts in the first two quarters. Doyle has yet to figure out a consistently effective approach to short-yardage situations either. It feels harsh to judge Doyle too much without Jackson at quarterback, but he still has to be better at adjusting once opposing defenses begin to catch up in games.

full_text: Sep 7, 2025; Orchard Park, New York, USA; Buffalo Bills running back Ty Johnson (26) is pushed out of bounds by Baltimore Ravens safety Kyle Hamilton (14) in the first quarter at Highmark Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark Konezny-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect *sigh* Another week of Lamar Jackson Ankle Watch in Baltimore. The Ravens badly need their star quarterback back on the field for their upcoming visit to Buffalo, but his high ankle sprain could sideline him for another week. Head coach Jesse Minter was noncommittal about Jackson’s status during his Monday presser, effectively indicating that the ninth-year passer remains day-to-day. His return to practice last Wednesday was an encouraging sign, but he will likely need to be upgrade to full participation for at least one day this week. Unfortunately, there is reason to believe that Jackson will miss another week. He revealed last week that he was dealing with a high ankle sprain, an injury that typically takes at least four weeks to heal. The two-time MVP indicated that he can play at less than 100%, but he still has yet to reach his minimum standard to take the field. Jackson also said that his attempts to play through injuries last year were “dumb, a little bit,” indicating he could take a cautious approach to his return. There are some similarities between his current injury situation and last year’s. Jackson missed three weeks with a hamstring injury, returned to practice in a limited capacity, and did not start the next game, due in part to a short turnaround before a Thursday night matchup the following week. This year, the Ravens are hosting the Jaguars just four days after their trip to Buffalo, which could give the team another reason to rule Jackson out for one more game in the hopes of a strong return in Week 9. Betting markets, however, have a sunnier outlook of Jackson’s availability in Week 8. The Ravens opened as 3.5-point underdogs against the Bills ( via FanDuel Sportsbook ), but another Tyler Huntley start would be much more of an uphill battle. title: NFL trade deadline: Buffalo Bills trade candidate – Antoine Winfield Jr.
summary: How about another safety as a potential trade target for the Buffalo Bills at the deadline? This time, let’s venture into the NFC South. Today I’m highlighting Buccaneers safety Antoine Winfield Jr., a seven-year steady veteran with a Super Bowl ring and nine games of playoff experience who currently plays free safety on a now […]
full_text: How about another safety as a potential trade target for the Buffalo Bills at the deadline? This time, let’s venture into the NFC South. Today I’m highlighting Buccaneers safety Antoine Winfield Jr., a seven-year steady veteran with a Super Bowl ring and nine games of playoff experience who currently plays free safety on a now 2-5 Tampa Bay team. This article is the sixth in the trade-candidate series I plan to sprinkle onto the site until the actual trade deadline until November 10, which is 15 days from now, and lands after Week 9. Past installments in this series: Derwin James , Brian Thomas Jr. Jessie Bates , Tariq Woolen , Amani Hooker Age: 28 The Buccaneers made Winfield Jr. a second-round pick in 2020 after an illustrious, ball-magnet career at the University of Minnesota. He was an instant-acclimation piece on the Tampa Bay defense, as he amassed 94 tackles with six pass breakups, three sacks, and an interception as a rookie. Ever since, Winfield Jr. has been one of the game’s steadiest playmaking safeties. While he only has nine career picks, Winfield Jr. has been a magnet to the football in the NFL by way of tackling. Despite being typically aligned at free safety throughout his career, he averaged 107 tackles per season from 2020 – 2025. Winfield Jr. was a first-team All-Pro in 2023, and has over 6,000 career snaps on his resume, 620 of which have come in the postseason. 2026 snap splits Box: 29.4% Free safety: 58.9% Slot corner: 7.6% Defensive line: 3.8% As per usual, Todd Bowles has asked Winfield Jr. to patrol the deep portion of the field in his defense. That’s where he excelled in college and where he’s flourished in Tampa Bay. At 5’9” and 203 pounds, he is built similarly to his dad, former Bills and Vikings great Antoine Winfield Sr., and he tackles like him too. Winfield Jr. has a super-low 8.5% career missed tackle rate, and that figure hasn’t been above 9.5% since his second season in the NFL in 2021. He’s long been one of the best tackling defensive backs in football. How he’d fit with Bills Again, we aren’t sure how the Bills feel about youthful depth options at safety right now. If they want a sure thing alongside Cole Bishop — to spell or even replace C.J. Gardner-Johnson — Winfield Jr. would be a sensational add. Presumably not quite as expensive as Jessie Bates but a clear step above someone like Amani Hooker, Winfield Jr.’s instincts, speed, ball skills, experience, and on-field charisma would work wonders for Buffalo’s back end. His stabilizing presence at free safety would allow the larger Bishop to align closer to the line of scrimmage more frequently, and Winfield Jr. could conceivably mentor the likes of Jalon Kilgore and Jordan Hancock along the way. Financial obligation for Bills to trade for him 2026 salary: $19.5M If the Bills trade for Winfield after Week 9, they’d be on the hook for $9.75Min prorated 2026 base salary. In 2027, Winfield has a non-guaranteed base salary of $18.1M and a $1.5M roster bonus. He’s set to become a free agent after next season. Projected cost to acquire Using Syndicate32.com’s trade machine , and adding the “fire sale” stipulation to the assessment, the projected cost to trade for Winfield Jr. is a mid Round 2 pick in 2027. That feels about right for Winfield Jr.. He’s still reasonably young and has long been one of the game’s best, all-around free safeties who makes plenty of plays in coverage and against the run. Should the Bills trade for Antoine Winfield Jr.? Winfield is probably still a player who is worth and deserves the contract under which he’s currently playing. But because there is no guaranteed money left on his current Buccaneers deal, if a trade to Buffalo were to occur, it feels like the classic scenario in which the trading team would agree to a new deal with the acquired player that lowers his current-year cap hit in exchange for future financial security for the player via guaranteed dollars. In essence, the Bills likely wouldn’t want to pay that prorated salary of nearly $10M for Winfield Jr. in 2026. They don’t really have the money for it either, although accounting gymnastics are always an option. In the process of all this, Buffalo could convert Winfield’s 2026 salary to a signing bonus, thereby spreading out the vast majority of it over the next few seasons while giving him guaranteed money into 2028 or beyond. Safeties can play high level into their early 30s, and Winfield Jr. won’t be 30 until right before the 2028 season begins. I’m not sure if the Bills would want to trade second-round picks in consecutive drafts for established veterans in their late 20s, but Winfield Jr. is exactly the type of safety this defense could use, someone whose presence could have an enormously positive ripple effect on the rest of the back seven in Buffalo. This would be viewed as the type of expensive “all-in” move many Bills fans have been wanting the team to make for a while now.

full_text: With the 14th pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, the Baltimore Ravens selected Penn State guard Vega Ioane, and he’s been a rock-solid addition to the team’s offensive front in the first seven games of this season. But the rookie blocker almost assuredly be on the field against the Bills in Week 8 after he suffered a knee injury in Baltimore’s Week 7 loss to the Bengals at home. #Ravens first-round guard Vega Ioane, one of the NFL’s best rookies this season, suffered an MCL sprain against the #Bengals , sources tell me and @MikeGarafolo . It’s considered to be a short-term injury, though he will miss a little time. pic.twitter.com/fSkoHvg4mn — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) October 27, 2026 Fortunately for the Ravens, the injury isn’t considered to be a long-term ailment, per Ian Rapoport, but once can surmise from the report, Ioane won’t be on the field this week against the Bills. The 6’4”, 320-pound blocker has only allowed eight pressures on 225 pass-blocking snaps to date and has been a road-grader for the Ravens run game in the first seven contests of this season. While Ioane is a right guard by trade, he actually manned the center spot in Weeks 4-6 for Baltimore. It’ll either be veteran Andrew Vorhees or 2025 third-round pick Emery Jones filling in for Ioane during his absence. Vorhees was a seventh-round pick in 2023 — he would’ve been picked higher but was selected with a torn ACL — and was Baltimore’s full-time starter at left guard in 2025 yet struggled mightily. Jones is a 6’5”, 315-pounder from LSU who played 48 snaps as a rookie and has appeared on 228 snaps thus far in his second season in Baltimore. He’s allowed five pressures on 127 pass-blocking snaps to date.

title: Is this the worst defense Josh Allen has ever played with?
summary: If you’re on social media for the Buffalo Bills you’ve likely seen the same graphic I have. The Buffalo Bills have won about 42 games when allowing the other team to score eighty zillion points or so, while understandably most teams struggle when giving up eighty zillion points or so. The conclusion is supposed to […]
full_text: If you’re on social media for the Buffalo Bills you’ve likely seen the same graphic I have. The Buffalo Bills have won about 42 games when allowing the other team to score eighty zillion points or so, while understandably most teams struggle when giving up eighty zillion points or so. The conclusion is supposed to be simple: Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills offense are really, really good. It’s a metric meant to show that the Bills are winning shootouts. While that’s fun, it wasn’t so long ago that we were enjoying blowouts. So that begs the question, is this the worst defense Josh Allen has had to support him? Well? Is it? But first, some methodology I’m going to attack this from a couple different ways. The first and easiest is points per drive. Note that all metrics used are rate states with an emphasis on per drive metrics. You can blame Matt Warren for getting me fixated on a drive = opportunity; which is a near perfect unit of “what do you do when given a chance?” Anyway, the simple analysis will be points per drive as that’s sort of the mission for defenses; to prevent points. That said, I will also do a more complex analysis using seven metrics that I think are good measures of defensive performance. Soon you’ll see a table which has the Bills’ rate in each metric and league ranking with #1 being the best of course. That allowed me to create a total score to weigh defenses against each other (lowest score is best). Here are the metrics and rationale (I don’t claim this to be perfect, so feel free to use it as a launch pad for success): Pts/drive – Included for obvious reasons. Yards/drive – Included as a metric for how advantageously they help put Allen into position. The shorter the distance given up, the less room Allen needs to score. Time/drive – Similar to yards per drive. The more time you put Allen out there, the better. Score % – This is like looking at a failure rate. Some overlap with pts/drive but not entirely. Pts/drive factors in type of score whereas this metric is more about “did we get a stop?” Turnover % – This would be a type of success rate but not a complete one. It’s included to show capability to force a drive to end. Sack % – Included just because it’s fun. OK, maybe it’s included because this could be tied to capability to rattle the opposing offense and create opportunities. 3rd down % – Included as a sort of “clutch” metric. How often can you get a stop when the stop is right in front of you? One last quick thing when you see the chart. I did a heat map based on my rule of four metrics (top four teams are elite, next four are good, the middle 16 are average, then a group of four that are bad, and the last four are labeled as “terrible”). The Chart Well, that sure was easy. Either way you slice it, this year’s defense is comfortably the worst that Josh Allen has ever been paired with. Using our simple metric of points per drive, Josh Allen has never been on a team giving up more. Their worst finish prior to this was 18th which is thoroughly average. When we get to our more complex rating system, the heat map tells us right away we have a problem. Only in one metric are the Bills even average (turnover rate). And even in THAT metric, it’s still their worst rating in the Allen era. As a matter of fact, it doesn’t matter which metric you pick out of these seven, the 2026 season if it holds true will be the worst in all of them. Now, I want to try to dismiss any claims of cherry picking. I chose the categories first as I felt they covered a broad swath of areas and was honestly not expecting this clear of a picture. I’m also aware of metrics where they aren’t the worst, like rushing yards per attempt. I didn’t isolate yards by type for this as I felt it was too granular but want to acknowledge the 2026 Bills are NOT worst at everything, but they’re significantly worse in many major metrics. And again, points per drive is atrocious. I can keep rubbing salt in the wounds like pointing out how Greg Rousseau had been leading the league in sacks for a bit and is still third in the league. I’m glad he’s doing well, but the team really isn’t on sack rate. I could go on. And on. The chart really covers most of it pretty well though. I’ll note the ranking system/score has some flaws but I stand by it as a quick way to aggregate and compare. It helps show just how dominant the 2021 defense was. It’s incredible the Bills didn’t win the big one that year as it was also one of Allen’s best seasons. So what the hell happened, man? In a word? Volatility. Overall, this defense was insanely good, but they weren’t as steady as the averages suggest. They had 11 games allowing less than 20 points, including five at ten or under which had two shutouts. They also had four games allowing more than 30, including their loss in the Divisional Round. What about the other years when we look at it through this lens? Well 2018 and 2019 had average to bad Allen and the offensive firepower wasn’t there (notably not even making the playoffs in 2019). 2020 was Allen’s breakout season and again the word “volatility” comes up again. I would also note that by my scoring metric it was the second worst defense Allen had with Sean McDermott. In 2022 I would also use that word, but I would also point out that while the team’s eventual loss to the Bengals had a very shaky start to the game on defense, the offense was zero help for much of the game. The Bills gave up 27 which also doesn’t qualify as an epic collapse either. In 2023, they again lost a game by giving up 27 points, meaning the loss wasn’t entirely on the defense. These were both years with what appear to be very good defenses still and so some disappointment is justified. The 2024 season was the worst Sean McDermott defense Allen was paired with and it was the reason for their loss to KC. In 2025 the defense improved but was still the third worst for McDermott with Allen. The 33 points looks like a defensive collapse, but I would remind everyone that the Bills gave the ball away faster than Halloween Candy that game. It’s always a good idea to come back to the idea of volatility. I’d remind anyone still reading this far that yes, the defense has disappointed in some playoffs losses, but they’ve also been dominant in many playoffs wins. It’s frankly one of the laziest arguments in my opinion to blame the McDermott defense for the playoff failures. It’s a mixed bag. Now, am I trying to disguise this article as a way to show love for McDermott? Not at all. While I think he did a fantastic job and that his defenses get some very weird ire not supported by the evidence, I was OK with moving on. His defenses were generally quite good to elite, though imperfect for sure. The heat map also shows a pattern of decline. That could be a Brandon Beane conversation too if you want. No, the article is intended to just simply state one simple fact. If the Bills are going to win it all this year, they’ll need to do so despite the defense unless they hit some stride they’ve shown no evidence of having in them. I hope it happens, but this far into the season it’s hard to be confident with that. I do have one more thing for everyone though. This is the same chart, but with Sean McDermott’s first year thrown in, pre-Josh Allen. This year’s defense is still worse, but it’s not by remotely as much as any other McDermott year. Why does this matter? First, it’s natural to think something would move backward with a new coaching staff. Second, the Bills squeaked into the playoffs that year and held a red hot Jacksonville Jaguars team to ten points in the Wild Card round. That was also the year where McDermott pulled the plug on the Marcell Dareus extended audition mid-year which had the immediate impact of allowing the Bills to get their butts kicked for a bit while they sorted things out. That became the dawn of the Buffalo Nickel defense which transitioned into the elite years as shown on the chart. In other words,…

title: Bills pass offense about to undergo a specific two-week test
summary: The Buffalo Bills offense has been very good in 2026. Thank goodness for that, because the Bills defense has been bad. A bye week is just what the doctor ordered to get the defensive side of the ball hopefully on a better path for the remainder of the 2026 season, but the Bills passing offense […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills offense has been very good in 2026. Thank goodness for that, because the Bills defense has been bad. A bye week is just what the doctor ordered to get the defensive side of the ball hopefully on a better path for the remainder of the 2026 season, but the Bills passing offense is the unit that will be put under an unexpected microscope as the team prepares to face the Baltimore Ravens and Minnesota Vikings over the next two weeks. Lost in the greatest of quarterback Josh Allen and the Bills expectedly-productive passing attack in 2026 is that it has come with it a strong performance for the unit against the blitz. In 2025, Josh Allen against the blitz registered the following results (amongst 41 QBs with at least 50 drop backs): 21st in success rate 27th in completion percentage over expected (CPOE) 19th in adjusted completion percentage 30th (lower is worse) in off-target throw rate 14th in expected points added (EPA) per drop back In 2026, those numbers have jumped up notably to: 4th in success rate 9th in CPOE 9th in adjusted completion percentage 14th (lower is worse) in off-target throw rate 2nd in EPA per drop back One of the most notable differences in results in the Bills offense in 2026 with former offensive coordinator Joe Brady at the helm as head coach is the passing game’s performance against the blitz, and this new trick couldn’t have come at a better time, because two of the most blitz-happy teams in the National Football League are on the docket for the next two Buffalo Bills games. The Baltimore Ravens have blitzed opposing offenses on 36.5% of opposing plays (8th most in the NFL), while defensive coordinator Brian Flores and the Minnesota Vikings continue to absolutely shell shock offenses with a staggering 73.9% of the time (handedly #1 in the league). The results from each team’s blitzing has been different, though, and we should judge the Bills performance against each team’s blitz differently. The Ravens are 23rd in the league in EPA per play allowed when blitzing, and the Vikings are 4th in the NFL in that same metric. In fact, the Ravens have a statistically significant delta between their EPA per play allowed when blitzing (+0.16) and when rushing with four (-0.02), so each team can be considered “blitz heavy”, but a.) not to even close to the same degree and b.) to not the same degree of effectiveness. Each one will provide a test against a Bills team that has only faced one defense that’s inside the top 10 in blitz rate (New England, #5 at 41.3%) and produced a season low success rate of 45.5% in that game. The Bills have been good overall against the blitz in 2026, but they’ve only had to deal with a single blitz-heavy team and it produced their only loss of the season. The next two weeks will go far to outline if the team is actually much better against the blitz compared to 2025 or if they just haven’t faced enough blitz experts. …and that’s the way the cookie crumbles. title: Panthers vs Buccaneers game review: Catastrophe
summary: It’s not often that a Carolina Panthers game has me breaking out the dictionary to confirm that my instinct on word choice is appropriately grave enough for the situation. Okay, it’s not often this season for me to have to do that. Sunday’s meltdown, however, had me reaching for a Websters. The definition for catastrophe […]
full_text: It’s not often that a Carolina Panthers game has me breaking out the dictionary to confirm that my instinct on word choice is appropriately grave enough for the situation. Okay, it’s not often this season for me to have to do that. Sunday’s meltdown , however, had me reaching for a Websters. The definition for catastrophe was ‘utter failure’, by the way, so I’m calling that suitable. Normally, I would try and find an element or takeaway from the game that was interesting or inspired some curiosity. Then I’d look into that and add some additional context or interesting tidbits. For that game? I’ve got nothing. More accurately, there were too many points of failure to even attempt at singling any one area out. Offense? Terrible. Defense? Putrid. Special Teams? Grotesque. What did inspire me however was a note from someone on social media who pointed out that the Panthers are 0-6 when entering a game with a winning record under Head Coach Dave Canales. Any sliver of expectations is like poison for them lol https://t.co/kYzE64wgB7 — Unnecessary Bluntness Owner/Coach/QB (@DuncOnDemand) October 26, 2026 I couldn’t believe it to be true, so I had to look it up for myself. Don’t know why I doubted it, but it was true. For your amusement, here are those 6 games the Panthers entered into with a winning record. Week 8, 2025: 40-9 loss versus the Buffalo Bills (entered 4-3) Week 10, 2025: 17-7 loss versus the New Orleans Saints (entered 5-4) Week 12, 2025: 20-9 loss versus the San Francisco 49ers (entered 6-5) Week 15, 2025: 20-17 loss versus the New Orleans Saints (entered 7-6) Week 17, 2025: 27-10 loss versus the Seattle Seahawks (entered 8-7) Week 7, 2026: 43-13 loss versus the Tampa Bay Buccaneers (entered 3-2) From the team that brought you “can’t have a winning record in back to back seasons” you can now enjoy their new hit “can’t have a winning record in back to back games”. It’s become a Sisyphean task to maintain a winning record. I’m not sure what the answer is, or who made a deal with what devil, but this is a trend that Canales must figure out how to eliminate. We’re approaching levels of statistical ineptitude not seen since the reign of Matt Rhule’s record when opponents score more than 17 points. Speaking of 17 points, that’s the average margin of defeat among those 6 games. That’s a touchdown’s worth of points more than their average points scored in the same contests – specifically 10.8 points per game. There are very few things that could go have gone worse for the Panthers. Thankfully, it still only counts as one loss and they won’t have to wait long for their chance at redemption. The Panthers are up again on Thursday night versus the Green Bay Packers – so until then, keep pounding.

title: Chicago Bears week 8 power rankings roundup
summary: The Chicago Bears have a long layoff from Thursday to their next game on Monday night. And since they were the first game of the NFL weekend, it’s fair to wonder if they’ll be overlooked in this week’s rankings. It was quite a splashy weekend of headlines. Two undefeated teams fell, the Buccaneers showed up in a big […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 22: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears calls a play during the first quarter of a game against the New England Patriots at Soldier Field on October 22, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears have a long layoff from Thursday to their next game on Monday night. And since they were the first game of the NFL weekend, it’s fair to wonder if they’ll be overlooked in this week’s rankings. It was quite a splashy weekend of headlines. Two undefeated teams fell, the Buccaneers showed up in a big way, the Rams aren’t dead and the Lions showed some defensive teeth. Where will the Bears land after their 30-24 win over the New England Patriots? Let’s take a look. WCG – Aaron Leming 7. Chicago Bears (5-2) Quarterback Progress Report: Caleb Williams (A) The marriage between head coach Ben Johnson and Williams has gone about as well as hoped through a season and a half. In Year 1, Williams made plenty of big leaps, but through four starts in Year 2, he looks like a Top 5-7 quarterback. He’s continued to limit turnovers while taking more of what the defense gives him. That has led to a completion rate over 70%, yet he’s still taking plenty of accurate shots downfield. There’s still growth to be had, but he’s been night and day from what we saw in his rookie campaign. The Athletic – Josh Kendall and Chad Graff 5. Chicago Bears (5-2) Last week: 8 Thursday: Beat Patriots 30-24 Something spooky: Caleb Williams’ arm The Patriots got a lot of pressure on Williams, but he was routinely able to sidestep defenders and make some incredible off-platform throws downfield. And don’t look now, but Williams is completing 71 percent of his passes while averaging 8.2 yards per attempt. Things are looking up in Chicago. NFL.com – Nick Shook 9. Chicago Bears (11) The Bears won a Thursday nighter by simply making more key plays than the opposition. The screen to Luther Burden III for a touchdown was a treat to watch unfold, and Caleb Williams remains one of the most captivating watches in the entire league. His third-and-long pass to Rome Odunze, fired from the shadow of his own goal post, made my jaw drop. It might still be on the floor. ESPN/NFL Nation – Courtney Cronin 7. Chicago Bears (5-2) Week 7 result: Beat the Patriots 30-24 Week 7 ranking: 9 Best offseason addition: S Dillon Thieneman Thieneman and fellow rookie DB Malik Muhammad II have nearly identical stat lines this season, but the No. 25 pick gets the nod here for how he has handled the highest snap percentage of any Bears defender (97.58%). Thieneman is No. 1 or tied for the team lead in total tackles (47), passes defensed (five) and interceptions (one). He also has 1.5 sacks and three QB hits. Thieneman has had his share of learning moments, but the stability he has provided can’t be overstated for a secondary that has dealt with moving parts since the start of training camp. — Courtney Cronin CBS Sports – Pete Prisco 8. Chicago Bears (13) Caleb Williams is playing the best football of his career right now. But the best news for this team: The defense has made strides. Yahoo Sports – Frank Schwab 5. Chicago Bears (5-2, LW: 6) The Bears have scored 30 or more points in three of Caleb Williams’ four starts. The fourth was a surprising three-point effort against the Vikings, which probably says a lot about how good Minnesota’s defense is this season. Chicago’s offense might be just as good as Ben Johnson said it would be. One thing that had been a question about Williams coming into the season was him missing too many passes. His completion percentage was 58.1% last season. He was one of two quarterbacks with on-target percentage of less than 70% last season, according to Pro Football Reference, and the other was J.J. McCarthy. This season, that has flipped. He has a completion percentage of 71%, just off the league lead. His on-target percentage is up to 79.6%, third in the NFL. He has gone from one of the most inaccurate quarterbacks to one of the most accurate in his third season. Williams has played just four games this season, but it appears he has arrived as one of the NFL’s best QBs. Profootballtalk – Mike Florio 8. Bears (No. 10; 5-2) : The NFC Championship matchup we almost got in January happens on Monday night. USAToday – Nate Davis 2. Chicago Bears (4): QB Caleb Williams has been lights out since his return. But after failing his Week 2 test against the Vikings, he’ll try to pass this week’s against Seattle’s equally formidable D − and on the road this time. What do you think of where the Bears are ranked this week? Is the top 2 too high?

title: Can Kyler Gordon continue making a big impact for the Chicago Bears?
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year, we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bears fans and fans across the country. It’s only been two games, but Chicago Bears nickelback Kyler Gordon is showing exactly why defensive coordinator Dennis Allen talked him up so much when he […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 22: Kyler Gordon #6 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after a play during an NFL football game against the New England Patriots at Soldier Field on October 22, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year, we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bears fans and fans across the country. It’s only been two games, but Chicago Bears nickelback Kyler Gordon is showing exactly why defensive coordinator Dennis Allen talked him up so much when he was hired in 2025. Allen loves giving offenses plenty to think about pre-snap, and Gordon’s versatility lets Allen line him up anywhere. In Gordon’s two games this year, he has already set a career high in sacks (4), forced fumbles (2), and tackles for loss (5). It’s a small sample size with just 48 defensive snaps, but he’s only allowed 2 receptions in coverage for 5 yards. Various injuries limited Gordon to just 3 regular-season games last year, but the Bears won all three. Maybe it’s a coincidence, but in those three wins, the Bears defense gave up an average of 300 yards and 17.6 points, far below their season averages of 362 and 24.4. Gordon has already blitzed 10 times this season, but he may be asked to cover more in their next game against the Seattle Seahawks and wideout Jaxon Smith-Njigba, who does a lot of work out of the slot. Since coming off the PUP list, Kyler played 26 total snaps in his first game and 35 snaps in his second, so we could see that pushed closer to 50 on Monday night. title: Chicago Bears Stock Watch: Wide Receivers Up, Defensive Backs Down
summary: After two games in five days, the Chicago Bears now have two games in the month. Schedule quirks like that are weird, but this one benefits a Bears team that could stand to get some rest. Right now, the Bears get 11 days between their Thursday night game and their next match, a Monday night […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 22: Luther Burden III #10 and Rome Odunze #15 of the Chicago Bears celebrate during the fourth quarter of the game against the New England Patriots at Soldier Field on October 22, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images After two games in five days, the Chicago Bears now have two games in the month. Schedule quirks like that are weird, but this one benefits a Bears team that could stand to get some rest. Right now, the Bears get 11 days between their Thursday night game and their next match, a Monday night game against the Seattle Seahawks. It’s a tough game against the defending Super Bowl champions. This Bears team appears to be built to take these sorts of games. At the conclusion of the game against the Patriots, it really started to sink in. This isn’t a dream; it’s not an anomaly. The Chicago Bears are a good football team, led by a good coach, with a really good quarterback. Ben Johnson has built a mentally tough team. How many Bears teams in the past would we see melt, or at least let a mistake like the 14-second touchdown drive the Patriots had before halftime, linger? Not this team though. They got the ball coming out of halftime, went down the field, scored a touchdown and never looked back. When they missed a field goal and it felt like the game was beginning to teeter, they got the ball back and went on another long drive. Then they let the kicker get a shot at redemption from further out, at a distance he’d never before made in a game. Mentally tough. Lifting each other. Staying cool under pressure. It is so much fun to watch. Stock up Rome Odunze, WR – There has been well-deserved criticism of Rome’s play. And questions about his future. The word bust has been floating around. And I’m not saying it was all absolved on Thursday. But it went a long way. After another bad drop in the endzone, with an offensive pass interference penalty tacked on, too, it looked like another disappointing night for the former first-round pick. However, he came alive late the game and made a big third-down catch after a big third-down catch. He finished with four catches for 69 yards. In the last two games, he has 7 catches for 118 yards. Luther Burden III, WR – Burden recorded the first 100-yard receiving game of the season. He caught four passes for 140 yards and a touchdown. He had yards after the catch, he made guys miss and he got open. Burden is truly becoming the star many thought he would be based on his offseason. D’Marco Jackson, LB – Six tackles, an interception and a pass breakup. Jackson was everywhere for the defense and made plays all over the field. He’s a bit of an unsung hero for the defense and his play has picked up a lot in the last couple of weeks. Stock down Devin Bush, LB – Bush hasn’t really been that impressive to me. He has played fine, but I haven’t noticed his speed quite as much as I had hoped. He got beat in coverage early against the Patriots and finished with just four tackles. Jaylon Johnson, CB – I don’t know if he can go lower at this point, but it is a crime he’s still getting trotted out there week after week. I get that the defensive backfield has limited options, but man he looks bad every single week. Cameron Lewis, S – Cam Lewis has unfortunately not made a difference for the secondary. This season, he’s been targeted 12 times, allowing 11 completions for 139 yards and two touchdowns for a 154.5 rating when targeted. Against the Patriots, he was targeted three times; all three were completed for 74 yards and a touchdown.

(Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears have a 16-man practice squad, but the list will be fluid, and we’ll update it throughout the year. UPDATE (10/27): The Bears signed running back Zavier Scott to the 53-man roster. Caden Barnett, OG Christian Jones, OT Salvon Ahmed, RB Kaden Davis, WR J.P. Richardson, WR Scotty Miller, WR Stephen Carlson, TE Qadir Ismail, TE Miller Moss, QB Wayne Matthews III, LB Buddy Johnson, LB Keidron Smith, S Elijah Jones, CB KC Eziomume, CB Beau Gardner, LS Practice squad injured: Anthony Johnson Jr. (S) Here are the qualifications for practice squad eligibility and some rules to remember. A 17th player is permitted as long as he qualifies for the NFL’s International Pathway Program. Players with no accrued seasons (rookies) and those with fewer than nine regular-season games in their lone accrued season. A maximum of ten players are allowed who have earned no more than two accrued seasons. Up to six players with unlimited accrued seasons are permitted on the practice squad. However, the number of players in the last two categories cannot exceed 10 total players. Teams can elevate up to two practice squad players for each game, but they can still only have 48 players active on game day. After the game, the elevated player(s) will revert to the practice squad. A player can be elevated up to three times, but if he’s needed after that, the team would be required to sign him to the 53-man active roster. Players on practice squads are free agents who can be signed to another team’s active roster. A player’s current club can’t block him from leaving; they can only make a counteroffer to keep him. Ultimately, it’s the player’s decision. If a player is signed away, his new team must keep him on its 53-man roster for three weeks, but if he’s released, he’ll revert to his previous team. Players signed to another active roster are also guaranteed three weeks’ salary. A practice squad player can’t sign with his team’s upcoming opponent unless he does so six days before the upcoming game or ten days prior if his team is on its bye week.

title: 10 Thoughts on the NFL: Caleb Williams breaks the internet in the best way
summary: 1. When’s the last time we left a quarterback duel between two young, emerging stars and came away feeling completely contented about both players? (I’m sure it’s happened, I just need a refresher.) Because last Thursday’s battle between Caleb Williams and Drake Maye, the respective No. 1 and No. 3 picks in the 2024 NFL […]
full_text: CHICAGO, IL - OCTOBER 22: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the New England Patriots during an NFL football game at Soldier Field on October 22, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images 1. When’s the last time we left a quarterback duel between two young, emerging stars and came away feeling completely contented about both players? (I’m sure it’s happened, I just need a refresher.) Because last Thursday’s battle between Caleb Williams and Drake Maye, the respective No. 1 and No. 3 picks in the 2024 NFL Draft, was just about perfect, especially since Williams’ Bears came out on top. Both guys balled out, with Maye putting on a one-man show to keep New England alive and Williams doing… stuff like this . If we saw this matchup again on the second week of February, it could feed families. 2. There’s been a lot of conversation about this throw from Williams and catch by Rome Odunze—some from people who know ball and some who don’t. So let’s be clear: this is an unbelievable grab by Odunze, who had an incredible fourth quarter to bounce back from an early penalty/touchdown drop. But this is a deity-level throw from Williams into a keyhole I can’t believe he had the temerity to throw it through. Dozens of receivers could make that catch, as brilliant as it was. There might not be another quarterback in the league who can make this throw. Hope that helps. Glad the Bears have a guy who can do that. 3. We have gone from Deshaun Watson being on his career deathbed to him leading the Cleveland Browns to an AFC North-leading 5-2 record—tied with Aaron Rodgers’ Steelers. (They play each other next.) We are officially in the Twilight Zone. Or the Upside Down. Or whatever place you go where nothing makes sense. Maybe that Todd Monken guy knows what he’s doing after all. 4. Speaking of quarterbacks from the 2024 class…a couple of them made some statements this past Sunday. Michael Penix continues to prove Tua Tagovailoa shouldn’t touch the field again as long as Penix is healthy, playing a clean 3-TD game against the previously undefeated San Francisco 49ers, while formerly cast-off fellow first-round pick J.J. McCarthy (20-of-28, 252 yards) got off the scrap heap and helped the Giants knock off the Texans in overtime. I trust the former a lot more than the latter still, and I’m not convinced a mere change of scenery will erase all McCarthy’s flaws. But credit where it’s due. I do love a good comeback story, after all. 5. There are different ways of playing to win a game, and they manifest themselves differently depending on the situation. On one hand, you could say Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs sliding down inside the 5-yard line rather than simply scoring a go-ahead touchdown with Detroit and Green Bay tied 17-17 was lame. (Then again, you’re probably a gambler if you think that.) Why not “take the points?” There’s something to be said for not just playing for the win, but doing as much as you can to also ensure the other team can’t win either. I’ve watched arrogance come back to bite teams who believed they had it won in the last minute, going up seven points and watching with frustration as the other squad tied the game before the end of regulation. Sometimes, you have to play smarter, not harder. Well played, Dan Campbell. 6. The more aggressive side of that coin, unsurprisingly, was Campbell’s old protégé in Detroit, Ben Johnson, last Thursday. Because throwing the ball on third down and inviting the possibility of a sack when you’re trying to kill clock and kick a game-winning field goal is a risky proposition, and it bit the Bears in that situation. When Williams went down around the 40-yard line, it didn’t even enter my mind that Johnson would try a 58-yarder with Cairo Santos, who famously doesn’t have the strongest leg in the world (at Soldier Field, no less). I thought they’d punt it and play the field position game for sure. My bad, dawg. Johnson wants to win, not play to avoid losing. And Santos stepped up and rewarded his coach’s faith in him. That’s football right there. 7. I understand the frustration some Ravens fans have with Lamar Jackson not being able to get back on the field and make the difference in a game like Sunday’s rout at the hands of the Cincinnati Bengals, in which Tyler Huntley and Baltimore’s offense couldn’t get anything going in the second half. But for people who want the Ravens to “look into” the quarterback position for next season, I’m going to need to know what that means. If you’re talking about drafting a young kid at the back end of the first round or sometime on Day 2 to groom in Jackson’s stead, I don’t hate that. If you want to look for an upgrade over Huntley, that’s fine, too. (Good luck with that, though.) But if you mean letting Jackson walk or trading him, that’s wild. When healthy, he’s still one of the five best quarterbacks in the league. There will come a time when keeping Jackson around won’t be the right move. I don’t think now’s that time. 8. If you want anyone on the Indianapolis Colts roster, the Vikings probably just did you a big favor. This latest Indianapolis loss, which drops the team to 2-5, has reportedly all but sealed their fate as fire-sale candidates at the trade deadline coming up in a few weeks. Why yes, I would happily take a DeForest Buckner, thank you very much. (Only eight years after I personally would’ve preferred him on the Bears, but so be it.) For the first time in a while, I will actually be disappointed if the Bears don’t make a move before the deadline passes. With Caleb Williams playing like this, it’s go-time. Trade: Colts have agreed to send eight-time Pro-Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks, per me and @rapsheet . Nelson is on an expiring contract and the Colts are opting to get back draft capital now before they could lose him in free agency. But an all-time Colt now… pic.twitter.com/uKlAEYkPnZ — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) October 27, 2026 9. Nothing in the NFL is easy, including kicking. (Especially if, like me, you can’t kick anything .) But man, there have been some brutal performances from kickers in recent weeks. Packers kicker Trey Smack had a case of the yips, missing two kicks inside of 40 yards against Detroit. (I’m sure Packers fans feel great about having yet another kicker you can’t trust in crunch time.) Kansas City’s Harrison Butker continued his fall-off as well, missing wide right again against Seattle. Even Santos missed a 53-yarder off the upright, a sound Bears fans never want to hear again. But hey, at least Santos got it together when it mattered. 10. Talk about calling your own number… Jay-Z saw all these young guns, namely Kendrick Lamar and Bad Bunny, putting up record numbers and decided to put himself on the stage for this upcoming Super Bowl. Given his commercial success and status as one of the best to ever do it, I’m predicting a successful show from one of rap’s GOATS. (Just think of all the people he can summon on stage to perform with him, including Queen Bey herself.) But what made the last two performances so special was the storytelling, not just the songs. And I won’t lie…I’m not sure what Jay-Z has to say aside from simply playing the greatest hits. But hey, must be nice being the guy in charge.

title: Chicago Bears Pass Protection Analysis on the Sacks Allowed vs Patriots
summary: The Chicago Bears allowed three sacks to a very good New England Patriots defense, and as has been the norm this season, the Pats came after Caleb Williams with the blitz. According to Next Gen Stats, Williams was blitzed on 61.5% of his dropbacks in their Thursday night game, which raised his league-leading blitz rate […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 22: Leonard Taylor III #93 of the New England Patriots sacks Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears during the second quarter of an NFL football game at Soldier Field on October 22, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears allowed three sacks to a very good New England Patriots defense, and as has been the norm this season, the Pats came after Caleb Williams with the blitz. According to Next Gen Stats, Williams was blitzed on 61.5% of his dropbacks in their Thursday night game, which raised his league-leading blitz rate faced to 55.3%. Of the four teams he played, only the Atlanta Falcons blitzed him less than 50% of the time. Playing blitz-happy Brian Flores and the Minnesota Vikings in Week 2 obviously skews Williams’ blitz rate faced, but he’s pretty far ahead of number two on the list, Atlanta’s Michael Penix Jr. at 43.9%. New England’s blitz didn’t faze Caleb, who threw for a career-high 205 yards and a touchdown on 12 of 20 (60.0%) passes on those plays. The Patriots must have thought they discovered a weakness on the Bears because their 61.5% blitz rate was the highest they’ve had this year and the third-highest by a Patriots defense in a game in the entire Next Gen Stats era. No on to the Sackwtch! Sack 16: 2nd Quarter – 1-10-NE 29 (10:55) C.Williams sacked at NE 31 for -2 yards (L.Taylor) Williams was reading the defense from left to right, and the Patriots had everything covered up. New England’s middle third safety took away Rome Odunze on the post, so if Williams had the time to get back to the right and Luther Burden III, he could have rifled the ball in on the deep cross. New England defensive tackle Leonard Taylor III got the sack, but that’s because right guard Jonah Jackson lost leverage after Williams was flushed up. Patriots rookie Gabe Jacas rushed around Chicago left tackle Ozzy Trapilo because Ozzy gave the edge up too quickly. Look at the depth of the pass rushers on each edge on the screenshot. Right tackle Darnell Wright is in a good position to work his defender around the pocket, while Trapilo lost the corner and couldn’t slow Jacas at all. This one is on Trapilo, but before moving on, check out Burden again and notice how quickly he broke off his route when he saw Caleb scramble. That’s good coaching and good recognition by Burden; there just wasn’t enough time for Caleb to make a play. Sack 17: 2nd Quarter – 2-10-NE 17 (:27) (Shotgun) C.Williams sacked at NE 24 for -7 yards (M.Jones) The Patriots brought the nickel blitz here by sending Marcus Jones off the Bears’ right side, and the Bears picked it up. Wright left outside linebacker Elijah Ponder (#91) for right guard Jackson, and Wright protected the edge and picked up Jones. But Jacas got Trapilo on the left side again. This time Ozzy was in a better position to cut Jacas off from getting around the edge, but he had to turn and open his hips to get depth. That left him without the base to stop Jacas’ inside move. Sack 18: 4th Quarter – 3-5-NE 30 (1:46) (Shotgun) C.Williams sacked at NE 40 for -10 yards (C.Barmore). NE – C.Barmore was injured during the play. Timeout #3 by NE at 01:39. You guys already know where I’m going with this one. Caleb took the sack but was bailed out by Cairo Santos’ career-long 58-yard field goal. While it was the wrong play, I do appreciate his reasoning and accountability. After the game, Williams was asked what he was thinking when head coach Ben Johnson sent Santos out for the 58-yard try. “I didn’t know how far it was. I know I took the sack. We’re going to go back and look at that,” he said. “I thought I could take the sack in that situation, keep the clock going, or make them use their last time out. But you know, in that situation, we’ll go back and look at it. I’ll learn from it so when we get in that situation again.” In his Friday press conference, Johnson was asked what the conversation was like with Caleb before this third down play that ended with the sack, and Johnson took accountability as well. “Yeah, I didn’t do a good enough job communicating to him (Williams) in that situation,” he said. “I mean, I have to do a better job letting them know that the yards are more important for us in that spot than the clock running or burning timeouts on the opposition or anything of that nature. So, 100% on me.” Calen and Ben will learn from this. title: Week 8 NFL Power Rankings: Grading Each Team’s Quarterback Situation
summary: With the conclusion of Week 7, we are quickly inching closer to the midpoint of the season. While there’s still plenty of season left to be played, certain teams have separated themselves, while others are experiencing plenty of adversity through the way of injuries. The playoff picture has yet to take shape, but with the […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - OCTOBER 25: Quarterbacks Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs and Sam Darnold #14 of the Seattle Seahawks embrace after a game at Lumen Field on October 25, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images) | Getty Images With the conclusion of Week 7, we are quickly inching closer to the midpoint of the season. While there’s still plenty of season left to be played, certain teams have separated themselves, while others are experiencing plenty of adversity through the way of injuries. The playoff picture has yet to take shape, but with the trade deadline just weeks away, the league’s dynamics will start to shift in the coming days/weeks. Before we turn the page ahead to Week 8, let’s dive into our updated Week 8 WCG NFL Power Rankings, reflecting on the week that was, headlined by each team’s quarterback play through seven weeks. 1. Buffalo Bills (5-1) Quarterback Progress Report: Josh Allen (A) Josh Allen is an alien, and even when things aren’t perfect around him, there might not be a better quarterback in the league. Although his numbers aren’t otherworldly so far, he’s the primary reason why the Bills are sitting at 5-1 after their bye week. Assuming receiver D.J. Moore gets back healthy at some point soon, his numbers should increase. Either way, the Bills are one of the best teams in the AFC yet again; we’ll see if their defense can hold up their end of the bargain this season. 2. San Francisco 49ers (6-1) Quarterback Progress Report: Brock Purdy (A) By the numbers, Purdy should be considered a front-runner in the MVP race so far this season. His hot start has been impressive, although I would argue that his last three games have been a bit of a “come back to earth” type of situation. That’s not meant to take away from what he’s done, but the decision-making is becoming shaky, and it needs to be mentioned. Overall, he’s playing at a high level, but he needs to course-correct a little bit for the 49ers to maintain their high level of play. 3. Minnesota Vikings (6-0) Quarterback Progress Report: Kyler Murray (C-) Quarterback play was a big issue for the Vikings last season, but all of that bad luck they experienced in 2025 seems to be overcorrecting so far this season. What’s funny about this situation is that the quarterback play hasn’t been noticeably better, whether that’s Kyler Murray or Carson Wentz. Then again, does it really matter with this defense? Murray has been OK, but he’s also left a lot to be desired. We’ll see what shakes out over the final 11 games of the season, but so far, he’s been “good enough” but nothing more. 4. Kansas City Chiefs (5-1) Quarterback Progress Report: Patrick Mahomes (A) Overall, there was a rush to judgment about the Chiefs’ 2025 season. Even if Mahomes hasn’t been playing at the MVP level lately, the way he’s come back from a torn ACL (among other issues) in such a short time is nothing short of impressive. The numbers haven’t been gaudy, but looking at the offensive depth chart, I’d say he’s playing well above what he should. The Chiefs appear to be back, and so does Mahomes. Considering the injury he suffered at the end of last season, his “comeback” has been extremely impressive. 5. Jacksonville Jaguars (4-2) Quarterback Progress Report: Trevor Lawrence (A) The resurgence of the former No. 1 overall pick in 2021 has been quite the sight to see. Head coach Liam Coen has unlocked a level of consistency we haven’t seen since Lawrence entered the league. The offensive line has outplayed expectations, and even without Brian Thomas Jr. being a factor, this offense is humming. While I’m not sure I would categorize Coen’s hiring as a “career-saving” move, it was pretty damn close. 6. Detroit Lions (4-2) Quarterback Progress Report: Jared Goff (A+) No matter who the offensive coordinator has been in Detroit, it hasn’t seemed to matter a whole lot for Goff. Under Drew Petzing, Goff has been damn-near perfect, especially in the touchdown-to-interception ratio at an impressive 14-0 through six games. His completion percentage is slightly down from the 70% he posted in 2024, but it’s right on par with what it was last year. He’s targeting the middle of the field and going deep often, and still doesn’t have an interception. That’s about as good as you can ask for, and it’s probably about time for him to be included in the MVP conversation. 7. Chicago Bears (5-2) Quarterback Progress Report: Caleb Williams (A) The marriage between head coach Ben Johnson and Williams has gone about as well as hoped through a season and a half. In Year 1, Williams made plenty of big leaps, but through four starts in Year 2, he looks like a Top 5-7 quarterback. He’s continued to limit turnovers while taking more of what the defense gives him. That has led to a completion rate over 70%, yet he’s still taking plenty of accurate shots downfield. There’s still growth to be had, but he’s been night and day from what we saw in his rookie campaign. 8. Seattle Seahawks (4-3) Quarterback Progress Report: Sam Darnold (D-) Little did we know that when Darnold went down in Week 1, it wouldn’t be a season-ending injury, but instead an eye-opening experience in which backup quarterback Drew Lock has severely outplayed Darnold this season. This has kind of been the story of Darnold’s career, but he’s put enough good football on tape to make many believe he can bounce back. That said, if he doesn’t soon, they might need to change the quarterback to salvage the season. Either way, Darnold has been brutal, and it’s simply not something Seattle can afford to live with. 9. Denver Broncos (5-2) Quarterback Progress Report: Bo Nix (D-) Broncos fans will hope Sunday’s blowout win over the Cardinals was a “get right” game for Nix and this offense. So far, it’s been a jumbled mess, and no matter who the play caller is, Nix has struggled coming back from his ankle surgery. Mobility is a big part of his game, but the continued peppering at or behind the line of scrimmage on throws has been a big red flag. Denver is a very good team, but they’ll need their offense to do its part if they hope to contend for a Super Bowl again in January. 10. Cincinnati Bengals (4-2) Quarterback Progress Report: Joe Burrow (A-) The Bengals have been relatively inconsistent through the first seven weeks of the season, including on Sunday when they trailed 13-0 heading into the half against the Ravens. Then they figured it out and scored 35 unanswered en route to a convincing victory to overtake Baltimore in the division. Joe Burrow was responsible for four touchdowns, bringing his total to 15 on the year through six games. If the defense continues to play as they did in the second half, this will be a tough team to beat down the stretch. 11. New England Patriots (4-3) Quarterback Progress Report: Drake Maye (B+) It’s clear that Maye is bordering on elite territory, but a slow start to the season has kept his grade down for the season. Thursday night’s showdown with Williams was a great glimpse into two of the top drafted quarterbacks from the 2024 class, and the matchup did not disappoint. As A.J. Brown and the offensive line get healthier, Maye’s play should improve. He’s unlikely to be as high in the MVP conversation this year, but it’s clear that his yips are out of the way, and he is indeed a very good quarterback with plenty of ceiling still to chase. 12. Green Bay Packers (4-3) Quarterback Progress Report: Jordan Love (A) For the first time in his career, his offensive line has not been ideal. While it has improved in recent weeks, several reserves have been taking real snaps, creating issues. Add in a non-existent run game, and Love has been set up to fail. The start of the season wasn’t great, but over the last month, he’s been a completely different quarterback. Although his completion percentage has dipped and his interceptions have risen a bit, he’s taking way more deep shots and, overall, looks like a big-play hunter. All…
