title: Broncos at Cardinals: The No Bull Review
summary: Let this be a lesson to all of you out there in Broncos Country: don’t trust the talking heads with narratives about this team or its players.  Last week all we heard about was how terrible and inept Bo Nix was. No one in the mainstream media was talking about the quality of defenses the […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - OCTOBER 25: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos runs for a touchdown during the second quarter of the game against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Chris Coduto/Getty Images) | Getty Images Let this be a lesson to all of you out there in Broncos Country: don’t trust the talking heads with narratives about this team or its players. Last week all we heard about was how terrible and inept Bo Nix was. No one in the mainstream media was talking about the quality of defenses the Denver Broncos were facing or the lack of a competent run game. Most of them took their turns dumping on Bo Nix because none of them thought he was going to do anything coming out of the draft. He was mislabeled as a check-down merchant in Oregon, and that label will likely follow him every time he has a match-up against an excellent defense. Not to worry, Broncos Country. This team is who we here at the No Bull Review thought they were. This is darn near the same script we saw last season. Sit back and enjoy the ride for the rest of this season as the Broncos hit their stride. Offense Sean Payton continues to tweak the offense as he keeps the team growing and moving toward a better version of themselves as the season wears on. He gave a ton of snaps to young Jonah Coleman, signaling that he’s not satisfied with the best a back can gain on average is 3 yards. He had more plays for Mims in this game and designed a multitude of shots downfield to multiple receivers. There was still a nice balance of run (26) vs. pass (29). The big difference in this game was in explosive plays. The offense had 5 plays of 20 yards or more. There are still many things for them to clean up. Receivers had drops, linemen blew blocks, and the quarterback can place the ball better in spots for sure. I’m not saying that the offense is a group of world-beaters. I am saying this team played up to their potential and showed what they are capable of doing. Quarterbacks Bo Nix can throw downfield, in case you didn’t know. He attacked deep early and kept it up through the game. He had an absolutely masterful run for a touchdown. He threw a 27-yard pass to Waddle that was a laser. I’m going to reiterate that everyone in the media has misread the ankle injury completely. People keep mentioning it as if it is still an issue. The issue is not the ankle from a health standpoint. As we saw on his nearly 20 mph run to the promised land, the ankle is working just fine. The issue with the ankle injury comes from him getting back into his groove as a passer. His accuracy has been lacking early this season (much like it did last season). I think we’re seeing Nix rounding into form as the season wears on. He’s getting work each week finally, and as he settles his footwork down, his throws are only going to get better and better. Line I largely liked what I saw from the line this week. They only gave up one sack. The run game was blocked up well enough. Sure, we saw McGlinchey miss a stunt and block no one to give up a big pressure. We also had a couple of illegal formation penalties that should never happen. This line has had a rough start to the season. With a more efficient runner toting the rock, I’m optimistic about their progress and ability to round into form much like Nix. Running Backs A healthy Jonah Coleman is just what the doctor ordered for this ailing Broncos run game. He was in on 50% of the snaps for the team. He showed a runner who has vision, burst, and power. I loved his ability to cut back and head north when his designed holes were closing up. That seems simple enough, but we’ve seen far too many runs go for nothing because backs aren’t cutting when the play is smothered. He averaged 6 yards per carry on 9 runs for 54 yards. He also caught two passes for 15. Coleman is versatile in anything we ask the position to do in this offense. I’m excited to see what this rookie does with the rest of his season. R.J. Harvey is a home-run hitter. He took a screen pass to the house early in the 3rd quarter. It was a perfectly timed and executed play that had multiple blockers running free downfield to help Harvey jet into the end zone. He was pretty rough as far as output goes outside of that one play. His other 4 touches were plays for 2-3 yards each. JK Dobbins had 6 carries for 23 yards. On one hand, that’s an improvement over what we’ve seen from him in the past few games. On the other hand, there’s a reason he only saw 23% of the snaps in the game. One of his carries was a touchdown that he earned fighting through a tackle to lunge the ball over the goal line. Receivers Let’s give some love to Marvin Mims for getting more involved with the offense this week. He had a gain of 47 yards off a busted coverage play to the sideline. He’s another guy on this offense who is a threat to house the ball if they can just find ways to get him the ball in space. Cortland Sutton got the party started with an in-breaking route across the middle for a big gain of 20 yards. He’s still looking like a player who has lost a step, but his size and great route running open up plays for Nix. Jaylen Waddle had a couple of really nice catches in this game. He caught a low throw on a 14-yard out that was way tougher than it needed to be. Late in the game, he caught a 27-yard back shoulder downfield while taking a big hit from a closing safety. He ended the game with 4 catches for 48 yards. Troy Franklin was ice cold in this game, missing both of his targets. What I loved from him was his blocking for the Nix run. He blocked two guys to help Nix get into the end zone. Defense The Broncos defense again held the opponents to under 20 points. That’s excellent in today’s NFL. Vance Joseph didn’t have an answer for Trey McBride (he threw everything and the kitchen sink at him coverage-wise). Sometimes you can’t hold down a great player (just ask JSN). I want to say that Joseph had his defense playing inspired football to close out the game. The Arizona Cardinals got the ball down to the 1-yard line and the defense held them out for 7 straight plays. The effort never dropped even with a two-score lead. Front 7 Malcolm Roach, to me, was the defensive player of the game. He was absolutely killing it up front all game long. He had a sack, a tackle for loss, 4 quarterback hits, and a batted pass to seal the big goal-line stand at the end of the game. Alex Singleton stacked up another really solid game. It wasn’t a shut-out for him, as he had a couple of coverage plays with shaky coverage, including a 14-yard crossing route that got by him. He had an impressive 19-tackle game with a tackle for loss, 2 quarterback hits, and a sack on the day. Sai’vion Jones had the most impressive sack of the game, with a guy draped over him using one arm. He also had a tackle for loss and a quarterback hit. Secondary Riley Moss got flagged for pass interference for executing perfect pass defense to deflect a pass as it was caught. I’m honestly sick and tired of referees throwing a flag when they see Moss in coverage. The replay made me want to puke, honestly. Riley had a pass defense later in the game with far more contact than we saw on the pass interference penalty. Kris Abrams-Draine continued to impress me with his play this week. He had an excellent open-field tackle to keep a pass bottled up on a 2nd and 5. On a 4th and 13 play out to his side, he did a superb job not biting as the receiver lateralled the ball to a guy behind him. KAD recognized what was happening and kept himself in line to stop the play. Brandon Jones on 3rd and 2 got the defense off the field with smothering coverage on McBride. He gave a huge pass interference call up by being too handsy and also had a couple of missed tackles. McMillian darn near had 3 interceptions in the game. They all go down in the stat sheet as a pass defense, but my soul weeps a bit to see so many passes hit his hands and not get picked.…

title: Bo Nix quells doubts in Broncos’ offense with big win over Cardinals
summary: Good morning, Broncos Country! Denver’s win in Arizona on Sunday wasn’t just another check in the W column. It was affirmation to fans (and analysts) that this team is on the right track and the signal caller is the right guy at the helm. Of course, it shouldn’t have had to be that kind of […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - OCTOBER 25: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos looks on during the second quarter against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Good morning, Broncos Country! Denver’s win in Arizona on Sunday wasn’t just another check in the W column. It was affirmation to fans (and analysts) that this team is on the right track and the signal caller is the right guy at the helm. Of course, it shouldn’t have had to be that kind of message to Broncos Country because Denver was still 4-2 and second in the AFC West heading into the game. But the bumpy road to those four wins had fans questioning. And on Sunday Nix was the one bringing the answers. The criticism of Nix the past few weeks has focused a lot on his decisiveness in the pocket and overall aggressiveness to make a play, many questioning whether offseason ankle surgery was still an issue (and one idiotic announcer suggesting he just wasn’t competitive and was disrespecting the position). But when No. 10 ripped off a 62-yard touchdown run just minutes before halftime, clocking 19.9 mph in the process, he allayed a lot of concerns about both. “Once you start running, you sort of turn into a running back at that point and you’re worried about an explosive play and maximizing the plays,” Nix said, noting that the man-to-man coverage gave him a lot of room to run. “At that point, we had a great opportunity to run a long way.” GO BO GO 🐎 This 62-yard TD run is the longest by an NFL QB since November 13, 2022. DENvsAZ on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on #NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/dEuT25n6lT — NFL+ (@NFLPlus) October 25, 2026 Nix admitted that even though he’s never questioned his athleticism, he knows it often comes as a surprise to opponents that he can run so fast. “It’s really nice,” he said of getting to show off his running capability this week. “I guess until people really see [my speed], they never really believe it.” Zach Allen certainly believes. The defensive lineman goes against Nix every day in practice, so he knows what the QB is capable of. “We see in practice how athletic he is. Bo is Bo,” Allen said. “We’re glad he’s our guy; when he’s making plays, he gets the whole team juiced up. So, (I’m) really excited for him.” Nix also made a believer out of Broncos Country once again – and not just because of the long touchdown run. He managed the offense for four quarters, sustaining drives and completing passes all over the field to a host of receivers. The offense finally looked legit instead of just fortunate. “I felt that we played a good game offensively,” Nix said. “Still several things that we would like to get better at, but overall, we had a big win over a tough team on the road so it was really good for us.” Head coach Sean Payton always says the two best friends of a quarterback are a great defense and a solid run game. Until this week, the Broncos had really only had one of the two. 🗣️ RJ's loose‼️ How Dave Logan saw #DENvsAZ : pic.twitter.com/3PAfugFqLC — Denver Broncos (@Broncos) October 27, 2026 But with a little spark from the return of rookie running back Jonah Coleman, plus continued grinding from RJ Harvey and JK Dobbins, the Broncos finally put up respectable numbers in the run game – 159 yards total. Even if you took away Nix’s 62-yard long run, the total rushing yards would still have been close to 100 on the day, which was a marked improvement on the season. “He played well,” Payton said of the rookie running back. “The touches he had were explosive.” Payton noted that getting more playing time has to be earned, and Coleman is certainly doing that. Averaging 6 yards per carry on his nine touches got the attention of his head coach. “He looked really good,” Payton said. “Definitely have to get him more touches.” While the defense didn’t have to win the game for Denver this week, the fact that it can consistently wreak havoc for opposing offenses is reassuring. And this week it was the red zone stops rather than the turnovers being showcased. The Broncos allowed the Cardinals just one score from the red zone out of five trips inside the 20. “It’s huge,” said Allen, who was originally drafted to the Cardinals but picked up by the Broncos three years ago. “We invest a lot into the red zone (defense), so when we see success there, it means a lot. We’re excited about it.” And so is the head coach, especially given the number of starters on the defense who were out nursing some injuries. “Pretty impressive. You’re just thankful for the depth (and) those guys stepping up,” Payton noted. “A lot of guys played well.”

title: Detroit Lions add former Vikings nose tackle to practice squad
summary: Last week, the Detroit Lions hosted free agent nose tackle Taki Taimani for a visit. On Tuesday, they announced that Taimani has signed to their practice squad. To make room, the Lions released wide receiver Lawrence Keys from the practice squad. Taimani first entered the league in 2024 as an undrafted free agent out of […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MN - AUGUST 16: Minnesota Vikings defensive tackle Taki Taimani (94) looks on during the NFL preseason game between the New England Patriots and Minnesota Vikings on August 16th, 2025, in Minneapolis, MN. (Photo by Bailey Hillesheim/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Last week, the Detroit Lions hosted free agent nose tackle Taki Taimani for a visit. On Tuesday, they announced that Taimani has signed to their practice squad. To make room, the Lions released wide receiver Lawrence Keys from the practice squad. Taimani first entered the league in 2024 as an undrafted free agent out of Oregon. He was signed by the Minnesota Vikings and even made their initial 53-man roster in his rookie season. He played in seven games that year (70 total defensive snaps, 34 special teams) before an ankle injury landed him on injured reserve for the final 10 games. The following year, Taimani spent most of the season on the Vikings’ practice squad, seeing the call-up for just two games in the 2025 season. This past year, he was waived with an injury designation late in training camp, and was released from the team’s injured reserve list in mid-September. Taimani is a big man, last listed at 6-foot-1, 324 pounds. In his brief appearances in games for the Vikings, he played multiple defensive tackle spots, including nose tackle. Prior to his time in the NFL, he was praised for his strength and anchoring ability as a two-gapper. Detroit doesn’t have a ton of run-stuffing defensive tackles on their roster outside of Alim McNeill and Tyleik Williams, although they did re-sign rookie Aidan Keanaaina to the practice squad last week. More interestingly, the Lions play the Vikings this week. So can Taimani help Detroit prepare for their second straight divisional home game?

title: NFL Week 8 power rankings: Detroit Lions on the rise following victory over Packers
summary: The Detroit Lions (4-2) have now won two straight, after taking down division rival Green Bay Packers 20-17 in Week 7. Half of this week’s national power rankings saw the victory as significant enough to move the Lions into their Top 10, while the other four rankers have Detroit just outside. Let’s take a closer […]
full_text: Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell reacts to a fumble made by running back Jahmyr Gibbs (0) against Green Bay Packers during the first half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions (4-2) have now won two straight, after taking down division rival Green Bay Packers 20-17 in Week 7. Half of this week’s national power rankings saw the victory as significant enough to move the Lions into their Top 10, while the other four rankers have Detroit just outside. Let’s take a closer look at this week’s national power rankings. Sports Illustrated: 7 ( Previous rank: 11) From Connor Orr : The defensive performance from Detroit against Green Bay was season-altering. With Josh Jacobs returning and the Packers supposedly at full(er) strength, the Lions posted one of the lowest opponent success rates in the NFL on Sunday. Talk about needing to have it. The Athletic: 9 (Previous rank: 9) From Chad Graff and Josh Kendall : Detroit got an important divisional win on Sunday, but concerns remain about its pass defense even after Brian Branch returned to the lineup. The Lions have the league’s fourth-worst expected points added per play on dropbacks against them. If they got even middling play from their secondary, they could be serious contenders in the NFC. Yahoo Sports: 10 (Previous rank: 11) From Frank Schwab : The Lions got a big win Sunday and a big return to the lineup. Safety Brian Branch was back after tearing his Achilles last season, and he had four tackles and an interception. He can make a big difference in a defense that needs the boost. “That’s just who he is, man,” linebacker Derrick Barnes told MLive.com. “He a ballhawk, man. He run, he hits, man. He plays fast the whole game. That’s who he is, man. And a lot of people feed off the energy.” Branch played 45 snaps, which was 67% of the Lions’ defensive plays. That number will increase as he gets back to full strength. The Lions held the Packers to 17 points with Branch back in the lineup, which is progress from a unit that had struggled all season. CBS Sports: 10 (Previous rank: 11) From Pete Prisco : “The offense is, as usual, playing at a high level. Jared Goff has been really good. Dan Campbell needs to quit going for it all the time.” USA Today: 11 (Previous rank: 11) From Nate Davis : Maybe a little more MVP love for Jared Goff, the only quarterback to pass for at least 200 yards, a TD and zero picks in each of his team’s first six games? Ever. NFL.com: 11 (Previous rank: 12) From Nick Shook : Detroit played one of its uglier games of the 2026 season on Sunday, a true NFC North rock fight against a rival that devolved into a polite battle of “No, go ahead, you take the win,” before the Lions ultimately emerged victorious. Turnovers became a problem for the first time this season, but conversely, Brian Branch’s return helped a defense that desperately needed a boost. ESPN: 11 (Previous rank: 12) From ESPN Staff, excerpt from Eric Woodyard : “Detroit drafted Miller as the No. 17 pick to be a Day 1 starter, and the 22-year-old has lived up to the hype. He took on star edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson during training camp, and he hasn’t allowed a sack in five games this season (primarily at right tackle). Meanwhile, Detroit’s offense is producing the second-most points in the league (30.67 per game) behind the Bills (32.83). Miller still has room to grow, as he has committed five penalties this season.” Sporting News: 12 (Previous rank: 14) From Vinnie Iyer : “The Lions’ defense went from scary bad to intimidating against the Packers with Brian Branch back to help the secondary. When Jared Goff is playing so well off Jahmyr Gibbs’ running, Detroit is difficult to beat. It’s no surprise Detroit delivered its best game for Dan Campbell after the bye. The team needs to keep up the momentum with first-place Minnesota visiting next.”
author: Erik Schlitt

title: Film study: The good, the bad from Lions offense vs. Packers
summary: The Detroit Lions battled self-inflicted adversity as it scrapped out a 20-17 victory over the Green Bay Packers to start the season 1-0 in the NFC North. Not how the prognosticators drew it up, the Lions defense had its best game of the season, stepping up in critical situations to hold the Packers to just […]
full_text: Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (16) talks to center Cade Mays (64) before a snap against Green Bay Packers during the first half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions battled self-inflicted adversity as it scrapped out a 20-17 victory over the Green Bay Packers to start the season 1-0 in the NFC North. Not how the prognosticators drew it up, the Lions defense had its best game of the season, stepping up in critical situations to hold the Packers to just 17 points. Although, some had pointed out the Packers’ deep passing game is a paper tiger . Might want to bookmark that to revisit in Week 18. While the final score was 20-17, the Lions were definitively the better team on the field for most of the game. By comparison of success rate, this was the second largest margin of play of the Week 7 slate. Did we really get beat that bad? Comparing offensive success rates for NFL games in Week 7: pic.twitter.com/pqarLvhGCZ — Sam Hoppen (@SamHoppen) October 26, 2026 Unfortunately, costly turnovers and a failed fourth-and-goal in the second half held the Lions offense back from hitting its normal 30+ points per game output. For this week’s film study, I want to take a look at both the good things the Lions offense did, and then look at the bad to improve on moving forward. The good Always start with the good. Designed for Jameson Williams Below is my favorite schemed play of the game. Jameson Williams is a nightmare for defensive coordinators because he can take the top off the defense at any moment with his speed. But in the red zone, that vertical threat is mitigated by spacing. Here, offensive coordinator Drew Petzing does an awesome job designing a play for Williams using his speed horizontally. Below, Williams is set in motion presnap into the box behind the offensive line. At the snap, he continues horizontally into the flat. His speed is already hard to keep up with, but when he is hidden and mixed with the traffic and movement of the play action fake, it is a near impossible assignment for the defense. The other critical element of the play design is Amon-Ra St. Brown lining up at the wing slot, and inserting inside the B-gap with the run-action. Most safeties and/or linebackers have keys that read this action as a run principle resulting in the first steps of the play side linebacker and deep safety to be downhill at the B-gap. From there, it’s an easy pitch and catch for Jared Goff. Not-a-statue Jared Goff for MVP After another great performance, Goff is finally starting to get the national attention he deserves for his historic start to the 2026 season. Dan Campbell has been consistent in his praise for Goff and the consistent, elite quarterback play he is showing week-in and week-out. Goff does all of the things presnap that go unnoticed in the mental and command elements of the offense, and he does them at a high level. His trained eyes in the play action game is being recognized as being elite. But when it comes to MVP voting, it’s typically the highlight reel out-of-structure plays that win the day. Goff is never going to match Josh Allen, Lamar Jackson, or Caleb Williams in this part of the game, obviously. It is time, however, to dispel the narrative that Goff is just a statue in the pocket. An immobile pocket passer that once pushed off his spot, he’s in trouble. Below I want to spotlight two plays where Jared Goff uses his legs to create two big plays while while throwing off platform. The first one is the touchdown pass to Jameson Williams. While Penei Sewell sitting in the zone on the mesh concept has garnered the spotlight, take a moment to watch how Goff navigates the pocket, feeling the pressure and driving forward, stepping forward to complete the pass to Williams. Jameson even noted that it was a no-look pass from Goff . Goff extended the play with his legs Threw the ball off platform, across his body No-look pass while drawing defenders toward Sewell. On the second play below, Goff immediately recognizes the creeping safety and blitzing linebacker to his right and exits the pocket to his left. Shuffling his feet, Goff backs an accurate throw to Amon-Ra St. Brown on a dig route going in the opposite direction as Goff’s momentum. The combination of both his mental processing as well as his athleticism to throw on the run rendered the Packers blitz moot, a huge component that will come in handy when the Lions match up against the Minnesota Vikings historically blitz-heavy scheme. Strong signs from the offensive line With center Cade Mays making his return and first start as a Lions, plenty of attention was given situation as backup Juice Scruggs had played well in his absence. Below is a third-and-1 run resulting in a first down, a critical situational area of the game that also reared its ugly head in the fourth quarter (more on that later). The key point I wanted to highlight here is the recognition and pickup on this outside zone run following the late presnap shift from the Packers defensive line. The bad While there were strong signals from the offensive line, there were also a handful of missed assignments leading to negative plays. The first play here shows some missed assignment/miscommunication up front. With left guard Christian Mahogany combo-blocking the nose with center Cade Mays and left tackle Penei Sewell working up to the play side linebacker, the B-gap defensive tackle is left untouched to make the tackle behind the line of scrimmage. These types of mistakes are self-inflicted, and should become far and few between as the season progresses. The fourth-and-1 Let’s get to the big one. To start, I agree with the decision to go for it on fourth down here. Beyond the generic historical analytical models given the field position and time on the clock remaining, it’s important to consider the particular teams on the field. In most games, the Lions offense will likely be the single best unit on the field on either side of the football. The weight given to that part of the equation needs to be adjusted and considered above the generic historic analytical models. That is, take the generic historical analytical model and adjust the weights and parameters to get a personalized approach for each game context. Now, while I approve of the decision from Dan Campbell to go, I do not like the play call from Petzing in this situation. I will admit, there are advantages to the play design particular for this situation. The part I do not like is that it did leave the team vulnerable in the exact way that the Packers took advantage of. Let’s break it down in detail. First, the clip of the full play is provided below. Diagrammed, the unique part of this run concept is that it appears to blend duo and power gap concepts. On short yardage, duo has the positive element of preventing penetration and displacing the defensive front. Combining this with power elements (the pulling right guard and fullback trap motion), the offense creates a numbers and angle advantage for critical play side blocks. On paper, this checks all the boxes for a critical short yardage play. The flaw, in my opinion, is in the details. Spotlighted below is the backside of the formation. The vulnerability here is the presentation of the cornerback as an active run defender at the line of scrimmage. If the corner starts the play at the snap where he was when the offensive line made its presnap line call, he is not an impact player in the success of this down-and-distance play call. The other interesting note is that the inline tight end here is none other than wide receiver Isaac TeSlaa. First, credit to TeSlaa for sticking his nose in the play and taking on the edge player. Putting TeSlaa down at the line is not my criticism of the play. My guess is that Petzing designed the play this way to hold the cornerback from blitzing the way he did at the snap. TeSlaa is a big threat the release on a…

title: Lions vs. Packers Song of the Game: ‘Get Over It’ by OK Go
summary: If you’re a Packers fan, you have two ways to think about what happened on Sunday. One way of looking at this game is nothing less than comeuppance, justified retribution for the years of officiating that has benefitted Green Bay in critical moments. The other is that your football team was objectively worse in every […]
full_text: Oct 25, 2026; Detroit, Michigan, USA; Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur reacts after a call during the third quarter against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field. Mandatory Credit: Lon Horwedel-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect If you’re a Packers fan, you have two ways to think about what happened on Sunday. One way of looking at this game is nothing less than comeuppance, justified retribution for the years of officiating that has benefitted Green Bay in critical moments. The other is that your football team was objectively worse in every which way, and had it not been for fumbles your defense didn’t even cause, Sunday would have been a two-score game at a minimum. Choose your perspective, and get over it—you have “Thursday Night Football” to prepare for! Lions vs. Packers Week 7 Song of the Game: “Get Over It” by OK Go Take a break from your daily grind and come back with me in time—back to the year 2002. The Playstation 2 is all the rage in the gaming world, and you’ve just ripped the wrapper on your brand new copy of Madden NFL 2003. You’re excited to see how the Detroit Lions stack up against the competition, but after scrolling through the league, it might be easier to rebuild one of the NFL Europe teams in Franchise mode. You wonder how the Lions are always so bad, year after year, but this your cross to bear. There’s no amount of trades you can pull off to improve your team enough and actually enjoy playing the game, so you play God and take control of all 32 teams to carry out your bidding. (Except Mike McMahon—you and your 77 acceleration can stay under center.) The soundtrack to your menu scrolling—while stealing Torry Holt from the Rams and Ricky Williams from the Dolphins—brings you so many offerings, from Good Charlotte (ew) to Nappy Roots’ rock remix of “Awnaw” (bop). But there’s one track you can’t get enough of: “Get Over It” by OK Go. You get to the options for EA Trax and turn off whatever Bon Jovi song keeps playing, and you’re listening to “Get Over It” four or five times an hour. Let’s just cut to the chase: do you know what all of these memories and the Lions’ 20-17 win over the Green Bay Packers on Sunday has to do with one another? Manipulation! Corruption! Cheating! Oh, it’s such a drag, what a chore Oh, your wounds are full of salt Everything’s a stress, and what’s more Well, it’s all somebody’s fault Packers’ fans had a rough Sunday and Monday—we’ll see how Tuesday plays out—but it’ll be interesting to see if they continue to spin tales of the officials, the Lions, and the NFL at large conspiring to defeat their beloved team. Honey, your football team just isn’t very good. It’s nobody’s else’s fault that Green Bay sports the least efficient and productive rushing attack in the NFL since… 1994 . Yes, the Packers 2.9 rushing yards per attempt is the first time a team has been under 3.0 rushing yards per attempt in over thirty years . Green Bay’s deep-passing attack is what we thought it was when it’s not buoyed by immoral and unethical behavior. Detroit’s self-inflicted miscues were the only reason the Packers even had a shot in this one, but at the end of the day, they lost a morally good football game because the better team won. What a pain, well, it’s all a crying shame What left to do but complain? You better find someone to blame Absurd defensive penalties helped 3 Lions RZ trips. They scored 10 points on those trips, and the non-scoring drive required a fourth-down stop. That includes the game-winning drive. There's just no way around mentioning the impact the refs had on the game. — Peter Bukowski (@Peter_Bukowski) October 26, 2026 In my 19 years covering the Packers on a daily basis, I've never written a blame-the-refs story. Yeah, I get it, the Packers beat themselves, too, but what happened at Ford Field was unaccepable, an embarrassment and, to quote Xavier McKinney, bullshit. ⬇️ https://t.co/IJdIl1WAMe — Bill Huber (@BillHuberNFL) October 26, 2026 #Packers lose to the NFL/Lions partnership 20-17. Garbage game. Refs literally took that game over. A total embarrassment for the league and fans should take notice. This league should not be trusted anymore. Too much of this across the whole league. Far past this game. — Evan Massey (@massey_evan) October 25, 2026 What I'd really like to know is how this isn't taunting. They're facing an opponent and gesturing at them in "acts…that may engender ill will between teams", which would be a violation of Rule 12, Section 3, Article 1(c). https://t.co/2nNJZcjzqU — Packers History (@HistoricPackers) October 26, 2026 Packers All-Pro safety Xavier McKinney unloads on the officiating. Have a listen. Says he’d rather get fined and try and help his team. pic.twitter.com/zW6FIp4eUR — Matt Schneidman (@mattschneidman) October 26, 2026 these refs are blind — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) October 25, 2026 Its hilarious watching literally every NFL fanbase across the NFL criticize the officiating while Lions fans live in their own little world of denial. Im sure everyone else is wrong 😂 pic.twitter.com/cHUZDZFw6H — Packerfan Total Access- Clayton (@packers_access) October 27, 2026 Hey! Get, get, get, get, get over it! Hey! Get, get, get, get, get over it! Hey! Get, get, get, get, get over it! Get over it, get over it! Oh! title: Detroit Lions film breakdown: The trained eyes of Jared Goff
summary: Last week, a few people pointed out a great answer from Detroit Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing about what makes Jared Goff special as a play-action quarterback. Here’s the transcript of Petzing’s answer below. I’m going to highlight the key points: “One of the things that makes him so elite in that is his process. […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 25: Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions calls a play during the first quarter of a game against the Green Bay Packers at Ford Field on October 25, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last week, a few people pointed out a great answer from Detroit Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing about what makes Jared Goff special as a play-action quarterback. Here’s the transcript of Petzing’s answer below. I’m going to highlight the key points: “One of the things that makes him so elite in that is his process. It’s uncomfortable and you don’t do it a ton in college anymore where you turn your back to the defense. And you have to take in a ton of information pre-snap, and you have to know where your eyes need to go and who you need to locate on their side of the ball and on our side of the ball. And I think that’s a huge part of the action game. And it’s one of the reasons you see defenses try to disguise and try to show different looks so that when you do turn your back, you’re turning around and seeing a different picture. And he’s done it at such a high level that I think even when that happens, he’s able to calibrate quickly, figure out what’s going on and make the proper decision almost every time . And that’s really one of the main reasons I think he’s excelled in that area.” Here’s the video: Phenomenal explanation by Drew Petzing on what makes Jared Goff so elite at play action. https://t.co/UdyD8yL1zU pic.twitter.com/6BMv7bqnn0 — Eazy (@SpeakEZsports_) October 23, 2026 In short, play-action can be really tough for quarterbacks, because in today’s NFL, defense’s are so good at disguising coverages that the look you see before you turn your head to fake the run could be completely different than the look you see when you turn back around to look at the defense. The Green Bay Packers are one of those teams that have been expertly disguising coverages. With three stellar safeties at their disposal, there’s so much they can do. That’s why their pass defense was one of the best in the league going into Sunday’s matchup with the Lions. They ranked third in passer rating allowed (73.9), third in yards per attempt (5.9) and second in DVOA. But Goff had no problem dissecting the defense, particularly early in the game, and a lot of that had to due with Goff’s elite ability to identify coverages both pre- and post-snap. On play-action passes, Goff went 8-of-11 for 140 yards against the Packers. His +0.55 EPA/dropback on play-action passes was third-best of the week, and his 145.1 passer rating was second. One particular play shows exactly the skills Petzing was talking about. It’s the tail end of the first quarter and the Lions are kicking off their second series of the game. As Goff is ready to snap the ball, the Packers are showing a pretty ordinary cover-2 look. Both safeties are back pedaling at the snap, while the Packers are just widening their zones with Amon-Ra St. Brown’s motion—clear zone indicators. However, at the snap—literally the moment Goff turns his back for play-action, the right side safety—All-Pro Xavier McKinney (#29)—aggressively runs toward the line of scrimmage to play a shallow zone, leaving the other safety, Evan Williams, as the single high. So when Goff finally turns around, the coverage is MUCH different than it looked before the play-action. But Goff immediately clocks it, drawing his eyes to the safeties before even looking at his receivers: So he knows that McKinney has vacated the left-middle part of the field, where Amon-Ra St. Brown’s leak route just so happens to be brilliantly designed to attack—while Jameson Williams takes the play-side cornerback out of the play. Despite the Packers doing a great job not tipping their coverage design, Goff immediately identified it, found where the weakness was, and exploited it for a huge gain. Here’s it all working together in harmony: Jared Goff ID'ing the disguised coverage immediately and exploiting it for a big gain. pic.twitter.com/8WKfxnrEIM — Jeremy Reisman (@DetroitOnLion) October 27, 2026 Aided by strong protection from the offensive line, this is Jared Goff making the remarkable look unremarkable. And against a team like the Minnesota Vikings who will do everything they can to disguise things and confuse Goff this upcoming Sunday, it’s when having someone like him at quarterback is also extremely valuable.

title: Debating Detroit Lions’ 4th-down decisions, highlighting best players vs. Packers
summary: We’ve heard what Dan Campbell has said. You’ve likely seen what the analytical models have said. Hopefully, you haven’t bothered to see what Pete Prisco thinks. Now, it’s time for us to discuss the Detroit Lions’ fourth-down decisions in their 20-17 win over the Green Bay Packers. Without a doubt, this has been one of […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 25: Head coach Dan Campbell of the Detroit Lions looks on against the Green Bay Packers during the first quarter at Ford Field on October 25, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’ve heard what Dan Campbell has said . You’ve likely seen what the analytical models have said. Hopefully, you haven’t bothered to see what Pete Prisco thinks. Now, it’s time for us to discuss the Detroit Lions’ fourth-down decisions in their 20-17 win over the Green Bay Packers. Without a doubt, this has been one of Campbell’s most controversial decisions: going for it in a tie game from his own 22-yard line with 4:53 left. It’s a position where most teams would not ever even consider going for it. Just the optics of potentially giving the ball back to the opponent already in field goal position to take the lead late is enough to scare off most NFL coaches. However, Campbell’s explanation of how the clock was critical to his decision changed a lot of people’s minds. “With where that was, where the clock was at is I know what I’m conceding,” Campbell further explained on Monday. “If you don’t get that—I believe we were going to get that. I know what you’re conceding, but I also know without any doubt, any question, we are getting the ball back with plenty of time to answer and rebuttal whatever they’ve done. It was really that simple.” On this week’s PODcast, we debate that decision. Generally speaking, we all agree that there is plenty of good rationalization and thought process that went into Campbell’s decision, and anyone who says the decision was completely reckless is not understanding the situation well enough. But should more consideration have been given to the Lions’ struggles in short-yardage situations this year or how inconsistent their run game had been against the Packers on Sunday? We also make the argument that Campbell’s other fourth-down decision—going for it on fourth-and-5 from the Packers’ 6-yard line already up three points—may have been the more controversial and inexcusable decision. That entire discussion and debate is the first topic of discussion in our second segment, which starts around the 32:45 minute mark of the show (1:15:00 mark if you’re watching on YouTube or Twitch ). Before that, we talk about the biggest storylines of the game, including an outstanding performance from the secondary, Jared Goff’s big day against a great Packers defense, and a very up-and-down day from the Lions’ rushing attack. You can catch it all on this week’s show below: If you want more Lions vs. Packers talk, consider checking on this week’s PODcast on our YouTube page or Twitch channel . There we have a bunch more in-between segments chats, including more thoughts on officiating from the game.

title: Discussion: What was the most impressive part of the Detroit Lions’ win over Packers?
summary: There are no style points in the NFL, and a Detroit Lions win over the Green Bay Packers has enough inherent beauty that I’m not going to complain too much that Detroit probably should have blown them out. After all, there were plenty of things the Detroit Lions did very well on Sunday that earned […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 25: Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions warms up prior to a game against the Green Bay Packers at Ford Field on October 25, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images There are no style points in the NFL, and a Detroit Lions win over the Green Bay Packers has enough inherent beauty that I’m not going to complain too much that Detroit probably should have blown them out . After all, there were plenty of things the Detroit Lions did very well on Sunday that earned them that win. Say what you want about officiating or controversial fourth-down decisions, but the Lions led for the majority of that game, and made the final, critical plays to push them over the top. So let’s talk about the most impressive accomplishments from the Lions’ 20-17 victory over the Packers. Today’s Question of the Day is: What was the Lions’ most impressive part of their win over the Packers? My answer: The easiest answer would be to talk about Detroit’s pass defense, which limited Jordan Love’s ability to push the ball downfield. While I thought the linebackers struggled in coverage over the middle, Detroit’s secondary played their best game of the season. According to PFF, all of the defensive backs combined were responsible for just nine catches on 19 targets for only 82 yards, 0 TDs, 1 INT, and two pass breakups. And Love’s overall efficiency was among his worst performances of the year. Going into the game, here’s what Love averaged through six weeks: 91.8 passer rating 7.5 yards per attempt 0.131 dropback EPA 42.9 dropback success rate And here’s how he performed against the Lions: 83.0 passer rating 6.1 yards per attempt 0.142 dropback EPA 35.4% dropback success rate Credit to the Lions’ defensive backs, and the smart strategy to rotate them and keep them fresh. But I also want to talk about the flip side of the ball. Detroit’s passing offense was spectacular against what was one of the best passing defenses through six weeks of the season. Going into the game, the Packers were allowing: 73.9 passer rating 5.9 yards per attempt -0.024 dropback EPA 45.5% success rate And here’s what Jared Goff and company did to that defense: 119.7 passer rating 9.5 yards per attempt 0.399 dropback EPA 57.1% success rate They absolutely blew them out of the water in a way Green Bay had not yet experienced this year. It wasn’t perfect, and the Lions were certainly slowed down in the second half, but that was still a damn impressive game from Goff and company. That should give Lions fans confidence that the offense should be able to move the ball relatively well even against some elite defenses. And what do you know? An elite defense is coming to town again this week. What (or who) was most impressive in the Lions’ win over the Packers on Sunday? Share your thoughts below. Join the conversation! title: Packers Injury Report: LaFleur hopes Matthew Golden plays on Thursday
summary: The Green Bay Packers are in an interesting position in terms of their injury report, because the team can mostly handle the issues they are suffering with just their internal options on the 53-man active roster. There are a couple of exceptions to that rule, which we’ll go over in this piece, and head coach […]
full_text: (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers are in an interesting position in terms of their injury report, because the team can mostly handle the issues they are suffering with just their internal options on the 53-man active roster. There are a couple of exceptions to that rule, which we’ll go over in this piece, and head coach Matt LaFleur discussed these injuries in depth in his post-practice press conference on Tuesday. Non-participants WR Matthew Golden (shoulder/foot) RG Travis Glover (knee) C Sean Rhyan (ankle) LB Zaire Franklin (shin) The following four players were the only players who didn’t suit up for the Packers’ walkthrough practice on Tuesday. Center Sean Rhyan and linebacker Zaire Franklin have already been ruled out of Thursday Night Football ’s action, and LaFleur said that the team hasn’t ruled out placing Rhyan on the injured reserve — which would open up a roster spot on Green Bay’s currently full active roster. On the subject of receiver Matthew Golden, LaFleur stated that hopes that the receiver will be available against the Carolina Panthers, but that the team is “still kind of working through it.” Travis Glover’s knee injury was not reported to the team until Monday, according to LaFleur, and the head coach has claimed that Kevin Zeitler will be ready to go if Glover can’t put on the pads on Thursday. Limited participants G Aaron Banks (knee/toe) DL Devonte Wyatt (ankle) DL Anthony Campbell (ankle) ED Brenton Cox Jr. (quadricep) The following players were limited participants in practice today, but it’s worth noting that all of them were able to finish Sunday’s game. In all likelihood, they will play against the Panthers. — So what are we on the look for in Green Bay? A 53-man roster getting worked down to a 48-man game-day roster is pretty simple for the Packers right now. They will almost certainly scratch three offensive linemen (including or not including injured players), running back Kaleb Johnson (who was a healthy scratch last week) and linebacker Zaire Franklin (who is out again with an injury). The only issue from a numbers perspective is if Matthew Golden can’t go. If he’s banged up, maybe the Packers end up elevating receiver Isaiah Neyor from the practice squad for the first time this season. — On the Panthers’ end of the injury report, starting edge rusher Jaelan Phillips and starting guard Damien Lewis remained non-participants for the second-straight walkthrough in Carolina this week. The Panthers are already dealing with a major loss in right tackle Taylor Moton, who went on the injured reserve on Monday. — Maybe the biggest injury news of the day was that LaFleur finally gave us a hint on the team’s timeline for edge defender Micah Parsons’ return. When asked if Parsons will practice next week, LaFleur stated, “I sure hope so.” When he was pushed on the subject, he said, “I’m saying there’s a chance.”

title: Remembering a Random Packers Game: The Carolina Panthers
summary: This season, I’ve been using a random number generator to pick a game between the Green Bay Packers and their opponent for that week. This week, the Packers are facing off against the Carolina Panthers, whom they’ve played just 19 times. The random number: 1, so we’re going to look at the first time these […]
full_text: (Photo by Allen Kee/Getty Images) This season, I’ve been using a random number generator to pick a game between the Green Bay Packers and their opponent for that week. This week, the Packers are facing off against the Carolina Panthers, whom they’ve played just 19 times. The random number: 1, so we’re going to look at the first time these teams ever met, which happens to be the NFC championship game played on January 12th, 1997. Entering the Game The 1996 Packers won 13 regular season games, which tied with the Denver Broncos for the league’s best record that year. A couple of weeks prior, QB Brett Favre had been awarded MVP honors for the second consecutive year, after throwing for 3,899 yards and 39 TDs (league best) for a career-best 7.2 TD %. They had also just won their Divisional Round matchup against the San Francisco 49ers, 35-14. The Packers were HOT. The Carolina Panthers were a relatively new team, having played their first games just one season prior. They went 12-4 during the 1996 season, and stunned the league by beating the reigning champion Dallas Cowboys in the Divisional Round, 26-17. A trip to the Super Bowl was on the line, and the NFC’s representative would be either one of the NFL’s oldest franchises, or its newest. Key Moments The first quarter was relatively uneventful as the teams went back and forth with punts. Then: LB Sam Mills intercepted Brett Favre as he attempted to throw to WR Don Beebe. Snagging the ball at the 12-yard line, Mills nearly took this one to the house until he was brought down just short of the endzone. The Panthers promptly scored after this, and held a 7-0 lead. As the second quarter began, Brett Favre completed a 29-yard TD pass to RB Dorsey Levens, and things were all tied up again. The Panthers would go on to take the lead again with a FG, but the Packers responded during their next drive with a TD by WR Antonio Freeman which would put them back on top, 14-10. With 42 seconds left to respond before halftime, the Panthers immediately turned the ball over to CB Tyrone Williams. Then, Brett Favre did his thing, and led the Packers into FG territory with 23 and 25-yard passes to WRs Andre Rison and Antonio Freeman, respectively. K Chris Jacke made another FG, and the Packers led 17-10 at halftime. The Panthers were unable to get anything going in the second half, outside of a FG they made to end their first drive, and the Packers would go on to absolutely dominate. Jacke made two more FGs, and RB Edgar Bennett found the endzone, and when it was all said and done, the Packers won 30-13. The Outcome For the first time in nearly 30 years, the Green Bay Packers were going to the Super Bowl. After some massive plays by QB Brett Favre and his receivers, returner Desmond Howard set the record for the longest kickoff return in Super Bowl history at the time with a 99 yard return for a TD. The Green Bay Packers then won their first Super Bowl since 1967, when they beat the New England Patriots 35-21. Howard’s performance as a punt and kick returner earned him Super Bowl MVP honors, and he is the only special teamer to ever earn the award. The 4-3 Packers and 3-3 Panthers face off at Lambeau Field on Thursday Night Football at 8:15 ET/7:15 CT.
author: Sam Kallien

title: Packers Film Room: Woulda Coulda Shouldas in Week 7
summary: It’s underselling it a bit to say that the Green Bay Packers had a few missed opportunities this past weekend, but there were a couple big ones that stood out that I wanted to spend a bit of time with. I already looked at the field goal operation, so today we’re going to look at […]
full_text: (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s underselling it a bit to say that the Green Bay Packers had a few missed opportunities this past weekend, but there were a couple big ones that stood out that I wanted to spend a bit of time with. I already looked at the field goal operation , so today we’re going to look at a couple of passing plays: the 4th down to Golden in the flat and the incomplete pass to Jacobs just before the blocked field goal. Play 1: 4th & 4, 4:20 remaining in the 2nd quarter Packers are in 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR) in a Quad Bunch Nub formation (a 4×1 formation with three receivers in a bunch to one side and the TE in-line on the opposite side of the formation). It’s 11 personnel, but the formation is a bit funky, with Pierre Strong [22] (the RB) the inside man in bunch, and Matthew Golden [0] (a WR) in the backfield. The Packers don’t shift or motion: they walk to the line, Jordan Love [10] gives a quick assessment, then they quick-snap, trying to catch the Lions mid-communication (something they did quite a bit in this game). They’re running a version of Mesh, with Tucker Kraft [85] and Pierre Strong running dueling drag routes, crossing a couple yards down the field. This version is Mesh Sit, with Savion Williams [83] following a drag then pulling up on a Sit route in the middle of the field. Christian Watson [9] is running a corner route and Golden is running a flat route. Typically the read on Mesh would be the vertical route first (Watson on the corner), then the Mesh point (Kraft/Strong, Williams), then the flat if none of those are open (Golden). This version out of Quads is slightly different, in that part of the whole thing is for the bunch receivers to create a wall of commotion for the Flat route. It’s a bit like Mesh Traffic in that regard (we’ll get to that). That would make DJ Reed the most important player on the defense. Love is reading Reed at the snap. With the push from the bunch and the initial angle from Reed, it looks like he’s going to get caught in the wall, which would leave Golden wide open in the flat. Instead, Reed does a really nice job of avoiding contact and maintaining speed over the wall, firing off the hip of Watson and driving down on Golden. Nice rep by Reed. If Reed gets so much as a bump, this is a TD. If Love feels he’s able to wait a tick to throw this, he could see Reed breaking and move off. If that were the case, he could have potentially been able to find Strong on the backside. Unfortunately for Love, Strong would be the 5th read on this play, which would make it tough to work back over to him. There’s a version of this play I like a bit better. A small little change but creates just a bit more traffic to navigate for the defense. This would see Golden align away from the bunch and release through the line (typically through the B gap). We’ve seen the Packers run this a few times over the years. It doesn’t have quite the same pop if it’s a WR in the backfield, but it could still be enough to get the job done. It introduces a few more moving pieces for the offense (slightly longer to set up, hoping the o-line doesn’t get shoved back into the release point, etc.) but it’s a beautiful play. I am certainly not saying that this play absolutely would have worked, but it’s a slightly different take on the same idea. It’s also one of my favorite Mesh variants, so I will bring it up as often as I can. Play 2: 3rd & 5, 3:30 remaining in the 4th quarter Fast forward to the last offensive play of the game for the Packers. Game tied 17-17, facing 3rd & 5. They are – once again – in 11 personnel. Bunch right, RB aligned away from the bunch. The Lions are showing a single-high safety and a lot of bodies around the line. Kraft shifts wide before the snap, leaving a two-man stack of Watson and Golden just outside the right hash. They’re running a little shallow crossing concept between Golden and Kraft, while Watson runs a corner route over the top. On the left side, Josh Jacobs [8] motions out at the snap, giving him outside leverage on his defender. With the initial release of both Savion Williams [83] and Jacobs, it looks like they may be running Arches, a popular concept in this down and distance. Instead, Jacobs gives a little shake and releases vertically up the field, while Williams releases vertically to the inside. On this play, Jacobs would be the Alert (throw this at the top of the drop if given a specific look or simply don’t look at it at all after an initial assessment post-snap). The goal of concept is to work the concept on the right (look to Watson initially, then work to Golden/Kraft underneath) if the Lions rotate back to a two-high safety look after the snap. With the Lions staying in single-high – and Jacobs getting outside leverage on the motion – Love takes the vertical route to Jacobs. The Lions staying in single-high means there are more bodies around the line, making the shorter concept from Golden/Kraft pretty muddy. They had already hit Jacobs on a couple choice routes close to the line earlier in the game, so the defense likely had those in mind. Midway through the 2nd quarter they hit Jacobs on an Angle route on the Texas concept. Then, early in the 3rd, they hit him on an out route (and he scored a TD on it). Derrick Moore [8] is in good coverage down the field, but the hesitation from Jacobs at the assumed break point gives him the initial separation he needs. Love lofts the ball over the top, dropping it in the bucket. I believe Derrick Moore [8] may get a fingertip on this, but it hits Jacobs in both hands and he can’t bring it in. Not too different from the route he ran against the Broncos last year that ended in a TD. Except for the part where he caught the ball. That part was different, I guess. title: Green Bay Packers News: Packers’ running game continues to struggle
summary: The Packers cannot get their ground game in gear. They cannot run with MarShawn Lloyd. They cannot run with Chris Brooks. They cannot run with Pierre Strong. They cannot run with Kaleb Johnson, a healthy scratch this week despite the Packers giving up a draft pick for him. They can’t even run with Josh Jacobs, […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-OCTOBER 25: Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs (8) carries the ball under the pressure of the Detroit Lions linebacker Malcolm Rodriguez (44) during an NFL football game between the New York Jets and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Sunday, September 27, 2026 (Photo by Amy Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images The Packers cannot get their ground game in gear. They cannot run with MarShawn Lloyd. They cannot run with Chris Brooks. They cannot run with Pierre Strong. They cannot run with Kaleb Johnson, a healthy scratch this week despite the Packers giving up a draft pick for him. They can’t even run with Josh Jacobs, who returned from his not-suspension against the Lions to grind out 36 yards on 11 attempts. 10 of those 36 yards came on one carry, meaning he averaged a paltry 2.6 yards per attempt on his other runs. Not great! Will it ever get better? All signs point to no at this point, but who knows? The Packers’ 2026 season has been anything but predictable, and they’ve been able to figure out some of their issues on the fly. Maybe the ground game will miraculously improve. It feels like it would take a miracle at this point. Maybe Kevin Zeitler finally gets into the lineup and ignites a change in fortunes. Maybe Josh Jacobs discovers the fountain of youth. Maybe MarShawn Lloyd figures out how not to get lost between his backfield position and the line of scrimmage. Maybe Jordan Love turns into a dual-threat savant. A lot of things could maybe happen! I’m not hopeful, though. Even when the Packers have faced some of the league’s worst run defenses, they haven’t been able to get it going on the ground. They peaked at 86 rushing yards against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and that included 58 yards on two carries from Kaleb Johnson and Chris Brooks. Unless the Packers can figure out a way to rip off a couple of big runs — or maybe fall into one by accident — it’s hard to see a big week of rushing output on the horizon this year. But who knows? Anything can happen. Maybe the real ground game has yet to be discovered. title: The Day After the Day After: Houston Texans fall to the New York Giants of New Jersey 27-21
summary: The Day After the Day After…when the raw, immediate emotions from the aftermath of a game diminish into the realm of clarity and the proverbial (or literal) hangover no longer haunts the mind. With that, a review of Week 7 Penalties…YIKES!!! 10 Penalties for 80 yards. After seeing the Giants rush for 188 yards, that […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - OCTOBER 25: Cam Skattebo #44 of the New York Giants celebrates a touchdown during the fourth quarter against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Kenneth Richmond/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Day After the Day After…when the raw, immediate emotions from the aftermath of a game diminish into the realm of clarity and the proverbial (or literal) hangover no longer haunts the mind. With that, a review of Week 7 Penalties…YIKES!!! 10 Penalties for 80 yards. After seeing the Giants rush for 188 yards, that is the next number that jumps out at you reading the box score. This game was in Houston, with an experienced team, facing a Giants team that hadn’t looked all that great in their last two games. Of Houston’s flags, 4 were of the mental mistake variety (3 x False Starts, 1 x Encroachment). Additionally, 3 of the penalties were offensive holding, which cost Houston 31 yards of rushing offense. The consistent lack of discipline points the finger squarely at the coaching staff. This with at least 3 flags declined, so the flag numbers could have been even worse. Bad enough when this was in Year 1 with a relatively young team. In Year 4 of the Ryans regime, with an experienced team, and at home…inexcusable, and to borrow the McClain catchphrase “pathetic”. If the Defensive Line can’t take control.. .The driving force for Houston’s defense is the defensive line. With Danielle Hunter and Will Anderson Jr., the theory is that they should be enough to disrupt an offensive line, with the resulting impact aided the rest of the defense. However, the Giants offensive line basically negated their impact. Will Anderson Jr was a practical non-factor. While Houston sacked McCarthy 3 times, only one of those sacks came from the defensive line. Half of that total (1.5), came from defensive backs blitzing, as the final 0.5 of a sack came from a blitzing LB. If you need your defensive backfield be the catalyst of getting pressure/sacks, then this defensive scheme is not having a great day. Additionally, the Texans came into this game with a top 5 rushing defense in yards allowed/game. However, the defensive interior could not lock down the Giants’ rushing attack, especially in the 4th quarter and OT, when Houston surrendered 101 yards on the ground alone. Went from allowing less than 82 yards/game to now allowing over 98 yards/game on the ground. Home is not where the heart is: Under Ryans, the Texans entered the 2026-7 season with an 18-8 home record (2-0 in playoff games). In the previous three seasons, Houston lost no more than 3 games at home in a season. They’ve already exceeded that total this year. At best, Houston will end the season at 4-4 at home…at best. They still get all three division rivals at home, along with the Ravens, so there is potential for the home crowd to get something for their money. This will be Houston’s worst home record since 2022 (0-7-1), but unlike that time, Houston should be able to win at least one home game…right? THE CRITICAL PLAY: 8:23 in OT; NYG Ball @ NYG 28; 2nd and 1; RB Cam Skattebo 42-yard run up the middle. Perhaps it was inevitable. The Texans had momentum coming into the extra frame, having just tied the game, as well as just missing out on a possible INT ball on the Giants’ final regulation drive. However, the Texans went a quick 3-and-out, punting the ball back to the Giants, who set up shop at their 19-yard line. A quick McCarthy pass got the Giants to a favorable 2nd and 1. The Giants lined up in a run formation, and McCarthy went with the handoff to Skattebo. The Giants line, aided by FB/TE Ricard, who lined up as the 2nd TE on the right side of a 3-TE set on the Giants’ right side of the line, blasted through the defensive front of the Texans. The Texans did not have a body covering the second level beyond the DL, and Skattebo had perhaps the best running lane of his pro career. From there, it was a foot race between Skattebo and the Texans’ secondary. Lassiter finally brought him down, but by then, the Giants were well within FG range. Even with their struggling kicker, it is hard to imagine that they would miss. Since Houston busted on its first OT possession, the Giants were likely going to win. Singletary’s nifty 30-yard run on the next play resolved the questions about how the Giants would clinch. FUN WITH NUMBERS: 2-0: JJ McCarthy’s record at NRG/Reliant Stadium: Combining his college and pro career, he’s played two games in Houston. This past Sunday, and when he was the starting QB for Michigan when they won the 2024 National Championship over Washington. Still has never thrown at TD in Houston, but he’ll take the combined 30 for 46 for 392 yards with no INTs and no loses. 7: Number of NFL teams since 2002 that started 2-5 and made the playoffs: If you still hold out hope, you can look to this. One of those was the 2015 Texans, who started 1-4 and 2-5, and managed to win the AFC South with a 9-7 record. They hosted another team that season (Kansas City) who also started 2-5. It did not go well . GAME BALLS: WR Xavier Hutchinson: All of the WRs on the Texans’ roster, and the most versatile one in this game ended up being Xavier Hutchinson. On the final drive, he ran for a 1st down on a jet sweep-type play, was slated to throw a WR pass and then caught the game-tying TD pass. Go figure. His final line: 3 receptions for 17 yards and 1 TD, 2 rushes for 12 yards, 3 kickoff returns for 74 yards. WR Tank Dell: Not bad when your first game action in almost 2 years after a devastating injury saw you take a pass you weren’t the primary for 43 yards to set up a tying score late in the 1st half. Also sparked the 4th quarter tying drive with his 14-yard punt return. Final line: 1 reception for 43 yards, 1 rush for 2 yards, 1 punt return for 14 yards. Giants FB/TE Patrick Ricard: He followed Harbaugh from Baltimore to East Rutherford. Good pickup. He logged no stats in the standard box score, but his blocking from the FB and the TE positions sprang the three biggest runs of the game for the Giants: the fake tush-push 3rd Down run from Skattebo for 19 yards, and the two big runs in OT combining for 72 yards and clinching the win. This game needs to lead off his future contract negotiations. SHOULD BE FORCED TO LISTEN TO JOHN MCCLAIN RAMBLE ON ABOUT THE BAYLOR COACHING SEARCH WHILE DROPPING HIS TRADEMARK “PATHETIC” DESCRIPTION ABOUT THE TEXANS ON REPEAT ALL WEEK. DC Matt Burke/Defensive Backs Coach Dino Vasso. Words I would not have uttered to start the year, but this pair might be sacked come Black Monday. The secondary once again was picked apart, this time by a known mercurial QB. Yes, Pitre and Blankenship were out for this game, but the communication between DBs in respective zone coverages seemed lacking, with the Giants able to rack up some explosive plays in the Texans’ defensive backfield. It is far too late in the season to be suffering comms break-downs. Throw in a defensive line that could not take advantage of a newish QB and LBs that allowed themselves to be shut down by Giants’ blockers, and you have a recipe for what you saw Sunday. Yes, Ryans is calling the plays, but whatever is going on in practice is either not translating onto the field (bad), or the performances from practice are translating to what is happening on the field (worse). OC Nick Caley/HC DeMeco Ryans :Actually, let’s put the offensive coaches as well as the overall coaching staff on this one. The offense was a bit too stubborn trying to get Marks going with the running game when turning Stroud loose might have worked out better, even given some of the pressure the Giants put on him. Ryans, well, this game had all the hallmarks of a trap game (back from big overseas win with a bye week coming), and he let the team step right into it without hesitation. title: It may be hard to stomach but this is exactly what the Colts need to do
summary: Fires can be good, at least in the sense of forest fires. No one wants to see a fire raging out of control and wreaking havoc, but a fire, especially a controlled or non-life-threatening one, is essential. A fire removes dead debris and makes way for new life. It encourages diversity and the chance for […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 25: DeForest Buckner #99 of the Indianapolis Colts takes the field before the game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Fires can be good, at least in the sense of forest fires. No one wants to see a fire raging out of control and wreaking havoc, but a fire, especially a controlled or non-life-threatening one, is essential. A fire removes dead debris and makes way for new life. It encourages diversity and the chance for new opportunities for different species to thrive. The Indianapolis Colts are experiencing their own version of a controlled burn, and while it may be painful to witness, it is exactly what’s needed. Two pillars of the team are gone. Captains Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner have new teams. No, these men aren’t “dead debris” but they are older players with expiring deals. For this metaphor, we will consider them to be the underbrush that needs to be parted with to make room for new growth. They probably won’t be the last either as Grover Stewart, Jonathan Taylor, Josh Downs, and others are floating around the rumor mill as trade candidates. If all of those players leave, the Colts will resemble a burned-out forest, dead and a shell of its former self. That’s when the magic can happen, though. New players can rise to take their place. Those that might not have gotten much of a shot will get to demonstrate what they can do now that the path has been cleared. Through the restocking of draft picks, the new growth begins as well. Fresh faces and an infusion of young talent can start to take root and stand where the mighty pines once did. There is no guarantee that it all works out and the forest returns to its mighty glory. That could take several burns and restarts. What is guaranteed is that this current iteration of the Colts isn’t going anywhere. By trading the men they have, the Colts are accomplishing two things: they are providing cherished players an environment in which to thrive and are reaping draft capital to help restore what has been missing in this organization. The moves have been twofold so far and completely necessary. The top canopy of the forest is gone. When Chris Ballard was fired, it left the whole forest exposed. The Colts looked around and realized how desperately they needed a refresh. When the fire is calculated and controlled, it is most effective. Fans have to trust the Irsays to keep it that way, and if they do, this organization can reap the benefits. Watching long-time players leave is tough, but removing the old and restarting with new can bring a world of possibilities. The fire itself isn’t usually pleasant, but for the Colts, this one is essential to their future.
