title: Reaction from Colts trading franchise trench pillars: Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner during tough day
summary: The Indianapolis Colts made two significant moves today by trading offensive guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner—both of whom were longtime veteran leaders for the franchise, team captains, and even have their player banners prominently displayed on two of the four outside corners of Lucas Oil Stadium. Each Pro Bowl lineman was a […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - OCTOBER 12: Indianapolis Colts guard Quenton Nelson (56) warms up prior to the start of an NFL game between the Indianapolis Colts and the Arizona Cardinals on October 12, 2025 at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis, IN (Photo by Jeffrey Brown/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts made two significant moves today by trading offensive guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner—both of whom were longtime veteran leaders for the franchise, team captains, and even have their player banners prominently displayed on two of the four outside corners of Lucas Oil Stadium. Each Pro Bowl lineman was a cornerstone in the middle of their respective line’s trenches and were consistently among their unit’s best players in Indianapolis during their standout tenures. It was a tough day for the franchise, seeing highly regarded leaders and franchise mainstays leave their locker room for the final time, but one, that at least in some regards, was arguably necessary in the hopes of finding better days ahead for the Horseshoe. Let’s take a look at each trade and recap my initial reaction: Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks Trade Return: Seahawks’ 2027 3rd round pick and 2028 5th round pick This move wasn’t totally unexpected given where the Colts sit at 2-5, and much closer to now a full-on rebuild than title contention, but I’m a little surprised that: 1) Big Q was the first domino to fall regarding the fire sale, and 2) that Indianapolis moved him despite only receiving a 2027 3rd round pick and a future 4th rounder. Yes, I know that the 3rd round pick was “ unprecedented value for a Pro Bowl guard ,” but I just don’t see that return being all that meaningful for a perennial NFL All-Pro guard, future Hall of Famer, and homegrown Colts’ Ring of Honor candidate, who projects to have at least 3-4 elite years of football left in him at starting left guard. The Colts would be lucky to find a high-impact starter with a late 3rd round pick (as Seattle should be pretty good for the remainder of this season), that would match the 3-4 seasons of Hall of Fame guard play they would’ve received had they just kept Nelson on a lucrative, long-term deal extension that would’ve set the market again. Even when Nelson’s athleticism and playing strength dips in his early thirties, his technique and fundamentals are so impeccable that he’d still theoretically be a great technician at the guard position. We’ve seen other future Hall of Fame guards age rather gracefully until their mid-thirties too. Not saying it’s an exact science for Nelson by any means, but I don’t see any reason why he can’t have at least a handful of high level years still left in him. As recently as last week, Nelson indicated publicly that he loved being a Colt , so unless that stance changed internally, and he explicitly told the team’s brass behind closed doors that he wanted to be traded or play for a title contender during his remaining playing career prime, then I don’t see why: 1) Indianapolis rushed to trade him with time still left before the NFL’s upcoming November 10th deadline, and 2) Traded him for the Seattle package they ultimately decided upon (* although there is a report that the Colts actually took less from Seattle per Nelson’s choice, who they wanted to do right by, over a possible trade with Washington ). Even if the Colts couldn’t work out a long-term contract extension with Nelson, they still had the franchise tag as leverage, so if the latter didn’t sign the tag with Indianapolis, then he essentially wouldn’t play in 2027. For what it’s worth, I never got the indication that Nelson didn’t want to remain a Colt long-term publicly, so it seemed more of a matter that Indianapolis didn’t want to pay him top guard money during a rebuild that will realistically take at least 2-3 years, and were still looking to recoup lost draft capital from last year’s Sauce Gardner deadline deal that also cost the Colts their 2027 first round pick. I understand the opposite perspective, but for me, even a young and rebuilding team like the Colts next offseason and for the next few seasons, realistically need a few elite, well-respected veterans in that locker room to establish a culture of leadership, work ethic, and accountability to emulate and develop in. You can cite Nelson’s win-loss record all you want, but QB wins isn’t a meaningful stat, much less for an offensive guard’s wins or losses. Former Detroit Lions legends and Hall of Famers Barry Sanders and wideout Calvin Johnson weren’t any less of genuinely great players or valuable because they consistently played on bad teams. I mean just look at Detroit castoff Matthew Stafford, who left the Lions to later become a Super Bowl Champion and NFL MVP with the LA Rams. Was he not valuable or a great player just because his teams largely stunk? Say what you want, but Nelson is a true ‘Horseshoe guy,’ who played the game the right way and brought it every day. He may not have been the most vocal leader, but I certainly think he led by example both on and off the field. It seemed like he genuinely loved being a Colt, unless those conversations were much different privately. As an Evansville, Indiana, native, I look at someone like Don Mattingly with the New York Yankees, who while never won a playoff series or World Series with the pinstripes was a beloved veteran leader later on in his career. His #23 is immortalized in Yankee Stadium’s monument park. Off the field, Mattingly, along with new manager Buck Showalter, were instrumental in setting up the winning culture of that clubhouse that helped develop their young core to eventually become a dynasty during the 90’s and early 2000’s . I fully understand moving a number of veterans including DeForest Buckner, and perhaps others such as Jonathan Taylor or Grover Stewart, but I would’ve kept Nelson as a Colt for life or at least, his remaining playing career prime. It’s invaluable to keep a highly respected veteran leader or two in that locker room. I think he’s one of the veteran pillars that the Colts should’ve kept to help bridge the next era, much like Reggie Wayne, Robert Mathis, and Adam Vinatieri did for the the transition from Peyton Manning to Andrew Luck. Alas, Nelson is somewhat shockingly no longer a Colt and will take his Canton-bound career to the Pacific Northwest to play for a legitimate Super Bowl contender again, who should be much improved with his latest big addition. DeForest Buckner Back to the 49ers Trade Return: 49ers 2027 4th round pick I was hoping the return would be closer to at least a 2027 3rd round pick, but this was the move that was always the most likely headed into this week following Sunday’s latest loss in Minnesota and the team reeling. In his recent post-game comments, Buckner seemed increasingly frustrated with the Colts persistent losing ways and was understandably rather non-committal about his football future here going forward, as a pending free agent. Wanting to win now, it didn’t seem like he had any intention of re-signing in Indianapolis and at his football age, he wasn’t a serious candidate to be considered for the Colts franchise tag this upcoming offseason. Coming off offseason neck surgery and at 32-years-old, Buckner probably has maybe one or two great seasons left in him (and maybe in his entire playing career), so it made sense for the Colts to do right by Buckner and send him back to where it all started in San Francisco to seriously compete for a Super Bowl title again. The breakout campaign of pending free agent defensive tackle Ade Adebawore at 25-years-old can certainly help fill some of the sizable shoes left by Buckner in the Colts interior defensive line for the remainder of the 2026 campaign, but Indianapolis needs to use some of this newly found cap savings to lock up Tomi long-term. Similarly to Nelson, Buckner embodied being a true ‘Horseshoe guy,’ with his…

title: BREAKING: Colts trade DeForest Buckner back to San Francisco 49ers for fourth-round pick
summary: The Indianapolis Colts are continuing their roster overhaul, trading three-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle DeForest Buckner to the San Francisco 49ers in exchange for a 2027 fourth-round pick, according to NFL insider Tom Pelissero. The move comes just hours after Indianapolis traded eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks for a 2027 […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - SEPTEMBER 27: Indianapolis Colts defensive tackle DeForest Buckner (99) reacts after the NFL game between the Houston Texans and the Indianapolis Colts on September 27, 2026, at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Allio/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts are continuing their roster overhaul, trading three-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle DeForest Buckner to the San Francisco 49ers in exchange for a 2027 fourth-round pick, according to NFL insider Tom Pelissero. The move comes just hours after Indianapolis traded eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round selection. With the Colts sitting at 2-5 and having lost three consecutive games, the organization appears to be fully embracing its role as a seller ahead of the November 10 trade deadline. For Buckner, the trade represents a reunion with the organization that originally selected him seventh overall in the 2016 NFL Draft. He spent his first four seasons in San Francisco, developing into one of the league’s premier interior defensive linemen and helping the 49ers reach Super Bowl LIV following the 2019 season. Indianapolis acquired Buckner in March 2020 in exchange for the 13th overall pick in that year’s draft, immediately signing him to a four-year, $84 million extension. The move was one of the most significant acquisitions of former general manager Chris Ballard’s tenure and provided the Colts with an established defensive star who would become the centerpiece of their defensive line for more than six seasons. Buckner certainly lived up to expectations individually. He earned First-Team All-Pro honors during his first season in Indianapolis, recording 9.5 sacks and establishing himself as one of the most disruptive interior defenders in football. He followed that performance with several more productive seasons, earning additional Pro Bowl selections in 2021 and 2023 while consistently providing the Colts with a reliable pass-rushing presence. Even at 32 years old, Buckner has shown few signs of slowing down. Through seven games in 2026, he has recorded 31 tackles, four sacks, eight quarterback hits and three passes defended, remaining one of the team’s most productive defensive players despite its struggles throughout the season. However, with Buckner playing out the final year of his contract and Indianapolis potentially entering a rebuilding period, retaining him for the remainder of the season became increasingly difficult to justify. Following the Colts’ embarrassing loss to the previously winless Tennessee Titans, Buckner openly expressed his frustration with the organization’s continued struggles. After more than six seasons in Indianapolis without sustained postseason success, an opportunity to return to San Francisco and compete for a championship could be beneficial for both sides. He showed his frustration again after the Vikings loss. DeForest Buckner on his current level of frustration, via @RomeovilleKid : "I don’t know. How about you guess. Yeah, I’m frustrated. Same thing, we lost." pic.twitter.com/2P3VfPVkaW — Underdog NFL (@UnderdogNFL) October 25, 2026 In my recent evaluation of Buckner’s trade value , I projected that Indianapolis could realistically receive a 2027 fourth-round pick for the veteran defensive tackle, the exact compensation the Colts ultimately acquired. San Francisco was also among the potential destinations identified, given its need for additional defensive line help and Buckner’s previous connection to the organization. Although a fourth-round selection might appear underwhelming for a player of Buckner’s caliber, his age and expiring contract significantly limited his market value. The Colts also faced the possibility of losing him in free agency without receiving any guaranteed compensation, making the opportunity to secure a draft pick in 2027 considerably more appealing. His departure also creates an opportunity for Adetomiwa Adebawore, who has shown encouraging development along Indianapolis’ defensive line. The former fourth-round selection recorded two sacks against Minnesota on Sunday and could receive a significantly larger role over the remainder of the season as the Colts evaluate their younger players. For San Francisco, Buckner provides an established interior pass rusher who could immediately strengthen its defensive front. The 49ers have dealt with injuries throughout their defense, including the loss of Nick Bosa, and bringing back a familiar face with Buckner’s experience and production gives the organization another proven weapon as it pursues a playoff berth. Meanwhile, the Colts have now acquired three additional draft selections through their trades of Nelson and Buckner, including two picks in 2027. With Indianapolis already without its first-round selection next year following the Sauce Gardner trade, replenishing draft capital has become increasingly important for a franchise preparing for significant organizational changes. Buckner’s departure also raises questions about which veterans could be moved next, particularly Jonathan Taylor, Josh Downs and Grover Stewart, whose names have surfaced in trade discussions over the past several days. The Colts have made their intentions increasingly clear. Less than two weeks after firing Ballard, Indianapolis has already parted ways with two of its most accomplished players, and there may be more changes ahead before the deadline.
author: Andrew Aziz

title: BREAKING: Colts trade All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson to Seattle Seahawks
summary: The Indianapolis Colts have officially begun selling ahead of the November 10 NFL trade deadline, sending eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks in exchange for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round selection, according to ESPN’s Adam Schefter and NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport. The move comes just over a week […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - AUGUST 29: Indianapolis Colts guard Quenton Nelson (56) during a NFL preseason game between the Detroit Lions and the Indianapolis Colts on August 29, 2026 at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis, IN. (Photo by Jeffrey Brown/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts have officially begun selling ahead of the November 10 NFL trade deadline, sending eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks in exchange for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round selection, according to ESPN’s Adam Schefter and NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport. Compensation update; The Seahawks are sending a 2027 third-round pick and 2028 fifth-round round pick to the Colts in exchange for Quenton Nelson. https://t.co/17B0bR47yV — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) October 27, 2026 The move comes just over a week after owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon fired general manager Chris Ballard following the team’s embarrassing loss to the Tennessee Titans. Indianapolis has since fallen to 2-5 after another disappointing defeat against the Minnesota Vikings, leaving the organization in a difficult position as it considers the future of several established veterans. Nelson, 30, was selected sixth overall by the Colts in the 2018 NFL Draft and quickly established himself as one of the league’s premier offensive linemen. He earned First-Team All-Pro honors in each of his first three seasons and has since accumulated eight consecutive Pro Bowl selections and six total All-Pro honors, putting together a résumé that could eventually earn him a place in the Pro Football Hall of Fame. Despite his many years in the league, Nelson has shown virtually no signs of slowing down. He currently holds an 86.6 overall grade from Pro Football Focus, ranking third among qualifying guards, while allowing just six quarterback pressures and no sacks through seven games this season. His consistency and physicality have made him one of the most dependable players on the Colts’ roster throughout his career, and replacing his production will be an enormous challenge. However, Nelson was playing out the final year of the four-year, $80 million extension he signed in 2022, making him an unrestricted free agent following the season. With Indianapolis seemingly approaching another organizational rebuild, the front office ultimately decided to secure draft capital rather than risk losing him for potentially nothing in free agency. Interestingly, in my recent analysis of Nelson’s trade value , I projected that the Colts could realistically receive a third-round selection in exchange for their All-Pro guard. While a second-round pick would have been a more attractive return, the market for veteran interior offensive linemen has historically been relatively modest, as demonstrated by Kansas City’s decision to trade Joe Thuney to Chicago for a fourth-round pick in 2025. Indianapolis ultimately received slightly more than that projection with the additional fifth-round selection in 2028, although the compensation still feels relatively underwhelming for a player of Nelson’s caliber. The implications extend well beyond the departure of one offensive lineman. Nelson has been instrumental in Jonathan Taylor’s success throughout his career, providing elite run blocking on the left side of an offensive line that has consistently ranked among the team’s strongest position groups. Losing him will place additional pressure on Taylor and an offense that has already struggled considerably this season. There is also the question of who replaces Nelson at left guard. Indianapolis has several young offensive linemen on its roster, including Matt Goncalves, Dalton Tucker and Jalen Farmer, but none offers anything close to the reliability and production Nelson provided over the past nine seasons. The Colts will now have to reshuffle their offensive line while attempting to navigate the remainder of an increasingly disappointing campaign. For Seattle, the move represents a significant addition to an offensive line that has struggled to consistently protect quarterback Sam Darnold and establish an effective running game. Nelson immediately becomes one of the team’s most accomplished offensive players and could provide a substantial boost as the Seahawks attempt to defend their Super Bowl title. The trade also raises questions about what comes next for Indianapolis. DeForest Buckner, Grover Stewart and Jonathan Taylor have all been mentioned as potential trade candidates, and Nelson’s departure suggests the organization is increasingly willing to part with established players in exchange for future assets. With the Colts already without their 2027 first-round pick following last season’s blockbuster acquisition of Sauce Gardner, replenishing their draft capital has become particularly important. However, losing one of the best players in franchise history for a third- and fifth-round selection is a difficult price to pay, even if the move makes sense from a long-term roster-building perspective. Nelson leaves Indianapolis as one of the greatest offensive linemen in franchise history, and his departure may ultimately represent the beginning of a much larger roster overhaul as the Colts look to establish a new direction following the Ballard era.
author: Andrew Aziz

title: Under pressure, the Colts are collapsing
summary: Great things can come from pressure. You need enough pressure to make diamonds, and in the sports world, pressure makes for the greatest players and moments. When the stakes rise and the pressure increases, some meet the challenge and others collapse under the weight. The Indianapolis Colts are proving they subscribe to the latter. The […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 25: Blake Cashman #51 of the Minnesota Vikings sacks Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts in the second quarter at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. The Vikings defeated the Colts 16-10. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images Great things can come from pressure. You need enough pressure to make diamonds, and in the sports world, pressure makes for the greatest players and moments. When the stakes rise and the pressure increases, some meet the challenge and others collapse under the weight. The Indianapolis Colts are proving they subscribe to the latter. The pressure was evident all afternoon against the Vikings. Brian Flores doesn’t sit back in Cover-2 and bend but not break. Flores might as well be nicknamed the “Instapot” based on the amount of pressure he builds on opposing offenses week in and week out. The Vikings blitzed 85.2% of Daniel Jones’ dropbacks. That’s the highest rate since it started being tracked. Talk about pressure. The Colts didn’t turn into diamonds, though. Four sacks and 108 yards from the quarterback was the result. The line couldn’t hold up, and the ball didn’t go where it needed to enough to win. Not only did the Colts not meet the challenge of the physical pressure, they didn’t handle the atmospheric pressure either; the pressure that is palpable as the game winds on and possessions become gold. Late in the third, with a chance to extend the lead, Spencer Shrader missed a long field goal. Then, to tie, he missed again. All hope wasn’t lost as the Colts had the ball needing a touchdown and extra point to take the lead. Jones buckled and threw a game-clinching interception instead. This happened while the beads of sweat formed on Shane Steichen’s forehead as he struggled to maintain control. The result was another early lead, followed by the weight of pressure finishing the Colts off. The theme has been consistent. How many times have the Colts been the first team to score a touchdown? How many times has this team wilted as the pressure grew? The Vikings were the perfect embodiment of the type of pressure the Colts have faced. A blitz is coming every single day. “Find a Way” is creating pressure, and as the games get tight, the Colts aren’t rising to the occasion. Pressure can make diamonds. It can also be incredibly destructive. The Colts are finding out how destructive it can be.
author: Jon Spradley

title: Horsepower or Horseplay? Highlighting Colts’ individual performances from Week 7
summary: The Indianapolis Colts (2-5) fell to the Minnesota Vikings (6-0), 16-10, and now have a three game losing streak, with whatever slim playoff hopes they had quickly evaporating in what’s shaping up to be another lost season. There’s no need to relive another tough loss in great detail by any means, but I did want […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 25: Dallas Turner #15 and Harrison Smith #22 of the Minnesota Vikings sack Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts in the second quarter at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts (2-5) fell to the Minnesota Vikings (6-0), 16-10, and now have a three game losing streak, with whatever slim playoff hopes they had quickly evaporating in what’s shaping up to be another lost season. There’s no need to relive another tough loss in great detail by any means, but I did want to highlight a few of the individual performances from Sunday—both the positive and negative: Horsepower Colts Running Game: Would’ve put Jonathan Taylor here individually, but after a few pass blocking gaffes that led to big plays by the Vikings defense, I’ll go with the Indianapolis ground game collectively instead and give kudos to their offensive linemen up front as well. Taylor rushed for 95 total rushing yards and a touchdown on 18 carries, averaging 5.3 yards per carry. He had the Colts lone big offensive play of the day, with his opening drive 38-yard touchdown run . DT Ade Adebawore: The Colts rotational defensive tackle continues to have a breakout 2026 campaign, and was incredibly disruptive in this one with 5 tackles, 2 tackles for loss, 2.0 sacks, 2 QB hits, 5 QB pressures and a pass defensed. It may hurt to lose DeForest Buckner in an imminent trade before deadline day, but Adebawore may help Colts fans sleep a little easier filling D-Fo’s rather large shoes for the remainder of this increasingly disappointing season. Indianapolis needs to lock Adebawore up long-term. S AJ Haulcy: There’s been a lot of growing pains for the Colts’ 3rd round safety, who’s been lost in coverage at times with blown assignments. He stood out in run defense (with a season high +78.1 run defense grade) and led the Colts with 9 tackles (5 solo) in this one. Hopefully, Haulcy is starting to find his groove in the backend of the secondary and get past that initial rookie learning curve. He’s playing better ball. Horseplay Daniel Jones: No one’s expecting Jones to be Superman here, but he at least has to provide the Colts consistently average to good starting quarterback play out there if they’re going to win another game this year. Head coach Brian Flores’ dominant Vikings defense blitzed the heck out of Jones , with great success the majority of the time. An issue that’s plagued Jones since around midseason of last year. Specifically, Jones completed 13 of his 22 pass attempts for a minuscule 4.9 yards per completion average, amassing just 108 total passing yards and the game-sealing interception with 1:15 left in regulation. Colts Edge Rush: Fill in cornerback Cam Taylor-Britt had more sacks than any Colts edge rusher in this one. This has been a season long issue, but can we please get consistent pressure from any edge? Buehler? Spencer Shrader: Look, Shrader’s been a great special teams story so far this year, reclaiming his Colts kicking job after a devastating season-ending 2025 knee injury and going a perfect 19-19 from field goal range up until Week 7’s dud. That being said, in a game where the Colts lost by just six points, his misses of 56 yards and 48 yards in the second half loomed large and proved to be the difference in tying this one up.
author: Luke Schultheis

title: Jaguars bye week staff roundtable: Travis Hunter is about to go nuclear
summary: Welcome to Big Cat Country’s staff roundtable! This week, we’re discussing big-picture topics on the Jacksonville Jaguars as they come out of their Week 7 bye. Question 1: It’s rarely constructive to assign blame for a narrow loss from the past. That said… were there any issues from Jacksonville’s Week 6 loss that you fear […]
full_text: Sep 27, 2026; Jacksonville, Florida, USA; Jacksonville Jaguars wide receiver Travis Hunter (12) celebrates after an interception during the second quarter against the New England Patriots at EverBank Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Morgan Tencza-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Welcome to Big Cat Country’s staff roundtable! This week, we’re discussing big-picture topics on the Jacksonville Jaguars as they come out of their Week 7 bye. Question 1: It’s rarely constructive to assign blame for a narrow loss from the past. That said… were there any issues from Jacksonville’s Week 6 loss that you fear could rear its ugly head again in close games later this season? Dillon Appleman : I’ve said it in earlier roundtables, but the defense’s inability to get a stop when it absolutely has to is becoming a real problem. Both of this year’s losses ended with the opposing offense taking the ball and finishing the game. We were a half yard away against Cincy from making it three, and eight seconds away against Philly from making it four. Right now Travis Hunter feels like the only guy consistently making impact plays in the big moments, and as great as he is, one player can’t carry that load. I think a certain expensive pass rush duo needs to start showing up when the game is on the line. If that doesn’t change, it’ll bite us again in a playoff-caliber game. Travis Holmes : I truly believe the Houston Texans are simply a bad matchup for the Jacksonville Jaguars, primarily because they understand the many ways to stress both the Jacksonville offense and defense. You never quite know whether Houston will have a dominant day defensively or offensively, but one thing seems clear: The Texans will find a weakness to exploit, largely because of the extensive history between these two teams. With that said, the Jaguars’ secondary in explosive passing situations and their run defense against jumbo personnel are two areas where I believe other teams will take notice and look to attack in future matchups. Gus Logue : I think Jacksonville’s playcallers are still learning how to manage big-time games. Liam Coen was actually great against Houston, but he had some silly calls against Philadelphia and got out-schemed against Denver. In the Texans game, he trusted Cam Little to make a 60-yard field goal AND his defense to stop a red-hot C.J. Stroud instead of his own quarterback to convert a 4th-and-4 to win the game. As for Campanile, he could’ve simplified his calls after his starting safeties went down with injuries against Houston, and his defense sure doesn’t feel trustworthy late in games. Henry Zimmer : I think the secondary not only getting thrown on a bunch, but the overall health of the unit, is an issue. If that group doesn’t get healthy at the safety position, the Jags could be in trouble. The lack of pass rush adds to more time. More time leads to more completions. And if you don’t even have your starters out there, it only cycles into more bad stuff happening. Health in the secondary is a quiet, but very real, issue. Question 2: The Jaguars put themselves in a good spot by going 4-2 over the toughest part of their schedule. What aspect of the team are you most excited to see after the bye week? Dillon : I’m most excited to see this team play cleaner football, because I’m certain that’s coming. Getting to 4-2 through the toughest stretch of the schedule on inconsistent play is a great sign, especially with how up and down the season has been on both sides of the ball: sloppy stretches, a ton of penalties, and too many empty red zone trips. Teams that win through that kind of mess tend to tighten up as the year goes on, and that’s exactly what happened during last year’s playoff push. I fully expect a much more consistent product by season’s end. Travis : The looming return of rotational edge rusher BJ Green is something I’m looking forward to over the coming weeks. With the Jacksonville defense still struggling to find its footing, particularly when it comes to generating a consistent pass rush, Green could be the final puzzle piece capable of moving the needle in that area. If he’s unable to help this rush group, in the immortal words of Vic Ketchman, “Help isn’t on the way.” Gus : I’ll say it: Travis freakin’ Hunter! His Week 7 performance was so, so encouraging. It took him 13 NFL games to record his first 1 TD/1 INT game — something only two other players have done since the 1970 merger — and it wasn’t just the fact that he did it. It was how he did it. Hunter shadowed Nico Collins and fooled C.J. Stroud into throwing a redzone interception by purposefully stumbling in man coverage. (Guess he must’ve learned a thing or two from his former Hall of Fame head coach.) And on the other side of the ball, Liam Coen unleashed him in the closest thing we’ve seen to Cooper Kupp/Puka Nacua/Chris Godwin usage in Jacksonville. Each of his 4 targets were big-boy designer looks, a notable step up from the basic RPO packages Hunter was used in just a few weeks ago. He’s arrived. Henry : Who would have guessed we would even be slightly complaining about a 4-2 start heading into the bye?! The offense has been really exciting and I have been impressed with the aggressive running ability of Bhayshul Tuten and Chris Rodriguez Jr. I want to see more of them popping pads against defenders and hopefully the Jags getting a 100-yard rusher in a game. Question 3: Should the Jaguars deal Brian Thomas Jr. to the highest bidder, or are you not ready for him to leave Jacksonville? Are there any other moves you’d like to see the Jaguars make (or not make) ahead of the Nov. 10 trade deadline? Dillon : I flip back and forth on this one. The depth of the receiver room is a huge strength, because defenses can’t key on any one guy without the rest making them pay. But it’s been so bad for BTJ that I don’t think teams even respect his speed anymore, which is the one move left in his bag, and if the Jags are going to get anything of substance for him, it’s going to be in-season, so I can understand a deal. As for other moves, a veteran ball-hawking safety like Jessie Bates really stands out to me, or getting Quenton Nelson on a one-year rental for a Super Bowl push would be awesome too. Travis : I feel the Brian Thomas Jr. saga may have run its course in Jacksonville. With Josh Cameron and Travis Hunter already in the building, the Jaguars would be wise to listen to offers from the highest bidder. That is especially true if they believe they can secure a second-round pick or better for the former Offensive Rookie of the Year finalist. However, Jacksonville doesn’t have to trade him. With BTJ still under contract through next season and the team holding his fifth-year option, the Jaguars could choose to keep him through the offseason before making a decision. As for additional moves, I believe Jacksonville would be wise to explore potential trades for defensive tackles Zach Sieler of the Miami Dolphins or Daron Payne of the Washington Commanders. Gus : I suggested Jacksonville deal Thomas a few weeks ago , before his trade value plummeted even further. He has not caught a football since that article was published. I still think Jaguars should deal him to the highest bidder, though. Pretty much anything they could get in a trade would probably be more valuable than the 0.1 EPA/target Thomas has provided Jacksonville’s offense. (That figure ranks 82nd among 131 receivers this season, between 34-year-old Keenan Allen and 31-year-old Calvin Ridley.) Thomas has continued to underwhelm, to put it politely, but the real reason that Jacksonville could finally pull the trigger is the blossoming of Josh Cameron and Travis Hunter. Henry : If there are any bidders for BTJ, you have to listen. We have now seen two explosive spurts on offense from Travis Hunter and the emergence of Josh Cameron. Aside from the idea of BTJ’s ability that defenses may fear, what is he providing? If the Jags can deal him for…

title: Chiefs-Seahawks: 5 stats to know from Week 7 loss
summary: Numbers never lie, right? There are so many statistics to parse through during the NFL season that some can be misleading. After each game, it’s a good exercise to review NFL “Next Gen Stats” and “Premium Stats” from Pro Football Focus and find the numbers that paint a picture not only of the game, but […]
full_text: (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images) | Getty Images Numbers never lie, right? There are so many statistics to parse through during the NFL season that some can be misleading. After each game, it’s a good exercise to review NFL “Next Gen Stats” and “Premium Stats” from Pro Football Focus and find the numbers that paint a picture not only of the game, but of what to expect from the Kansas City Chiefs moving forward. Here are three statistics from the Week 7 win over the Seattle Seahawks and what they could mean for the rest of the season: 1. L’Jarius Sneed was targeted on 55% of his snaps in pass coverage According to NFL Next Gen Stats , Sneed was in coverage for only 11 snaps, but the Seahawks threw six passes his way and completed five for 83 yards. He allowed a passer rating of 118.8 despite a season-low average yards of separation (1.5) on his throws. It was similar to Week 2 against the Indianapolis Colts , when Sneed was targeted on 56% of his coverage snaps and allowed 121 yards on 10 catches. In Seattle, it seemed as if defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo adjusted by keeping Sneed on the sideline more as the game went on, but high-end receivers will continue to be targeted heavily if Sneed is matched up on them from the slot. 2. The Chiefs ran a season-low 12 plays from under center Kansas City ran it five times and passed it seven times to gain 51 yards from under center against the Seahawks. Coming into the game, the team had called at least 21 under-center plays in each game and run the ball at least 11 times. The Chiefs totaled 100 fewer under-center yards than the second-lowest total this season (151 against the Colts). The offensive switchup, which made the unit look eerily similar to its 2025 version, may have been a preference for quarterback Patrick Mahomes after right tackle Jaylon Moore (concussion) was unable to play; it’s speculation, but under-center plays make the quarterback have to turn his back to the defense, and it may have been hard to trust that in this specific matchup. If Kansas City wants to get back on track, this can’t become a trend. 3. Ashton Gillotte registered 4 Stops in 28 run-defense snaps Translation: Gillotte kicked ass when he was on the field Stops, according to Pro Football Focus , are tackles that constitute a failure for the offense based on down and distance. Only linebacker Drue Tranquill (5) had more than Gillotte among the Chiefs’ defense in Seattle, and Gillotte’s tackles came only against handoffs. Ashton Gillotte is a big part of the Chiefs' solid early-down defense. He finds the ball. 4 'Stops' (PFF) was 2nd on the team despite not starting The whole DL kicked ass against the run and set up 3rd-and-longs vs. Seattle, who just traded for Quenton Nelson pic.twitter.com/NWMk3ohcKM — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) October 27, 2026 It highlights the role Gillotte has settled into after a plantar fascia injury during training camp disrupted his start to the season. He is a strong, high-effort run defender who finds the ball and gets the ball carrier on the ground. That was on full display against the Seahawks, helping the Chiefs get to favorable third-and-long situations. Nose tackle Khiyirs Tonga (3 Stops in 27 run-defense snaps) was also a key factor there. There’s little to be critical about when talking about Kansas City’s run defense. 4. Patrick Mahomes was pressured on 39% of his dropbacks 38.9% is the second-highest mark of his season, behind the Week 4 win over the Las Vegas Raiders , but Mahomes overcame it in Las Vegas, throwing for 225 yards and two touchdowns with a 97.2 passer rating. In Seattle, it was 165 yards and two turnover-worthy plays. You have to tip your cap sometimes; the Seattle defense is very good. However, the offense will struggle if the run game is bottled up and Mahomes faces pressure on more than 1/3 of his dropbacks. Outside of Jaylon Moore’s return, there isn’t much else the Chiefs can do to consistently provide clean pockets on obvious pass downs, so the run game has to keep them out of those spots. 5. The average Patrick Mahomes throw from a clean pocket traveled 3.6 yards downfield Mahomes was kept clean 47% of the time he dropped back against Seattle, a very low number that speaks to the constant pressure he dealt with, but even when he was protected, he rarely found a downfield throw to make. He checked it down to a running back often because of this; overall, the offensive scheme didn’t manufacture anything downfield against a very good Seattle defense.

title: NFL Power Rankings Week 8 Roundup: Chiefs drop after first loss
summary: In Week 7 of the 2026 NFL regular season, the Kansas City Chiefs lost to the Seattle Seahawks in front of a primetime audience. Let’s see how the national media reacted to it in this week’s sampling of power rankings: ESPN: 4 (Down from 2) Best offseason addition: RB Kenneth Walker III Despite his disappointing […]
full_text: (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images In Week 7 of the 2026 NFL regular season, the Kansas City Chiefs lost to the Seattle Seahawks in front of a primetime audienc e. Let’s see how the national media reacted to it in this week’s sampling of power rankings: ESPN : 4 (Down from 2) Best offseason addition: RB Kenneth Walker III Despite his disappointing return to Seattle on Sunday, Walker has perhaps been the biggest reason the Chiefs are atop the AFC standings. He is second in the league with 701 rushing yards; his production has made life easier for quarterback Patrick Mahomes , who has excelled at play-action passes. At this point last season, the Chiefs realized they didn’t have any explosion in their running attack. Now the Chiefs’ biggest strength on offense has been when Mahomes hands the ball off to his new teammate. — Nate Taylor — Nate Taylor The Athletic : 3 (Down from 2) Something spooky: An offensive blip That was the first time in Patrick Mahomes’ career that his offense didn’t reach the end zone in some fashion. And frankly, it could’ve been even more lopsided if not for a Sam Darnold interception in the end zone. Still, the Chiefs should be fine. That game probably said more about Seattle’s defense than it did about Kansas City’s offense. — Chad Graff and Josh Kendall Pro Football Talk : 5 (Down from 2) They badly need help at receiver. — Mike Florio CBSSports.com : 4 (Down from 2) They are just too limited on offense without a big-play threat receiver. They need to make a move to get Patrick Mahomes some help. — Pete Prisco Yahoo! Sports : 4 (Down from 2) The Chiefs are allowed one bad game, in a hostile road environment against a great defense. They couldn’t get anything going in a 20-3 loss. But it was troubling how little Kansas City did on offense once Kenneth Walker III was taken out of the equation. Walker had 36 rushing yards. Nobody else made an impact; no other Chief posted more than 44 yards. Rashee Rice was out and that affected the offense. However, the Chiefs still have to be considered a candidate to make a trade for a receiver before the deadline to alleviate their recurring issues in the passing game. “So you got to feel it on that plane ride home and understand that it sucks. But then how can you build off of it?” quarterback Patrick Mahomes said, via Chiefs Wire. “The biggest thing is as we get back and get back to that film study on the Broncos, you got to see where you made your mistakes and how they’re going to try to execute, and then do stuff to combat that and play better. So, obviously, it sucks right now, but we’ll be full steam ahead, trying to do our best to find a way to win this next week.” — Frank Schwab USA Today : 6 (Down from 2) They don’t get the benefit of the doubt San Francisco does, and this could be a generous ranking after the first game of Patrick Mahomes’ career in which he never took a snap in the red zone. The offense’s 213 yards was also a new low under the three-time Super Bowl MVP … granted Mahomes could use better blocking and some help at wideout, especially against a unit like the “Dark Side.” — Nate Davis Sports Illustrated : 6 (Down from 2) What we saw on Sunday was the epitome of how incredible Kenneth Walker III has been over the first six weeks of the season. You can cover up a lot of question marks by rushing the ball for more than 130 yards a game. — Conor Orr Sporting News : 3 (Down from 1) The Chiefs met a frightening Seahawks defense on the road at night that gave Patrick Mahomes and Kenneth Walker III chills they hadn’t experienced together this season. It’s not often they look so flat and lost but it’s good to get some out of it out of their system ahead of a huge division clash in Denver. — Vinnie Iyer FOX Sports : 3 (Down from 2) The Chiefs were bound to stumble at some point, but that was one ugly way to do it. Patrick Mahomes managed just 165 passing yards and an interception against the tough Seattle defense. And RB Kenneth Walker III was held to just 36 rushing yards by his former team. Given how bad that was, it’s probably worth noting that the Chiefs haven’t exactly played a tough schedule. They are now set up for a very interesting rematch this week with the best team they beat: the Broncos. Stat To Know : During the 20-3 loss to the Seahawks, Kansas City never reached the red zone, the first time that has happened in a Patrick Mahomes NFL start, with Sunday being his 153rd career start, including the playoffs. — Ralph Vacchiano
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: The Chiefs’ defense struggled to get stops in Seattle
summary: In the 20-3 loss to the Seattle Seahawks, the Kansas City Chiefs’ defense played the bend-don’t-break style that coordinator Steve Spagnuolo has sharpened throughout his time in Kansas City. Through Week 7, the Chiefs still allow the second-fewest points per game in the NFL (17.2). The defense kept the team in this game — a […]
full_text: Credit: Joe Nicholson-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect In the 20-3 loss to the Seattle Seahawks , the Kansas City Chiefs ’ defense played the bend-don’t-break style that coordinator Steve Spagnuolo has sharpened throughout his time in Kansas City. Through Week 7, the Chiefs still allow the second-fewest points per game in the NFL (17.2). The defense kept the team in this game — a better kick from 45 yards by Harrison Butker would have brought the game to within a score in the fourth quarter — but regardless of the point total, the Seahawks’ offense stayed on the field. Seattle converted 11 of 16 third downs and sustained five possessions for nine or more plays. The Seahawks ran 19 more plays than Kansas City and held possession for nearly 12 more minutes. The three longest drives were key turning points, and each featured third-and-longs the Seahawks converted: 1st half: 15 plays and 96 yards for a field goal 3rd & 9 and 3rd & 7 converted Second quarter: 10 plays and 66 yards for a touchdown 3rd & 6 and 3rd & 9 converted Third quarter: 13 plays and 62 yards for a field goal 3rd & 9 and 3rd & 10 converted Let’s take a closer look at why the Chiefs couldn’t get off the field when it needed to in Seattle: Man coverage lapses Early on, Spags deployed man coverage on third downs, and quarterback Sam Darnold targeted slot cornerback L’Jarius Sneed regardless of the matchup. On the opening drive, he allowed a chains-moving third-down catch out of the slot, but the Chiefs eventually forced a punt. Third-and-9 on the second drive: With wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba, the reigning NFL Offensive Player of the Year, as the primary threat on a pass down, the Chiefs have near-safety help over the top. Here, safety Chamarri Conner brackets Smith-Njigba with cornerback Mansoor Delane in trail-man coverage, taking away a throw at the sticks. However, slot receiver Cooper Kupp — who goes in pre-snap motion to identify Sneed as his man-coverage defender — will receive the pass with a quick pass over the middle. Kupp sets Sneed up outside and beats him back across; there’s no help over the middle because linebacker Nick Bolton is in the pass rush. Darnold’s quick release was a theme of the game, especially in the first half. He averaged 2.45 seconds to throw, the third-fastest time of his career according to NFL Next Gen Stats . He completed 13 of 14 passes when throwing in 2.5 seconds or less. Third-and-7 on the same drive: In a similar man-coverage setup, it’s now Sneed who is manned up on Smith-Njigba, with safety Alohi Gilman anticipating an out-breaking throw at the sticks in help coverage. However, Sneed loses the inside leverage by overdoing his jam at the line of scrimmage. Gilman cheating outside opened the floodgates for the 33-yard catch-and-run over the middle, and Conner’s poor angle on the missed tackle didn’t help either. The Seahawks relentlessly attacked the Chiefs’ man coverage over the middle until Spags adjusted. Not finishing the play When the Chiefs turned to zone coverage, typically when closer to or in the red zone, it wasn’t as easy for Darnold to find an option to move the chains. Kansas City held Seattle to a field goal on the previously discussed possession by playing tight zone coverage on the ultimate third down. Third-and-6 from late in the first half: The Chiefs dropped seven into zone coverage with a four-man rush, and Darnold rolls to his right after not his initial reads are taken away. That sets up defensive end George Karlaftis to wrap him up for a game-changing sack, leaving Seattle on fourth down and deciding to kick a roughly 60-yard field goal. Instead, Darnold jukes Karlaftis and outruns defensive tackle Chris Jones to the sticks. It was one of the first times the Chiefs’ defensive lineman had a chance at a sack, and No. 56 in particular couldn’t come through. A few plays later, Darnold delivered a perfect pass in rhythm to Smith-Njigba, who caught the touchdown down the sideline through tight coverage by Delane on third-and-9. Third-and-9 in the third quarter: Another four-man rush with zone coverage forces Darnold out of the pocket, and without a throwing option, cornerback Nohl Williams and linebacker Nick Bolton can’t react in time to stop him from crossing the marker. A late fake by Darnold fools Bolton. Third-and-10 from the same drive: Zone and a four-man rush work once again, with a stunt by Karlaftis dissuading Darnold from a downfield throw and forcing a checkdown. Yet Bolton and Williams are again too passive in rallying to the ball, allowing the running back to gain the first down. Edge rusher R Mason Thomas’s visible frustration after the play, in which he pressured Darnold, reflects how many in Chiefs Kingdom felt. Nothing seemed to go Kansas City’s way on third-and-long in Seattle. The bottom line Despite a frustrating night, the Chiefs’ defense was close to having a winning formula. The problem is, we say the unit is “close” way too often when analyzing negative plays, whether it’s the pass rush or coverage. On the flip side, it suggests that the players on the field simply need to perform better. However, there need to be personnel wrinkles, including at slot cornerback. Sneed (14 snaps) seemed to see his playing time decrease as the night went on, and that should continue as Chris Roland-Wallace rises in that same position. We finally found a role for Jeffrey Bassa in the Chiefs' defense He played 2 snaps in Seattle, both as a QB Spy. Remember this for the Buffalo matchup pic.twitter.com/CZYX1U8TzS — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) October 27, 2026 Another wrinkle that the Chiefs teased on Sunday night was second-year linebacker Jeffrey Bassa playing a Quarterback-spy role. He was in on two third-down red-zone stops as part of a unique defensive formation that deployed just two pass rushers, flooding coverage with as many defenders as possible. Look out for Bassa on the field as a spy moving forward, especially against mobile quarterbacks like the Buffalo Bills ’ Josh Allen.

title: Chiefs News: The Chiefs are reportedly ‘calling around’ about a trade
summary: On Monday, after the Kansas City Chiefs failed to reach the red zone in a blowout loss to the Seattle Seahawks, rumors swirled further about the Chiefs’ interest in trading for a wide receiver. Ever since the injury to wide receiver Tyquan Thornton (dislocated ankle), it has felt like the insiders have been talking a […]
full_text: (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Monday, after the Kansas City Chiefs failed to reach the red zone in a blowout loss to the Seattle Seahawks , rumors swirled further about the Chiefs’ interest in trading for a wide receiver. Ever since the injury to wide receiver Tyquan Thornton (dislocated ankle), it has felt like the insiders have been talking a lot about Kansas City regarding the trade deadline, which is two weeks from today. The latest Kansas City Chiefs news New NFL Trade Rumors as Chiefs, Steelers Target Key Position Before Deadline | Bleacher Report “You look at the Kansas City Chiefs, they are calling around at least to see what they can potentially add,” ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler reported Monday. “Now they should get Rashee Rice back, he’s been out with that hamstring for the last three weeks. … They could look to add a piece in the next few weeks just because all the injuries they’ve had at that position.” Suddenly, the Kansas City Chiefs are facing a lot of questions | Andscape A key contributor to the franchise’s three Super Bowl victories in the decade, Butker has been among the most clutch postseason kickers of the Super Bowl era. But since the beginning of last season, he has been, well, way off. In fact, according to research by The Associated Press, his 15 missed kicks (10 attempted field goals and five PATs) during that span are the most in the NFL. “Warmup wasn’t great,” Butker said Sunday. “It’s just something that you have to roll with and try to fix it in the game and do the best that you can. Patrick Mahomes needed help in Seattle. That help was sitting at home | The Kansas City Star Two days after head coach Andy Reid requested that we focus purely “on the guys playing,” the Chiefs proved the relevance of those who are not: left tackle Josh Simmons and wide receiver Rashee Rice. That shouldn’t be construed as an excuse, because as difficult as it is to win without your left tackle and No. 1 receiver, the Chiefs pitted themselves into that corner. A barometer game against the defending Super Bowl champions required they play at their best, and yet their best is reliant on two players who have proven themselves unreliable. So what are the odds we will see this team at its best? Seahawks ‘put on a clinic’ shutting down Kenneth Walker III, Patrick Mahomes in blowout win over Chiefs | NFL.com Macdonald’s D so thoroughly whipped the Chiefs, Mahomes looked dazed and confused by the end of the game. K.C. generated just 213 yards, went 3 of 11 on third downs and netted 11 first downs while averaging 4.3 yards per play. For the first time in a Mahomes start, the Chiefs didn’t even sniff the red zone. The QB completed 19 of 33 passes for 165 yards and an interception. The domination frustrated Walker, who didn’t shake hands with his former teammates after the contest. “S—, we lost,” Walker said, via ESPN. “I was frustrated. That’s about it. I [saw] them over there celebrating and s—. That’s about it.” NFL legend Calvin Johnson wants Chiefs to trade for this superstar WR | Chiefs Wire During an October 26 appearance on ‘Up and Adams,’ NFL legend Calvin Johnson revealed that he wants the Kansas City Chiefs to trade for New York Jets wide receiver Garrett Wilson. A former first-round pick and 2022 NFL Rookie of the Year, Wilson is widely considered to be one of the most dynamic pass-catchers in the league and will be a hot commodity if New York decides to make him available before the November 10 trade deadline. Around the NF L Eagles vs. Cowboys score: Dallas routs depleted Philadelphia in NFC East showdown | CBS Sports Dallas’ offense was unstoppable most of the night. Dallas scored on four of its five possessions in the first half and took a 20-14 lead at halftime. Philadelphia briefly took the lead in the second half before the Cowboys’ offense mounted three unanswered scoring drives. Dallas put the game away when Javonte Williams found paydirt from two yards out with 2:21 left. Conversely, it was a tremendous night for Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott, who threw two touchdown passes to CeeDee Lamb and another to George Pickens. Prescott was complemented by Williams, who rumbled for a career-high 155 yards on 25 carries. Jay-Z selects himself to perform Super Bowl 61 halftime show | The Athletic SoFi Stadium last hosted Super Bowl 56, which was played on Feb. 13, 2022. That halftime show featured an ensemble of performances by Dr. Dre, Eminem, Kendrick Lamar, Mary J. Blige and Snoop Dogg. Jay-Z, whose given name is Shawn Carter, released his first album, “Reasonable Doubt,” 30 years ago. It has been 25 years since the release of his acclaimed album “The Blueprint.” Aaron Glenn says Garrett Wilson’s outburst ‘overblown,’ defends Jets’ offense | ESPN On the CBS telecast, Wilson was seen barking at someone on the bench during the fourth quarter. The announcers said it was quarterback Geno Smith, but it was actually passing game coordinator Seth Ryan, who relays communication from offensive coordinator Frank Reich in the booth. On Monday, Glenn was asked how he feels about a player yelling at a coach. He turned the conversation back to Wilson and Smith. “Well, I think sometimes that’s overblown as far as what people think is happening,” Glenn said. “Sometimes those conversations could be totally something else. And, listen, I know for a fact that Geno and Garrett, it was more or less, ‘Man, let’s get going and let’s get the offense going’ more than guys bickering at each other. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride Chiefs’ offense had a historically poor showing in loss to Seahawks “We have to help [Walker],” Mahomes said. “When they put so many eggs in that basket of stopping the run game, we have to have the play-action game and the movement game to be able to throw the ball. title: Chargers PFF Grades at the bye: Akheem Mesidor, defense leads the way
summary: The Chargers were on a bye this week and unfortunately saw the Dolphins earn their first win against the Jets which leaves the Bolts as the lone winless team in the NFL this season. Through six weeks, one side of the ball has been much better than the other. The Chargers defense has 15 player […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 11: Tuli Tuipulotu #45 and Akheem Mesidor #90 of the Los Angeles Chargers react after a stop during the second quarter of the game against the Denver Broncos at SoFi Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Katelyn Mulcahy/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chargers were on a bye this week and unfortunately saw the Dolphins earn their first win against the Jets which leaves the Bolts as the lone winless team in the NFL this season. Through six weeks, one side of the ball has been much better than the other. The Chargers defense has 15 player graded at 60.0 or higher on the season while the offense has 10. The craziest part? Justin Herbert is not one of those 10 players. He’s actually among the bottom five as of now. Talk about a worst-case scenario-type season for the Chargers. Alas. Let’s go ahead and reflect on how the Chargers have done this season, individually, via Pro Football Focus. Offense Best WR Ladd McConkey – 74.4 OT Rashawn Slater – 73.7 OT Joe Alt – 71.6 OT Travis Burke – 70.5 FB Scott Matlock – 66.8 When McConkey is on the field, his ability to perform in this offense is night-and-day different from every other receiver on the Chargers. Without him, this system continues to look like it has no chance. Unsurprisingly, Slater and Alt are the Chargers’ best offensive linemen but both have missed multiple games so far this season. Slater will miss more after the bye while still on IR but Alt is reportedly set to return this week against the Rams after receiving good news on his neck injury. The rookie Burke has surprised in his surprise duties on the left side and he’s currently the fourth-highest graded player on the Chargers at the bye. Should the staff make a point to fit him into the lineup? Would that come at guard? I wouldn’t be surprised to see some effort made to keep him on the field, even after both starting tackles return. Best receiving grade: WR Ladd McConkey -73.0 Best pass block grade: OT Joe Alt – 77.3 Best run block grade: OT Joe Alt – 80.2 Best rusher: RB Kimani Vidal – 65.3 Worst OT/G Trey Pipkins – 37.1 OT Daniel Brunskill – 44.3 QB Justin Herbert – 44.5 C Jacob Spomer – 44.6 WR Brenen Thompson – 45.3 Pipkins has never been a good guard and it was only a mistake for Jim Harbaugh to force him into the lineup there. Pipkins’ trainer, Duke Manyweather, has been vocal about this on social media. I’d trust him over this staff at this point. Herbert’s been bad. Not the sole reason the team is bad, but reality is that he is not jiving with the offense and no one is winning, in any sort’ve way. Thompson has barely played this season and it’s unfortunate his small sample size came against the Raiders when he couldn’t hold on to the ball in big moments. I’m excited to see him come back, but for now his outlook does not look great. Defense Best EDGE Akheem Mesidor – 75.8 LB Troy Dye – 75.5 EDGE Khalil Mack – 75.2 S Elijah Molden – 73.5 EDGE Tuli Tuipulotu – 72.9 Mesifor is your highest-graded Chargers defender this season through six weeks. His worst grade is 60.6 in run defense, but all three of his pass rush, coverage, and tackling grades are all top three on the team. Dye has not played as much as either Daiyan Henley or Del’Shawn Phillips, but he’s made the most of his snaps with a pair turnovers forced. Mack and Tuipulotu continue to be rock-steady up front for a Chargers defense that continues to be the best part of this team so far in 2026. Best run defense grade: S Tony Jefferson – 79.9 Best tackling grade: EDGE Akheem Mesidor – 81.1 Best pass rush grade: LB Troy Dye – 82.9 Best coverage grade: CB Tarheeb Still – 76.6 Worst CB Rodney Shelley – 26.9 CB Deane Leonard – 40.2 DT Nick Barrett – 44.5 DT Teair Tart – 49.0 EDGE Bud Dupree – 52.0 Shelley has been bad just about every time he’s stepped on the field. He is the worst-graded Charger on the entire team by a good amount. Barrett is just a rookie, but he has sub-60.0 grades in both run defense and pass rush. His tackling grade is still good at 72.5, however. Tart has been best as a pass rusher this year but he’s received rough grades in both run defense and tackling. He needs to get those numbers up if he wants to keep earning the extension he received this offseason.

title: NFL MVP race: Running backs trying to steal award from a quarterback
summary: The NFL MVP race has long been dominated by quarterbacks, but could a running back finally challenge that trend in 2026? With the season approaching its midpoint, the conversation surrounding the league’s most prestigious individual award raises an important question: Is a quarterback’s value still enough to outweigh a running back putting together a historic […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - OCTOBER 18: Kenneth Walker III #9 of the Kansas City Chiefs celebrates after scoring a rushing touchdown against the Los Angeles Chargers in the first quarter of a game at Arrowhead Stadium on October 18, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images The NFL MVP race has long been dominated by quarterbacks, but could a running back finally challenge that trend in 2026? With the season approaching its midpoint, the conversation surrounding the league’s most prestigious individual award raises an important question: Is a quarterback’s value still enough to outweigh a running back putting together a historic season? Quarterbacks typically have the advantage because of their impact on the passing game, overall offensive production and ability to carry their teams to victories. However, an elite running back can change the complexion of an offense, control the tempo of a game and provide consistent production that opposing defenses struggle to contain. If that production translates into team success, the MVP conversation could become more interesting than usual. The challenge is that running backs face a difficult historical precedent. Quarterbacks have become the standard for MVP voters, making it increasingly difficult for players at other positions to break through. Still, a dominant individual campaign combined with a compelling team narrative could force voters to reconsider their usual approach. Could a running back do enough to steal the award from the quarterbacks this season? Let’s examine what it would take to make that possibility a reality. MY MVP TOP-5 1. Kenneth Walker, RB (KC) Walker is the second leading rusher in the NFL with 701 rushing yards to go along with 6 rushing touchdowns. In addition, he 116 receiving yards and 2 touchdowns. Walker has revitalized the Chiefs offense. His game-changing ability in the backfield is why the Chiefs are 5-1. The difference is that he has played 1 less game than Atlanta’s Bijan Robinson. RBs with 650 rush yards and 6 rush TD over their team's first 5 games of a season since the merger 1998 Terrell Davis* 2026 Kenneth Walker *won MVP and Super Bowl pic.twitter.com/WQAk46ropp — PFF (@PFF) October 18, 2026 2. Jaxson Smith-Njigba, WR (SEA) Fresh off of winning Offensive Player of the Year in the 2025 season, JSN is on pace to compete for the award again. He leads the league receptions, receiving yards, and receiving touchdowns. He could be the next Triple Crown winner, becoming the league’s 6th player ever to do so from the receiver position. The only two players since the merger with 700+ Rec Yards and 7+ Rec TD through the first 6 weeks of a season 2026 Jaxon Smith-Njigba 1986 Jerry Rice pic.twitter.com/ZrCiEx3gnl — PFF (@PFF) October 16, 2026 3. Brock Purdy, QB (SF) The 49ers are first in the NFC West and a lot of that has to do with Shanahan’s ability to playcall. But Brocky Purdy is playing near flawless football for the 49ers. He has 15 touchdowns to 4 interceptions while pacing the 49ers top 5 offense. Highest Passer Rating in NFL history (min 50 starts) Brock Purdy 105.4* Lamar Jackson 102.7 Aaron Rodgers 101.9 Joe Burrow 101.3 Patrick Mahomes 100.9 *made 50th start Sunday pic.twitter.com/Lgatpv3yJT — PFF (@PFF) October 12, 2026 4. Bijan Robinson, RB (ATL) Bijan Robinson is probably the best NFL player on the planet. Bijan is first in the league in rushing with 704 rushing yards and 4 touchdowns. 5. Jahmyr Gibbs, RB (DET) If Kenneth Walker are 1A and 1B in the league, Gibbs is the clear #2. Gibbs is fourth in the league in rushing yards with 620 yards but has a league best 7 rushing touchdowns. Since the Lions let David Montgomery walk in free agency, Gibbs is now taking bell-cow duties seriously… For those that think Jared Goff is MVP-worthy. Please do not kid yourself. Goff is not the engine of that offense. title: Projected trade cost for Rams to acquire Brian Thomas Jr
summary: The Los Angeles Rams would likely need to surrender at least a Day 2 draft pick to acquire Brian Thomas Jr, if the Jacksonville Jaguars ultimately decide to offload the former first-round wide receiver. For a Rams team looking to strengthen its receiving corps, the potential asking price could present a significant obstacle. Thomas, selected […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FL - SEPTEMBER 13: Brian Thomas Jr. #7 of the Jacksonville Jaguars reacts after a play during the game between the Jacksonville Jaguars and the Cleveland Browns on September 13, 2026 at EverBank Stadium in Jacksonville, Fl. (Photo by David Rosenblum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Los Angeles Rams would likely need to surrender at least a Day 2 draft pick to acquire Brian Thomas Jr , if the Jacksonville Jaguars ultimately decide to offload the former first-round wide receiver. For a Rams team looking to strengthen its receiving corps, the potential asking price could present a significant obstacle. Thomas, selected 23rd overall in the 2024 NFL Draft, offers the downfield speed and one-on-one playmaking ability Los Angeles could use to complement Puka Nacua and Davante Adams. However, acquiring that type of talent through a trade typically requires meaningful draft compensation, particularly when dealing for a young receiver with first-round pedigree. Brian Thomas Jr. has plenty of trade buzz. Marvin Harrison Jr. was traded for: 🏈 2027 2nd-round pick 🏈 2027 7th-round pick Houston sent back a 2027 6th-round pick. Both WRs are 24 years old and were drafted in 2024. Harrison: No. 4 overall Thomas: No. 23 overall Career… — Arye Pulli (@AryePulliNFL) October 26, 2026 A Day 2 selection would be the minimum starting point for any serious discussion, rather than an indication of Jacksonville’s final asking price. The Jaguars would have to determine whether moving on from Thomas makes sense for their long-term plans, while interested teams would need to weigh his potential against the cost of acquiring him. Based on the Arizona Cardinals decision to trade away former first round pick Marvin Harrison Jr, the general parameters have been set for what the projected cost of Brian Thomas Jr will be. Harrison cost the Texans a 2027 2nd-round pick and 7th-round pick. The Texans are currently 2-5, which means that 2nd-round pick has a lot of upside, being viewed as a top 50 pick. For the Rams, draft capital could complicate matters. Los Angeles already surrendered significant assets in its blockbuster trade for Myles Garrett this past offseason, leaving the franchise with limited draft capital for the 2027 NFL Draft. The Rams currently have just four selections: a second-round pick, a fourth-round pick, a fifth-round pick and a sixth-round pick. That limited inventory puts additional pressure on general manager Les Snead to make every remaining selection count. Using a 2nd-round pick and 6th-round pick to acquire Thomas would mean giving up one of the team’s most valuable opportunities to add an inexpensive, young contributor through the draft, while also stripping the Rams draft capital to just 2 remaining picks. Still, the Rams’ need for another reliable receiving threat could make the conversation worthwhile. Thomas would offer a potential long-term weapon alongside Nacua, but Jacksonville’s asking price and Los Angeles’ depleted draft resources could ultimately determine whether a deal is realistic. The Rams may have the motivation to pursue Thomas, but with only four 2027 picks available, they have little room for error in another major trade. But.. the Rams won’t have Matthew Stafford-Aaron Donald-Myles Garrett and Co. for forever. It may just be worthwhile to trade for the former first round pick. Besides, hasn’t Les Snead made it a habit, better yet, a career in acquring former first round picks on other teams? It just seems like destiny to make BTJ the latest in a long list of first rounders to join Snead’s roster. Hypothetical Trade Offer Rams Receive Brian Thomas Jr Jaguars pay $2 million in salary (2027) Jaguars Receive Rams 2027 2nd-round pick Rams 2028 6th-round pick Rams 2028 7th round pick

title: Seahawks trade for Quenton Nelson
summary: The NFC West arms race is back in full effect, as the Seattle Seahawks acquired eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson in a trade with the Indianapolis Colts on Tuesday. The 4-3 Seahawks are making a push to get back in the hunt for the NFC West title and catch up to the 6-1 San […]
full_text: The NFC West arms race is back in full effect, as the Seattle Seahawks acquired eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson in a trade with the Indianapolis Colts on Tuesday. The 4-3 Seahawks are making a push to get back in the hunt for the NFC West title and catch up to the 6-1 San Francisco 49ers, while the Los Angeles Rams sit at 3-4 and hoping to start a winning streak after beating the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday. After a summer that saw the Rams trade for Myles Garrett and Trent McDuffie, and the 49ers sign Mike Evans, the Seahawks have made their move several weeks before the 2026 trade deadline. Seattle is sending a third and a fifth-round pick to the Colts for Nelson. Compensation update; The Seahawks are sending a 2027 third-round pick and 2028 fifth-round round pick to the Colts in exchange for Quenton Nelson. https://t.co/17B0bR47yV — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) October 27, 2026 Is this a move the Rams should have considered making? Kevin Dotson has not had the type of season that fans are accustomed to seeing from him. However, Nelson has primarily played left guard in his career and Dotson is a right guard. Would Dotson push Steve Avila inside or to the right side? It’s essentially the same thing that has to happen in Seattle, as 2025 first-round pick Grey Zabel is the Seahawks’ left guard. The Seahawks and Rams don’t face each other until Week 16. Seattle has had major issues protecting Sam Darnold and running the football consistently, so they’ve made a move now. Will the L.A. Rams also make a move at the trade deadline? Brian Thomas Jr and other receivers are on possibility, but any move you can make to improve the team at any position is a move worth considering.
