title: Walter Rouse growing more comfortable after ‘whirlwind’ arrival in New England
summary: While in the process of trimming their roster to get below the league-mandated 53-man limit in late August, the New England Patriots also swung a pair of trades. They acquired running back Corey Kiner from the Arizona Cardinals, and offensive lineman Walter Rouse from the Minnesota Vikings. Seven weeks into the season, both have had […]
full_text: While in the process of trimming their roster to get below the league-mandated 53-man limit in late August, the New England Patriots also swung a pair of trades. They acquired running back Corey Kiner from the Arizona Cardinals, and offensive lineman Walter Rouse from the Minnesota Vikings. Seven weeks into the season, both have had their opportunities. But while Kiner’s increased relatively gradually, Rouse was thrown in at the deep end. Such is the life of an injury replacement. However, despite the fairly abrupt nature of his arrival in Foxborough, the 25-year-old has enjoyed the journey so far. “It’s been great,” Rouse said at his Gillette Stadium locker this week. “Of course, getting here from the Vikings, it’s been a whirlwind since then. But getting here, getting with my teammates and coaches, learning the playbook, it’s been a great adventure; just learning the process and whatnot.” A sixth-round draft pick by the Vikings in 2024, Rouse mainly served as a backup offensive tackle during his two years in Minnesota. For good reason: the 6-foot-6, 322-pounder played 3,400 snaps at left tackle during his college career at Oklahoma. The Vikings, however, quickly started giving him reps both on the outside and inside. Any experience he gained at guard, however, came in a relatively controlled setting either in practice or preseason. The few regular season snaps he took, meanwhile, all saw him line up at left or right tackle. That changed after his trade to New England, and in Week 3 of this season. Leading up to their game against the Jaguars, the Patriots specifically prepared Rouse to play right guard in case starter Greg Van Roten — himself an injury replacement for regular RG Mike Onwenu — became unavailable. That happened in the first half, prompting the team to employ its “break glass in case of emergency” option. The results were as had to be expected, and the next week Rouse was back on the bench. However, with the injuries continuing, he again was thrust in the spotlight in Week 6 versus the Jets; Rouse was brought on at left guard after both starter Alijah Vera-Tucker and backup Ben Brown exited the contest. Four days later versus the Chicago Bears, Rouse got his first career start. It was trial by fire, but also a chance for him to earn some much-needed game reps to aid his development. “All the way back from when I first got in the game in Jacksonville to last Thursday, I feel a lot better,” he explained. “Just more comfortable at the guard position whether it’s in pass pro or run blocking. I think it’s just continuing to grow and just being more comfortable in that guard spot.” With Onwenu, Van Roten and Vera-Tucker all on injured reserve, and with Ben Brown only returning to practice this week, there is a chance the Patriots will continue to rely on Rouse and fourth-string right guard Matt Pryor this coming Sunday against the Miami Dolphins. Regardless of the team’s eventual plans, however, Rouse’s preparation will look the same. Staying true to an oft-mentioned mantra at One Patriot Place this fall, he will continue to prepare as if he was a starter. “That’s the mindset you just need to have going all the way back to the Jets game, a next-man-up mentality,” he said. “That comes from just preparing like a starter and just continuing to do that each and every week no matter what’s going to happen, and of course again this week — preparing like I’m a starter and just be ready for anything that happens.”

title: Patriots vs. Bears position grades and film review from Week 7
summary: With the eyes of the nation on them, the New England Patriots have not played their best football so far. After losing the season opener in Seattle, they went 0-for-2 in prime time games last Thursday night versus the Chicago Bears. It didn’t have to be this way. The Patriots had their opportunities to come […]
full_text: With the eyes of the nation on them, the New England Patriots have not played their best football so far. After losing the season opener in Seattle, they went 0-for-2 in prime time games last Thursday night versus the Chicago Bears . It didn’t have to be this way. The Patriots had their opportunities to come away victoriously, but ultimately were undone by some untimely errors and an ability to make the big play when it needed to be made down the stretch. Let’s take a look at the film and hand out some grades. Patriots film review from NFL Week 7 Quarterback: Drake Maye briefly reverted back to his Week 1-3 self, when he saw a bad throw into the end zone intended for tight end Eli Raridon get intercepted in the second quarter — a pivotal moment in a one-possession game. However, other than that one miscue, the third-year QB played some impressive football. Case in point: even with the turnover, the second most-impactful play of the night in terms of expected points added or lost, he finished with the same EPA per play as Chicago’s Caleb Williams (0.34). In a way, it was Maye playing his usual brand of football between making difficult throws look routine, extending plays with his legs, and maneuvering around the pocket even when faced with pressure and a variety of blitz looks. | Grade: A- Running back: Together with his quarterback, Rhamondre Stevenson seemingly single-handedly willed the Patriots to competitiveness on Thursday. The veteran running back finished with the best receiving output of his career — 93 yards including an improbable 48-yard touchdown to close out the first half — and did what he could behind some underwhelming run blocking. He also looked good as a pass blocker, something that cannot be said for TreVeyon Henderson. The second-year back continues to be uneven in that area, while his feel for run-lane development is also still a major work in progress. Corey Kiner did not fare significantly better. | Grade: C + Rhamondre Stevenson set a career-high with 93 receiving yards vs the Bears pic.twitter.com/YEZJhMkSQy — Taylor Kyles (@tkyles39) October 24, 2026 Wide receiver: He didn’t have the same drop issues he struggled with against the Jets in Week 6, but A.J. Brown’s impact was still limited on Thursday. He did move the chains on all three of his receptions but also didn’t manage to find the same space he did against the Jets; he looked a bit slow at times while getting up to 101 snaps in a four-day span fresh off a four-week stint on injured reserve. Catching three passes, Brown was still the most productive Patriots receiver against the Bears in terms of volume. The others — DeMario Douglas, Efton Chism, Kyle Williams — were relatively quiet in their rotational roles. Some might have been by design and the running backs and tight ends seeing increased targets, but they also didn’t provide consistently-reliable outlets for Drake Maye to target. | Grade: D Tight end: Hunter Henry continues to be Mr. Reliable in the Patriots’ offense, and his chemistry with Drake Maye has been evident for multiple weeks now. On Thursday, he hauled in a team-high seven passes both from in-structure situations and while improvising to assist his quarterback on play extensions. He also continued to perform at a high level as a blocker, something that was not the case earlier in the year. Rookie Eli Raridon, on the other hand, is not there yet and continues to struggle with his run-block assignments. The Patriots are trusting him with a high-pressure role, but he hasn’t always been up to task. As a receiver, Raridon has looked a lot better and continues to find positive matchups against second-level defenders including on his 30-yard touchdown catch up the seam: the rookie simply ran past his man to get open for the score. | Grade: B- Offensive line: They did what they could, but at the end of the day the blocking was the mixed bag that had to be expected given the circumstances. Down starting guards Alijah Vera-Tucker and Ben Brown, the Patriots used Walter Rouse at left guard and Matt Pryor on the right side. Both showed flashes, but their run blocking in particular left some to be desired — unsurprisingly, given that they had only four days to prepare for the starting roles they were asked to fill. And considering how important cohesiveness is to a team’s run game, it looked the part on Thursday. Pass protection was a different story, with the O-line holding up surprisingly well and being responsible for just nine total pressures all game. | Grade: C Defensive line: The Patriots defensive line some positive moments, such as Milton Williams registering a tackle for loss and Christian Barmore taking down Caleb Williams for a 10-yard sack that could have been one of the biggest plays of the game had New England won. However, the highly-paid interior pairing was unable to consistently collapse the pocket from the middle and needs to make impact plays at a higher rate. The same is true on the edge, where Elijah Ponder found himself misplaced on multiple occasions, including a 4-yard D’Andre Swift touchdown run. Gabe Jacas, on the other hand, flashed his impressive skills and high-octane motor once again. He still has room for growth but the arrow is pointing up steeply. | Grade: C Linebacker: The Bears made it a point of emphasis of challenging the Patriots’ off-ball linebackers, and found some success by putting Robert Spillane and Christian Elliss into tough positions. The most notable of those moments came on back-to-back plays in the late first quarter. First, Elliss seemingly did not get the memo on a coverage adjustment which left wide receiver Luther Burden wide open on a 58-yard catch-and-run. The very next play, Spillane missed a tackle while Swift found the end zone on the aforementioned touchdown. Make no mistake, there was a lot of positive as well, but on the whole the pair was still involved in too many missed or big plays. | Grade: D+ Cornerback: By his own lofty standards, Christian Gonzalez did not play his best game on Thursday. The highest-paid cornerback in football, who was added to the injury report with an illness just two hours before kickoff, gave up two separate 21-yard completions and was flagged for illegal use of hands. On the whole, he still ranked fairly low on the list of New England’s issues against the Bears, but with high salary comes high expectation. As for the issues, Marcus Jones and to a lesser degree Charles Woods had plenty of them. The pair missed nine combined tackles, with Jones’ six a career-worst. The team captain also was involved in two touchdowns, including as the assigned coverage defender on a 12-yard touchdown to Colston Loveland in the third quarter. His lack of size and modest physicality was successfully tested by Chicago all night long. | Grade: D+ Safety: Colston Loveland also made plays when matched up with New England’s safeties, including when he beat Jaylen Reed for a 22-yard gain — one of just five reps on the night for the late-August trade pickup. As for the starters, they mixed some good with some bad. Craig Woodson and Kevin Byard both missed one tackle each, and failed to make impact plays even when in decent position — including when Byard was inches from breaking up a 3rd-and-9 completion to Rome Odunze in the fourth quarter. It wasn’t a terrible night for the position, but it didn’t help lift the defense either. | Grade: C- Special teams: New England has had better special teams days, with a 47-yard kickoff return (plus 5-yard penalty added on) as one of the worst plays of the season for the unit. In addition, it didn’t recover an onside kick that seemed to at least have a chance of being reeled in. The coverage groups also missed a pair of tackles on the day. From the positive department: new dad Andy Borregales made a 47-yard field goal and hit all three of his point-after attempts. | Grade: C- How would you grade the Patriots’ performance against the Bears? Do you agree with…

title: Patriots injury analysis after Bears loss in Week 7
summary: The New England Patriots dropped to 4-3 on the year and out of the current AFC playoff picture with their loss to the Chicago Bears on Thursday night. However, not all was bad: the injury-ravaged team received a much-needed reprieve. In fact, there were only two noticeable injuries after rewatching the contest. Patriots injury analysis: […]
full_text: The New England Patriots dropped to 4-3 on the year and out of the current AFC playoff picture with their loss to the Chicago Bears on Thursday night. However, not all was bad: the injury-ravaged team received a much-needed reprieve. In fact, there were only two noticeable injuries after rewatching the contest. Patriots injury analysis: NFL Week 7 S Kevin Byard III: Early in the second quarter, the veteran safety had to be checked out by trainers on the field due to an apparent left shoulder injury. He subsequently jogged off the field under his own power and into the blue medical tent, but reemerged after a brief evaluation. Byard ended up missing just four snaps before his return. He ended the game with a 94% playing time share , not missing any other reps down the stretch. DT Christian Barmore: Barmore made what could have been one of the biggest plays of the game in the late fourth quarter, sacking Caleb Williams for a 10-yard loss. Unfortunately, the play did not end up mattering — kicker Cairo Santos kicked a career-long field goal to effectively ice the game — while the sixth-year defensive tackle remained on the ground afterwards: he had landed awkwardly on his right hand and required medical assistance. Barmore walked off the field and with the Patriots playing no more defensive snaps did not get an opportunity to reenter the game. What this means for the Patriots While the injuries to both Kevin Byard and Christian Barmore could have been potentially concerning, it appears neither will be a long-term issue. Byard returned to the game, while head coach Mike Vrabel said about Barmore on Monday that “he’ll be fine.” Him and Barmore both being present at practice on Monday is concrete proof of that. For the Patriots, especially considering that they were on a short week, this is definitive good news. The team, after all, had at least lost some starters or key reserves to injury in almost every game this season so far. Now heading into a Week 8 contest against the Miami Dolphins off a mini-bye, they seemingly are trending in the right direction again. No major injuries were added on Thursday, while the team is getting healthier — as evidenced by the fact that guard Ben Brown (knee) also was back on the practice fields on Monday. The first injury report of the week will be published on Wednesday afternoon, and give more information about the current state of the team. Kickoff between the Patriots and Dolphins at Miami’s Hard Rock Stadium is scheduled for 4:25 p.m. ET on Sunday.

title: Patriots playoff picture after losing to the Bears in Week 7
summary: Their 30-24 loss to the Chicago Bears last Thursday put an end to the New England Patriots’ three-game winning streak, and also impacts their standing in the AFC playoff picture. Entering Week 7 as the fifth seed in the conference, they woke up on Friday morning out of the playoff picture and having dropped all […]
full_text: Their 30-24 loss to the Chicago Bears last Thursday put an end to the New England Patriots’ three-game winning streak, and also impacts their standing in the AFC playoff picture. Entering Week 7 as the fifth seed in the conference, they woke up on Friday morning out of the playoff picture and having dropped all the way to No. 9. Of course, a majority of Week 7 was still left to be played at that point. With those games now all in the books, let’s update the standings. AFC East standings Buffalo Bills (5-1) New England Patriots (4-2) New York Jets (2-5) Miami Dolphins (1-5) The Patriots remain in second place in their division even after losing to the Bears, and would have stayed put regardless of what the weekend slate would have brought. The Bills, after all, were on a bye, meaning New England would not have overtaken them even in case of a win. That said, what was a one-game deficit entering Thursday is now a 1.5-game gap that needs to be overcome. Elsewhere in the division, the Dolphins celebrated their first win of the year. After looking like arguably the worst team in the NFL, they beat the Jets 28-25 on the road to improve to 1-5 on the year — a likely morale boost heading into this week’s home game with the Patriots. The Jets, meanwhile, are now 0-2 in the division and in real danger of their season slipping away already. AFC playoff standings Kansas City Chiefs (5-1) Buffalo Bills (5-1) Cleveland Browns (5-2) Jacksonville Jaguars (4-2) Denver Broncos (5-2) Pittsburgh Steelers (5-2) Cincinnati Bengals (4-2) On the bubble: 8. New England Patriots (4-3) , 9. Baltimore Ravens (4-3), 10. Las Vegas Raiders (3-4), 11. New York Jets (2-5), 12. Indianapolis Colts (2-5), 13. Houston Texans (2- 5) Not yet eliminated, but let’s be real here: 14. Miami Dolphins (1-5), 15. Tennessee Titans (1-6), 16. Los Angeles Chargers (0-6) As noted above, the Patriots found themselves in the ninth seed coming out of Thursday’s game. However, the Bengals and Ravens playing each other on Sunday meant that at least one of those teams would drop below New England when all was said and done. It was the Ravens, who lost 35-13 despite taking a 13-0 lead into the locker room at halftime. That one game was not enough to catapult the Patriots back into the top seven, though, because both the Broncos and Steelers ended up winning their contests; the former won 30-16 in Arizona, and the latter 16-10 against the Saints in Paris. Both have a worse conference record than New England at the moment — with the Patriots also holding the head-to-head advantage over Pittsburgh — but remain ahead in the standings. At the top of the conference, the Chiefs suffered their first defeat of the season. Patrick Mahomes and company were unable to play competent offensive football against the Seahawks on Sunday night, losing 20-3.

title: What are some changes the Saints could make during the bye week?
summary: With the New Orleans Saints having only two wins entering the bye week, it’s an ideal time for some changes to be made. Although many may be ready for a head coaching change, that’s unlikely to happen just yet, even after a loss in Paris. So, I wanted to look at other areas of the […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - OCTOBER 18: Daniel Carlson #10 of the New Orleans Saints looks on during the third quarter against the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium on October 18, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images) | Getty Images With the New Orleans Saints having only two wins entering the bye week, it’s an ideal time for some changes to be made. Although many may be ready for a head coaching change, that’s unlikely to happen just yet, even after a loss in Paris. So, I wanted to look at other areas of the roster and staff where the Saints could make moves before deciding whether to move on from Kellen Moore. Cut kicker Daniel Carlson Let’s start with the most obvious move. The Saints took way too long to move on from Blake Grupe last season, which led to more losses. That was a mistake the Saints should have learned from, and hopefully they did. So far this season, Daniel Carlson has not been the signing many hoped for. He’s been very inconsistent, and like last year, it’s impossible for fans to feel comfortable with the kicker making a field goal. It’s not going to be a season-changing move, but one that will help. Move on from OL Coach Brendan Nugent If you look at the roster, the offensive line has been arguably the most disappointing unit. After major investment throughout, the players who should be playing well are underperforming. The comparison that I have been making is to the 2024 Saints defensive line coached under Todd Grantham. That group was really bad under Grantham, but that was with a younger Cam Jordan, Chase Young, and Carl Granderson. Once Grantham was gone, the entire defensive line played much better. This is why I think Nugent and the Saints should part ways. There’s a legitimate chance that some of the Saints’ offensive line issues could improve once Nugent is gone. Trade away some veterans Although this is more of a trade deadline conversation, the Saints can start working in the veteran trade market. New Orleans should be sellers at the deadline, and they have some veterans who could at least earn an early day 3 pick. Looking at some of the names on the roster that stand out as options: Justin Reid, Cesar Ruiz, and Pete Werner. Starting with Reid, the safety group is really struggling this year, and that should have been the consistent part of the DB room. Jordan Howden can step in, and the Saints can get a decent return for Reid. Next is Ruiz, and this is similar to Reid. To get some more draft capital, Ruiz can make that happen, and the Saints can keep Jeremiah Wright in. Last is Werner, and I’m not sure the Saints will be able to get much for the linebacker. But it may be time to make a deal happen. What changes do you think the Saints should make to their roster or staff?

title: Saints WR Barion Brown shines in Paris
summary: The New Orleans Saints struggled in Sunday’s loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers in Paris, but rookie Barion Brown provided one of the team’s few bright spots. Brown made an impact in all phases of the game, showcasing his big-play ability as a receiver while also one special teams. The rookie hauled in all three of […]
full_text: The New Orleans Saints struggled in Sunday’s loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers in Paris, but rookie Barion Brown provided one of the team’s few bright spots. Brown made an impact in all phases of the game, showcasing his big-play ability as a receiver while also one special teams. The rookie hauled in all three of his targets for 57 receiving yards, including a 49-yard reception that gave the Saints a much-needed spark. The former LSU Tiger also contributed in the return game, recording three kickoff returns for 77 yards with a long of 42 yards. He added another 20 yards on his lone punt return. According to Pro Football Focus, Brown earned a 90.5 offensive grade, an 89.2 receiving grade and a 90.4 special teams grade, which highlight just how effective Brown was on Sunday. While the Saints ultimately fell short against Pittsburgh, Brown’s performance offered an encouraging sign from a rookie who has proven he can contribute in several areas. His ability to generate explosive plays in the passing game and provide a spark on special teams could help him carve out a larger role as the season progresses.

title: Can Travis Etienne fix the Saints’ stagnate run game?
summary: The New Orleans Saints’ rushing attack has been so ineffective without Travis Etienne that it is fair to wonder whether the offense would look much better even if he were healthy. With Etienne currently on injured reserve due to a hamstring strain, the Saints have been left without one of their most explosive playmaker’s and […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - SEPTEMBER 27: Travis Etienne Jr. #3 of the New Orleans Saints looks on from the field during an NFL football game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Cesars Superdome on September 27, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints’ rushing attack has been so ineffective without Travis Etienne that it is fair to wonder whether the offense would look much better even if he were healthy. With Etienne currently on injured reserve due to a hamstring strain, the Saints have been left without one of their most explosive playmaker’s and the focal point of their rushing attack. His absence has been extremely noticeable, but Sunday’s performance against the Pittsburgh Steelers in Paris showed just how serious New Orleans’ problems have become. The Saints managed a measly 18 total rushing yards (five from Alvin Kamara, six from Kendre Miller and seven from Tyler Shough), an unacceptable performance for an NFL offense. Losing a productive tailback can certainly hurt an offense, but the Saints’ struggles go beyond simply missing one player. When a team cannot consistently move the ball on the ground, it becomes increasingly difficult to keep defenses honest and take pressure off the passing game and Tyler Shough. Etienne, who is eligible to return Week 9 against the Cleveland Browns, could provide a much-needed boost to a struggling operation. His return will add that explosiveness and home-run play ability to a backfield that desperately needs both. However, expecting one player to completely transform an offense that has struggled this badly would be asking a lot. The offensive line also has to be part of the conversation. If New Orleans can’t improve their blocking up front and establish a more effective ground game as a unit, Etienne could face many of the same challenges when he returns. The Saints can’t afford to keep having performances like Sunday’s against. Eighteen rushing yards is not going to cut it, regardless of who is carrying the football. Etienne’s eventual return should help, but it shouldn’t become an excuse for the team’s broader problems. New Orleans needs to figure out why the game has been so ineffective and make the necessary adjustments before expecting one injured player to provide all the answers. Until then, it is difficult to feel confident that Etienne alone would be enough to turn things around. Do you think that Etienne’s return could make a different?

title: New Orleans Saints News: Saints forget how to run the ball

summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as the Giants are in first place in the NFC East. Presser Points: Takeaways from GM Joe Schoen | Giants.com Jaxson Dart has been around the building during his rehab process. “He’s not weight-bearing yet. So he’s on his crutches. But […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as the Giants are in first place in the NFC East. Presser Points: Takeaways from GM Joe Schoen | Giants.com Jaxson Dart has been around the building during his rehab process. “He’s not weight-bearing yet. So he’s on his crutches. But he’s staying as positive as he can. He’s around, which I think is good, you know, mentally being around the guys, being around football still. And, you know, he still thinks if we make the playoffs that he’s going to be able to come back. So, you know, that’s just his mindset. That’s just his mindset. I mean, he got hurt in the Rams game. He’s in the locker room trying to do pass sets, dying to go back in the game. So, you know, he’s one of those guys you appreciate his toughness and grit.” The John Harbaugh effect The Giants completely overhauled the organization with one hire — John Harbaugh. pic.twitter.com/dr8Dn7jftv — PFT Live (@PFT_Live) October 26, 2026 How John Harbaugh put on a coaching masterclass in lead-up to Giants’ Week 7 win | The Athletic Harbaugh didn’t hesitate to address the biggest issues facing his team. He cut veteran running back Najee Harris, who had been ineffective and then griped about his role after getting only four carries against the Saints. That paved the way for Harbaugh to turn back to Skattebo, who handled a demotion against New Orleans with professionalism, then responded with a career-high 124 rushing yards against a stout Texans run defense. Making the right read on which buttons to push is an intangible quality for a coach. Harbaugh’s successful 18-year run in Baltimore provided belief that he had that touch when the Giants made the ballyhooed hiring this offseason. Harbaugh made all the right calls last week, which helped deliver the type of win that has him confident “We’re going to be in this thing until the end now.” The Winners and Losers of NFL Week 7 | The Ringer Winner: J.J. McCarthy, Giants Savior. One month after the Vikings gave up on the no. 10 pick in the 2024 draft by trading him to another NFC team for a future fifth-rounder, J.J. McCarthy has the Giants in the driver’s seat to win their division. The quarterback made his first start for New York as a double-digit road underdog against the Texans, and he pulled off the upset in a 27-21 overtime victory that’s the highlight of the Giants’ season so far. Vikings coach Kevin O’Connell once said that “organizations fail young quarterbacks before young quarterbacks fail organizations.” It’s a thought worth revisiting with McCarthy playing well so soon after his turbulent tenure in Minnesota came to an end. While a strained relationship with the Vikings’ coaching staff didn’t help, injuries were McCarthy’s biggest issue during his first few years in the league. If he can stay healthy, the Giants might have found something here—and it’s worth noting that Sunday marked only his 11th professional start. Abdul Carter urged Giants to empty the tank. Now go win the NFC East | The Record When Abdul Carter speaks up, the New York Giants pay attention. Because the messaging is often spot on. Jaxson Dart was the heart and Brian Burns the soul of the team, but both players are out for the season following knee surgeries. What’s become clear is Carter, for all intents and purposes, has an intrinsic ability to feel the Giants’ pulse. NFL Insider: Giants bully ball taking root “[The Giants are] playing a type of bully-ball that travels.” Manti making the case for the New York Giants as the team to beat in the NFC East 😤 pic.twitter.com/WkcFLi5CQK — Good Morning Football (@gmfb) October 27, 2026 NFL Week 7: Big takeaways, questions and fantasy spin from Sunday’s games | ESPN.com Trend to watch: Deonte Banks’ strong coverage. The rejuvenated Giants cornerback locked up Texans top receiver Nico Collins most of the afternoon. The Texans completed just four of seven passes for 25 yards when throwing in Banks’ direction, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. Collins finished with two catches on five targets for 6 yards, thanks in large part to Banks. J.J. McCarthy’s resurgence took root long before joining Giants — with plenty of room to grow | New York Post Despite his struggles with the Vikings, McCarthy said Sunday he began feeling more comfortable in the league in a Week 14 win over Washington. Coming off three straight losses in which he threw six interceptions and just two touchdowns, McCarthy — after missing a week in the concussion protocol — carved up the Commanders on 16-for-23 passing for 163 yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions. He then won his final three starts, though he missed another with a hand injury. “Just being able to really start feeling like the defense is slowing down and understanding concepts, intent of plays, understanding the situation,’’ McCarthy said. “There’s a lot of things that go into playing NFL quarterback and it takes a little bit to figure those things out. I really feel like I was on an upward trajectory after that game. I continue to just refine my craft and get better every day.’’ Baldy on the Giants run game Brian Baldinger on Week 7's run game — New York Giants (@Giants) October 27, 2026 Giants’ John Harbaugh echoes Cam Skattebo’s criticism of NFL for penalty | NJ.com “That’s how I felt about it,” he said. “I mean, I understand the idea, but I also understand human physiology and anatomy and the way the body works. Skatt runs low. You have to run low. You have to run low to protect the football. You have to run low to protect your body. You can’t run in there and give tacklers your chest. When you run low, your head is down there, too. You can’t move your head off your shoulders. It’s a physical impossibility. I’m quite sure Skatt’s not trying to use his helmet as a weapon, as a battering ram. “It’s not the way he’s thinking. He’s leading with his shoulder. That’s what he’s trying to do. He’s trying to keep his head in a good, strong, upright position. But his pads are down there low. He runs low to the ground. That’s the way you’re supposed to run. That’s how you protect yourself and the football. So I didn’t have a problem with the technique personally at all, but we haven’t heard from the league. Maybe they’ll be able to enlighten us a little bit on it, in terms of what they want us to teach. And that would be great.” From Big Blue View 4 takeaways from Giants GM Joe Schoen: Trade deadline, J.J. McCarthy, more Giants roster moves: RB Tyrone Tracy to IR, RB Greg Desrosiers signed Giants finally signing veteran defensive tackle Giants trade candidate: DT Dalvin Tomlinson a low-cost upgrade? How good a pass rusher is Abdul Carter? Colts trade OG Quenton Nelson to the Seahawks, per report Film review: J.J. title: 4 takeaways from NY Giants GM Joe Schoen: Trade deadline, J.J. McCarthy, more
summary: New York Giants general manager Joe Schoen addressed the acquisition of J.J. McCarthy, the upcoming NFL trade deadline, the impact of head coach John Harbaugh, and more during his bye week media availability on Tuesday. Here are some of the takeaways. Trade deadline: ‘Look at all the options’ At 4-2-1 and leading the NFC East, […]
full_text: Joe Schoen | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect New York Giants general manager Joe Schoen addressed the acquisition of J.J. McCarthy, the upcoming NFL trade deadline, the impact of head coach John Harbaugh, and more during his bye week media availability on Tuesday. Here are some of the takeaways. Trade deadline: ‘Look at all the options’ At 4-2-1 and leading the NFC East, the Giants obviously have a chance to win the division and make the NFC playoffs. The roster, though, could use supplementing in a few areas. Schoen and the Giants have to decide whether they want to be aggressive between now and the Nov. 10 trade deadline, or if they want to protect their draft assets for the future. They are currently without fourth- and fifth-round picks in the 2027 NFL Draft, though they are projected to receive a 2027 fourth-round compensatory selection. “There’s a lot of factors into it, in terms of where we are pick-wise. We don’t have a fourth or a fifth right now. So, you take that into account,” Schoen said. “In some situations, that may rule some players out. Maybe that’s what their value is. Maybe a third is too rich or a sixth isn’t enough, so then you start looking into future picks and contract status, where we are depth-wise. So, a lot of factors that we’ll look at and who’s going to be available, who’s really available.” The Indianapolis Colts began what might be a full-blown fire sale on Tuesday by trading star guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks . The Colts have several other players the Giants might be interested in, including running back Jonathan Taylor. “It’s easy to say, go sign X, Y, and Z position, but if a team’s really not ready to get rid of somebody where they’re asking too much, it doesn’t match up with where you see the value, then it doesn’t make sense to do it,” Schoen said. “So, we’re going to look at all the options that are available. And, there’s certain teams that have already started some trades, and we’ve been in contact with those teams and have a pretty good idea of who may or may not be available. And again, it’s got to make sense, short-term and long-term, when you make those moves.” Schoen said losing Jaxson Dart and Brian Burns “really won’t impact what we do” at the trade deadline. Valentine’s View It is important to remember that this is ultimately John Harbaugh’s show, not Schoen’s. Coaches notoriously think short-term more than long-term. If the Giants make a splash move, that will likely be because Harbaugh senses an opportunity and wants to do everything possible to try and capitalize on it. The Harbaugh effect Schoen said the Giants have “absolutely” taken on the personality of Harbaugh. “It started from day one in the spring. Coach came in here and just the details, the messaging, the leadership. His record speaks for itself as a head coach. The guy has won a lot of games. The players were eager to buy in,” Schoen said. “We have a good, young nucleus of players here that just want to win. Just want to win, whatever it takes. Coach Harbaugh and his staff have done a very good job of laying out the plan. This is what it looks like. This is how you practice. This is how you approach OTA’s. This is how you approach the off-season program. This is how you train in training camp. This is how you prepare in-season, week to week.” Valentine’s View Harbaugh is clearly this team’s best and most important offseason acquisition. The view from the top The fact that the Giants lead the NFC East is something many NFL analysts and fans are having a hard time wrapping their minds around. How does Schoen see what the Giants have done through seven games? “I’m happy where we are. I really like the team. I like the makeup of the players, the grit,” Schoen said. “I was thinking about it, just the end-of-game happiness that we’ve had, whether it was the last play of the game in Tennessee or Arizona or even Washington, the way that played out. And then the walk-off run by Motor on Sunday in Houston. So, just the resilience of the players, the way we performed late in games in the fourth quarter and overtime. “Just really proud of guys like that and the way they’re approaching it. Did I think we’d be here? You never know. Each team takes on a personality of its own, but I’m really happy about where the guys are. They’ve earned the right to be in first place in the NFC East, and we have meaningful games ahead of us that I’m looking forward to.” Now, Schoen and Co. will see what they can do to help the players out. “They’ve earned that right to be in these games, and I know they’re excited about it,” Schoen said. “And, again, we’re going to canvas the league and see what’s available and what the cost may be to upgrade the roster, and if it makes sense, we’ll certainly do that.” Are the Giants equipped for a playoff run? “We’re about to find out,” Schoen said. “Again, I like the group. They’re resilient. We have a quarterback that’s started one game for us and went out and performed at a high level. You know, he’s 23. He’s won his last five starts, and just having played the position, how hard that is to do, to come in with 20-plus snap counts and not really throwing to our receivers throughout a training camp or an offseason. You think about all the reps these guys get with their receiving corps and their teammates that, J.J., I don’t think it’s been a month. Maybe tomorrow will be a month he’s been here, and to go out and perform against that defense the way he did was impressive. So, again, I like the team … I’m excited about where we are and excited to see what the future holds.” Valentine’s View Whether the Giants make the playoffs or not, entering November with that as a possibility is certainly better than already being focused on the draft. ‘A good position to be in’ That is how Schoen termed the idea of having Jaxson Dart and J.J. McCarthy, both 23-year-old former first-round draft picks, on the roster. Including Dart, Schoen said the Giants’ quarterback room is “ probably one of the stronger ones in the league.” Schoen said McCarthy was the team’s target once they knew Dart would be lost for the season. “We obviously had intimate knowledge of J.J. throughout the [2024] draft. We knew where he was on the depth chart [in Minnesota]. We knew that Carson Wentz was playing. We had played them in the preseason, so watching him pregame there. And he was probably the targeted guy from the get-go that we were really interested in,” Schoen said. Schoen was also asked why the Giants gave Jameis Winston a two-year contract extension before the season began. “When you’re talking about a backup quarterback that also has leadership, that can lead not only that room, but the team. Can he go 2-2 in a four-game stretch? He went 2-1-1,” Schoen said. “And like I said, he’s led us in games where we’ve had leads in the fourth quarter or at least a tie. So you’re in the game in the fourth quarter with him and with a backup quarterback; that’s what you’re looking at. Not to mention the ability to lead not only that room, but the team. “And then a lesson I learned back when I was in Buffalo, and we took Josh Allen his rookie year, we didn’t have a veteran in the room. You’re always going to want a vet that can help the young guys while the coaches are up game planning and the quarterbacks are doing film on their own. Downstairs in the meeting room, to have a vet and just to know how valuable Jameis is to Jaxson and how valuable he will be to J.J. as well.” Valentine’s View No matter how well McCarthy plays this season, and everyone around the Giants should hope he plays exceptionally well, I have a hard time believing the Giants would want to enter next season with a quarterback competition/controversy. I believe that the better McCarthy plays, the more he helps the Giants with another issue Schoen addressed on Tuesday — a need to replenish their draft capital. “Obviously you want to have as many picks as you can. But, again, we’re glad we…

title: Giants roster moves: RB Tyrone Tracy to IR, RB Greg Desrosiers signed
summary: The New York Giants have made a trio of roster moves as they enter their BYE week. The Giants placed RB Tyrone Tracy on the injured reserve with a hamstring injury, per GM Joe Schoen. The team signed RB Greg Desrosiers Jr. off of the Los Angeles Chargers practice squad as the corresponding roster move. […]
full_text: New York Giants running back Tyrone Tracy celebrates a touchdown. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New York Giants have made a trio of roster moves as they enter their BYE week. The Giants placed RB Tyrone Tracy on the injured reserve with a hamstring injury, per GM Joe Schoen. The team signed RB Greg Desrosiers Jr. off of the Los Angeles Chargers practice squad as the corresponding roster move. The Giants are also adding veteran DL Dean Lowry to their practice squad. Tracy suffered the hamstring injury on a 7-yard run with 5:29 remaining in the second quarter against the Houston Texans. Tracy had been playing well in an increased role, scoring a touchdown earlier in the game, and that run helping to set up a Jameis Winston touchdown. Tracy’s injury is not considered to be a long-term one, however he’ll have to miss the next four weeks. The Giants will play the Philadelphia Eagles, Washington Commanders (Thursday Night Football), and Jacksonville Jaguars in that span. Desrosiers Jr. is an undrafted free agent rookie out of Memphis and weighs in at 5-foot-10, 205 pounds. He doesn’t have stand-out physical traits, but he did have an impressive preseason that was highlighted by a nine-carry, 118-yard, 1 TD performance in the final preseason game. He was an efficient runner in college, averaging 6.2 yards per carry over the previous four years, with averages of 8.1 and 7.4 per carry in 2023 and 2024 (respectively). 2025 was a “down” season and Desrosiers Jr. only averaged 5.7 yards per carry. Desrosiers Jr. is a versatile back with upside as a pass catcher as well as a kick returner, which should allow him to contribute immediately on special teams.
author: Chris Pflum

title: Colts trade OG Quenton Nelson to the Seahawks, per report
summary: We now know that All Pro guard Quenton Nelson won’t be a member of the New York Giants. The Indianapolis Colts are trading Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks for a 2027 3rd round pick and a 2028 5th round pick, per reports. Nelson, 30, is still one of the best guards in the NFL, however […]
full_text: Indianapolis Colts guard Quenton Nelson | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images We now know that All Pro guard Quenton Nelson won’t be a member of the New York Giants. The Indianapolis Colts are trading Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks for a 2027 3rd round pick and a 2028 5th round pick, per reports . Nelson, 30, is still one of the best guards in the NFL, however his age and the fact that he’s in the final year of a 4-year $80 million contract made him a likely trade candidate for a Colts team that seems to be entering a rebuilding phase. The Colts currently don’t have a first round pick, having traded it to the New York Jets for CB Sauce Gardner, and they could use all the draft picks they can get. The Nelson’s name has been tossed around as a possible trade target for the Giants, but he isn’t the only Colts’ player who could interest the Giants. If the Colts’ fire sale has truly started, the Giants might be interested in RB Jonathan Taylor, WR Alec Pierce, DT DeForest Buckner, or DT Grover Stewart. The Giants don’t have much in the way of trade capital, with picks in the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and two 6th round picks. The Giants may be in line to receive a compensatory 4th round pick, as well.

title: How good a pass rusher is Abdul Carter of the NY Giants?
summary: Since Joe Schoen arrived as New York Giants general manager, these have been his first-round picks: Kayvon Thibodeaux, Evan Neal, Deonte Banks, Malik Nabers, Abdul Carter, Jaxson Dart, Arvell Reese, and Sisi Mauigoa. Neal was a huge miss. Thibodeaux hasn’t been as good as you hope a No. 5 pick will be, but he plays […]
full_text: Since Joe Schoen arrived as New York Giants general manager, these have been his first-round picks: Kayvon Thibodeaux, Evan Neal, Deonte Banks, Malik Nabers, Abdul Carter, Jaxson Dart, Arvell Reese, and Sisi Mauigoa. Neal was a huge miss. Thibodeaux hasn’t been as good as you hope a No. 5 pick will be, but he plays an important, though unglamorous role oftentimes in the Giants defense.Mauigoa has gone through an adjustment period but played well against Houston. Banks looked like a flameout, but under Dennard Wilson he’s playing like a Pro Bowler. Nabers is now looking like his next Pro Bowl selection is on the horizon. Reese has been everything you could hope for so far. So has Dart, even though imported first-rounder J.J. McCarthy is looking like he could give Dart a run for his money. That leaves Carter. What shall we make of him? On the one hand, we consistently see him getting into the backfield on his pass rush. On the other hand, we rarely see him actually getting to the quarterback for a sack. Is the perplexing Carter a success or a failure? Edge defenders have multiple jobs, including run defense, sometimes coverage, and sometimes eating blocks so another edge defender can get to the passer. You draft a player No. 3, though, to sack or at least disrupt the quarterback, so let’s focus on that Job 1 of an edge defender. Sacking the quarterback is a drama in three acts: You have to first beat the block of the offensive lineman opposite you who is protecting the quarterback. In football metric language, this is called a pass rush “win.” A win is not the same as a pressure, because… You have to get close enough to the quarterback for you to affect his throw. That’s not the same thing as Act 1, because the QB may be lined up in the shotgun far behind the line of scrimmage, or he is rolling out to the side opposite the one the edge defender is coming from, or the play is a quick pass to the flat, etc. Only if you get close enough to make the QB get rid of the ball sooner than he wants or affect his throw in some other way do you get credit for a pressure. You have to hit the quarterback soon enough and hard enough to tackle him before he can get rid of the ball. Otherwise it counts as a QB hit but not a sack. So how good is Carter at all these things? Pro Football Focus thinks he is pretty darn good. In his rookie season, PFF gave him an 84.5 pass rush grade, which was 11th among all NFL edge defenders. The guys ahead of him were all the players who immediately come to mind as the NFL’s best pass rushers: Myles Garrett, Micah Parsons, Will Anderson Jr., Aidan Hutchinson, etc. But now it’s 2026, so how’s he doin’ this year? No. 4 in the NFL ain’t bad. But it gets better. PFF defines a subset of all pass rush snaps as “ True Pass Sets .” These throw out plays like screen passes, rollouts, and play-action passes that distort the impression of how well the edge defender is doing mano-a-mano against his blocker and the quarterback he is trying to get to. Here are the 2026 rankings of edge defenders for only true pass set plays: The far right column shows the pass rush grade for true pass sets only, and Carter is No. 1 in the NFL. We can go further. The NFL embeds RFID tags in players’ shoulder pads, so they have a pretty good idea of if and exactly how quickly an edge rusher beats his man. Here are the rankings as of Oct. 20 from ESPN Analytics : Carter is actually tied for the No. 1 edge rusher in the NFL in pass rush win rate (i.e., beating his blocker). He’s being double-teamed (DT%) at a slightly higher rate than others in the top 5 but a rate that is typical of the top 20 overall. So beating his man is not the problem. Getting to the quarterback in time after he beats his man is the problem. But it may not be his problem. Here is a thread from Ben Linsey of Sumer Sports on the topic: Abdul Carter is tied with Will Anderson Jr. for 3rd in the NFL in total pass-rush wins, but that hasn't led to an overly impressive pressure rate or sack total. Couple of thoughts on why Carter's still been an impactful pass rusher and the pressures + sacks should come below pic.twitter.com/e6s9wdYsio — Ben Linsey (@benlinsey_) October 26, 2026 You can see Carter right up there with the big guys in pass rush wins, but the pressures and sacks are much lower than the others. The pass rush wins, though, are having an impact: On plays where Carter wins as a pass rusher, the Giants are allowing -0.66 EPA/play. That's over 3x the value of a typical play where an edge rusher wins their pass-rush rep. Dealing with small samples and confounding factors here, but the NYG defense has been very good when… pic.twitter.com/nMopAX2UkD — Ben Linsey (@benlinsey_) October 26, 2026 The EPA per play for the defense as a whole on plays where Carter beats his man is three times more negative (a good thing for a defense) than the EPA per play on wins for the typical pass rusher, i.e., even though Carter himself is not getting to the quarterback as much as he’d like, he’s (apparently, my interpretation) forcing the QB to make a quicker decision than he wants to get rid of the ball to avoid the sack. That’s because he’s winning against his blocker so quickly: A big part of this is how quickly Carter wins. His 2.29s average time to pressure ranks fastest across qualifying edge rushers and 72% of his pressures come in under 2.5 seconds (also first). Opposing offenses have a 2.52s avg time to throw vs. the Giants (2nd fastest), in… — Ben Linsey (@benlinsey_) October 26, 2026 So Carter may not have the numbers himself but the defense as a whole is benefiting. The good news beyond that is that if Carter is like other edge rushers, the best may be yet to come: And players with Carter's profile through 7 weeks (15% + pass-rush win rate and 0.85 pressures per win or fewer), tend to see upticks in turning their wins into pressures and their sack rates from Week 8 onward pic.twitter.com/nxWtuVZUzk — Ben Linsey (@benlinsey_) October 26, 2026 If all of this is not just a coincidence, then apparently it means that opposing offenses are very aware of how quickly Carter is winning, it is forcing them to get the ball out more quickly, and it is hurting their ability to be successful on those passes, whether it be because they have to focus on shallower pass routes that develop quickly and produce less EPA, or they are just hurrying and less accurate with their throws. Either way, Carter seems to be in the heads of opposing defensive coordinators, and if the stats above are meaningful, we might expect his visible impact to increase in the second half of the season.

title: NY Giants finally signing veteran defensive tackle
summary: The New York Giants and veteran defensive tackle Dean Lowry have been linked together for weeks. It appears that Lowry and the Giants are finally coming together, with Dan Duggan of The Athletic reporting that Lowry will join the practice squad. A Giants source confirmed that Lowry is, indeed, signing with the team’s practice squad. […]
full_text: Dean Lowry with the Steelers. | Getty Images The New York Giants and veteran defensive tackle Dean Lowry have been linked together for weeks. It appears that Lowry and the Giants are finally coming together, with Dan Duggan of The Athletic reporting that Lowry will join the practice squad. A Giants source confirmed that Lowry is, indeed, signing with the team’s practice squad. To make room on the practice squad, GM Joe Schoen said at his Tuesday press conference that the Giants are releasing wide receiver Jason Brownlee. Lowry, 32, has played in 132 NFL regular-season games with 85 starts over nine seasons. A fourth-round pick in the 2016 NFL Draft, Lowry spent seven seasons with the Green Bay Packers. He has also spent a year with both the Minnesota Vikings and Pittsburgh Steelers. Lowry, 6-foot-6, 296 pounds, spent last season on IR with the Steelers after tearing his ACL in training camp. The Giants and Lowry were rumored to have mutual interest in early September, but a signing never happened. New York has continued to look for veteran defensive tackle help throughout the season to support D.J. Reader and Shelby Harris. Right now, the Giants have three younger players — Darius Alexander, Bobby Jamison-Travis, and C.J. Okoye — in rotation behind Reader and Harris. Perhaps Lowry can provide some help during the second half of the season.
author: Ed Valentine

title: NY Giants QB J.J. McCarthy looked like the real deal vs. Houston
summary: The New York Giants traveled to Houston to defeat the Texans 27-21 in quarterback J.J. McCarthy’s first start as a New York Giant. McCarthy went 20 of 28 for 252 yards, while suffering three sacks. He was calm, poised, understood where to go with the football, and his arm talent shone in the Lone Star […]
full_text: J.J. McCarthy | Getty Images The New York Giants traveled to Houston to defeat the Texans 27-21 in quarterback J.J. McCarthy’s first start as a New York Giant. McCarthy went 20 of 28 for 252 yards, while suffering three sacks. He was calm, poised, understood where to go with the football, and his arm talent shone in the Lone Star State. McCarthy didn’t use his legs, but the threat of his legs allowed Matt Nagy to effectively run concepts out of different formations that made McCarthy’s athletic ability a threat to the defense. Read defenders had to remain disciplined off the zone-read, lest McCarthy break contain with his speed and burst. The Giants’ run game, also, was much more physical at the point of attack, and the overall rushing attack accepted and thrived when challenged by John Harbaugh last week. Nevertheless, McCarthy’s presence helped make the offense multidimensional, allowing them to total 420 yards of total offense. McCarthy had two 40+ yard plays in the first quarter, and his velocity, ball placement, and ability to access all areas of the field were massive assets for Matt Nagy and the Giants’ offense. McCarthy had several high-level throws in the game. Here are six of them below. Q1, 6:59, First-and-10 The Giants got aggressive after picking up a crucial fourth-and-short on a Darnell Mooney jet sweep at the Houston 47 yard line: via GIPHY via GIPHY The Giants confirm the middle-of-the-field-closed, Cover-1 look post-snap, and McCarthy rips a beautifully placed back-shoulder pass to Malik Nabers outside the numbers. McCarthy held the safety in place well, creating an easy one-on-one matchup post-snap. Still, the outside ball placement allowed the elite receiver to adjust his body, locate, and secure the pass, which set up the Tyrone Tracy Jr. touchdown. Q1, 4:05, Second-and-17 On the first play of the next drive, J.J. McCarthy (18) drove a dime to Malachi Fields (88) that the rookie receiver took for 47 yard: J.J. zips it into Malachi Fields and he does the rest. NYGvsHOU on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/UifGLgnC8b — NFL (@NFL) October 25, 2026 The ball jumps out of McCarthy’s hand with excellent velocity and ball-placement; he hit Fields in stride and allowed the big receiver to walk the tightrope up the sideline. It appears to be quarter-quarter-half coverage and Fields pressed to the midline of the numbers before exploding outside. The cornerback does a solid speed turn, but the ball placement and timing were too perfect from McCarthy. Q2, 6:52, Second -and- 10 via GIPHY via GIPHY McCarthy found Nabers for 17 yards after evading a free rusher in the pocket. I appreciate how the young quarterback navigated the pocket but kept his eyes downfield to find Nabers on the dig route. Space was cleared by Darnell Mooney (17) and Jalin Hyatt’s (81) vertical routes vs. Cover-4. The dig was open in the middle of the field, but the vertical routes were both isolated in single coverage, both with a leverage advantage. It was a great call by the coaches, but McCarthy’s movement, throw, and ability to rip it off platform are all noteworthy. Q2, :29, First-and-10 McCarthy gets the Giants in field goal range with an elite throw. This throw, however, was with an expiring clock at the end of the first half: Look at that football jump out of JJ McCarthy's hand and then drop right over the underneath defender, in between the safety and outside the numbers 🤷‍♂️ pic.twitter.com/NwVAYYeg5f — Dan Schneier (@DanSchneierNFL) October 26, 2026 McCarthy was under pressure but fired the deep corner route against man. The accuracy was so precise that it allowed Nabers to secure the 27-yard pass and get out of bounds. Houston ran a successful T/E twist that got pressure but McCarthy stood strong in the pocket and delivered a pass that got the Giants into Houston’s part of the field. Zvada attempted a 44-yard field goal that was missed. Q3, 12:42, Third-and-4 Good god JJ McCarthy 😂…The subtle pump fake to hold the boundary CB.. the layered rip here that gets just over not one but two leaping defenders and then away from the coverage outside the numbers towards the sideline… WOW. Just… wow. pic.twitter.com/DkM8gHVYHQ — Dan Schneier (@DanSchneierNFL) October 26, 2026 This is an exceptional play by McCarthy that went for 20 yards to Fields along the sideline. Nagy dialed up a high-low with Devin Singletary (26) and Fields, and McCarthy held the underneath defender with his eyes before delivering a 20 yard pass to Fields along the sideline. His eyes allowed his arm to make this throw. Q4, 9:36, Third-and-9 This was an exceptional conversion by J.J. McCarthy, who delivered a far-hash rocket to Fields for a first down. The Texans paid attention to Isaiah Likely (9) on the underneath play, and the Cover-3 leverage was off and slightly to the inside. Fields ran a route and McCarthy delivered a good pass that hit the outside hip of Fields – move the sticks! Who are we even watching here, Giants fans!? 😂😂 Far hash throw lands PINPOINT in the WR's hands (no jumping necessary)… and just look at how fast the football travels from release to catch point for a far hash throw all the way to the sideline pic.twitter.com/uu58NTbFVX — Dan Schneier (@DanSchneierNFL) October 26, 2026 Bonus play This is just an unreal arm talent throw by McCarthy, who recognized the lapse in coverage and gave Darnell Mooney a chance from the far hash to make a play. Mooney is open a lot; it’ll break right for him soon, but securing footballs like this would be an excellent start. Here’s a highlight reel from McCarthy, including a few plays that were not elaborated on above: J.J. McCarthy highlights against Houston. pic.twitter.com/HDpuSbG6WL — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) October 26, 2026 Final thoughts The Giants were 10.5 point road underdogs with a young – new – quarterback, who was labeled a bust by his previous team. Yet, J.J. McCarthy answered the call and helped the Giants win an important game before the BYE week. The NFC East is up for grabs and the Giants sit in first place. Moving to McCarthy seemed to unlock the Giants’ ability to play multifaceted on offense, while giving the team a much higher ceiling than Jameis Winston. There’s an excitement around the Meadowlands – and it’s understandable!

title: NY Giants trade candidate: DT Dalvin Tomlinson a low-cost upgrade?
summary: The New York Giants sit at 4-2-1 after seven games, surprisingly leading a seemingly weakened NFC East as they move into their bye week. With the Nov. 10 trade deadline just two weeks away, the Giants face the question of how to balance helping this team try to make a run to the playoffs for […]
full_text: Dalvin Tomlinson | Getty Images The New York Giants sit at 4-2-1 after seven games, surprisingly leading a seemingly weakened NFC East as they move into their bye week. With the Nov. 10 trade deadline just two weeks away, the Giants face the question of how to balance helping this team try to make a run to the playoffs for the first time since 2022 vs. saving or adding assets that can help them beyond this season. It is a delicate balance. Making the playoffs would be an outstanding first season for John Harbaugh as Giants’ head coach. Doing so by mortgaging premium assets for short-term fixes that won’t help the Giants beyond this season is counter-productive. The Giants then have to wade carefully into the trade market. Where could they use help? Defensive line, wide receiver, maybe running back, maybe even edge or linebacker depth due to injuries could be areas of consideration. Between now and the deadline we will be looking at a variety of trade rumors and scenarios involving the Giants. Let’s start with a player who could help the Giants’ thin defensive tackle rotation. Potential trade target: DT Dalvin Tomlinson The Giants have been getting quality run defense from veteran nose tackle D.J. Reader, but the rest of the defensive line rotation has been a question mark. Thirty-five-year-old veteran Shelby Harris has had a couple of really good games, and a couple of ineffective games. Darius Alexander has been better against the run the past couple of weeks, but he is a work in progress. Rookie sixth-round Bobby Jamison-Travis was good Sunday against the Houston Texans, not so good in his debut the week before against the New Orleans Saints. C.J. Okoye has been unimpressive. The Giants could use a trustworthy veteran to fortify their rotation over the season’s final 10 games. What about Tomlinson? Why it would work A 2017 second-round pick by the Giants, Tomlinson is working for the Los Angeles Chargers on a one-year, $6.2 contract. At 0-6 and going nowhere fast, John Harbaugh’s brother, Jim, and the Chargers might be amenable to saving a little money and moving on from a 32-year-old player who really isn’t going to help them at this point. ESPN recently proposed the following deal for Tomlinson , a move that would amount to little more than a 2028 late-round pick swap: Giants get: DT Dalvin Tomlinson, 2028 seventh-round pick Chargers get: 2028 sixth-round pick If that is really a makeable deal, it’s a low-cost move that could provide the Giants with some incremental help without really dipping into future assets. Financially, the Spotrac trade machine shows that an acquiring team would be on the hook for only $1.97 million of Tomlinson’s $2.69 million base salary. Why it wouldn’t work Tomlinson is not the top-notch run defender that he was during four seasons with the Giants at the beginning of his career. Last season, he posted an awful 37.3 Pro Football Focus run defense grade, though he has bounced back this year with a slightly-above-average 64.9. This chart from Pro Football and Sports Network using its ‘Impact Score’ shows Tomlinson’s decline over the years: The PFSN baseline for an average score is 75.0, and you see that Tomlinson has not been meeting that mark in recent seasons. Could he give more in limited snaps as a run defender than someone like Okoye? Maybe. And, maybe a chance to play for a team in a playoff race would motivate him. Is this the type of deal you would make, Giants fans?

title: NY Giants news: Playoff possibilities, running game spark, more
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know about the first place team in the NFC East. full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know about the first place team in the NFC East. Is it time to … respect the Giants as favorites in the NFC East? | ESPN.com Does that feel sustainable? Not really. Narrowly winning (or tying) games over middling teams with late takeaways isn’t something you can count on every week, At the same time, somebody has to win this division. At 4-2-1, the Giants are two-plus games ahead of the Cowboys and Eagles, with the latter now starting Tanner McKee for the rest of the season and likely to be dealing players at the trade deadline. The Commanders, at 1-4-1, have spent the past few weeks embroiled in their own internal turmoil. ESPN’s Football Power Index gives the Giants a 39.0% chance of winning the NFC East, up from 10.5% before the season. Sometimes, teams claim divisions in triumphant fashion by dominating their competition. Others win by being the last team left standing. The Giants might be more likely to fall in the latter camp, but having not won a division title since 2011, I suspect their fans won’t care how they do it. Not a traitor to the defense Reese JUST misses the QB, hustles all the way back to make the tackle after the pass. Elite effort. Absolute stud for #BigBlue pic.twitter.com/xtHjMbXbCK — el Jefé (@JefePil) October 26, 2026 NFL’s most pleasant surprises: How real are Steelers, Browns, Giants, Vikings? Pick Six | The Athletic A coach who spun through McCarthy’s pass plays Sunday night offered the following insights: McCarthy’s fundamentals have improved some; he has not climbed the pocket unnecessarily as much as in the past; there were plays against the Texans on Sunday when he appeared comfortable in the pocket, delivering the ball accurately McCarthy still forces the ball too much (opponents have dropped three potential interceptions so far, including one in the end zone against New Orleans) He still throws a flat deep ball, making it tougher for receivers to find it, let alone run under it, as was the case for Malik Nabers more than once Sunday QB Report Cards for 2026 NFL Week 7 | Beacher Report JJ McCarthy may have revived his career with the New York Giants. While Sunday’s effort is merely a one-game sample size after a disappointing start to his career with the Minnesota Vikings, the 2024 first-round draft pick provided a spark for Big Blue. McCarthy set career-highs with 252 passing yards and a 71.4 completion percentage. He did so against the Houston Texans defense, which may not be playing quite as well this season but can still get after opposing quarterbacks. Less pressure is now on the third-year quarterback, because the Giants didn’t draft him in the first round or let Sam Darnold to walk in free agency before he won a Super Bowl with the Seattle Seahawks. McCarthy is not even expected to be the long-term starter. This opportunity allows the young signal-caller to get comfortable and just play. That’s exactly what he did Sunday. Grade: B+ NFL Week 7 winners and losers: Cam Skattebo, J.J. McCarthy lift Giants | CBSSports.com Winners: Cam Skattebo, J.J. McCarthy and the Giants. Call it the Cam Skattebo redemption game. One week after John Harbaugh relegated him to the bench, the New York Giants running back amassed 124 yards and a touchdown in a bounce-back effort against the Houston Texans. He broke loose for a 42-yarder, which set the Giants up to win in overtime. Plus, it was the first 100-yard game of his career. Skattebo also held onto the ball, which should put him back in his coach’s good graces after he opened the year tied for the most fumbles by a non-quarterback through six weeks. This is McCarthy’s fifth win in as many starts dating back to his time as the Minnesota Vikings’ No. 1 quarterback. If he can keep it up, this is precisely the kind of upside the Giants bet on when they made the low-risk investment in McCarthy. They can win with him and more than salvage a season that could have been lost when their Week 1 starter had his campaign cut short. Is there such a thing as double pancake block? Both linebackers drop out but Skattebo decides to help with protection anyways by barreling his nose into a defensive tackle's ribs pic.twitter.com/UYpKp0eOvj — Ted Nguyen (@FB_FilmAnalysis) October 26, 2026 With similar traits as Jaxson Dart, J.J. McCarthy gives Giants chance to win rest of season| SNY.tv McCarthy, still just 23 years old and making only his 11th career start, looked very much like a player worthy of his first-round draft selection. He didn’t turn it over. He bought time with his legs. He layered throws and threw with anticipation. He worked through his reads playing within the structure of Matt Nagy’s offense. The Giants traded for McCarthy after Dart went down believing, once caught up to speed, he’d allow their offense to function with similar principles and concepts to that of Dart, where much of that needed to be thrown out with the statuesque Winston. McCarthy hasn’t stopped smiling since arriving in New York. He’s connected with teammates on both sides of the ball. There’s a working, back-and-forth relationship with Nagy to marry his offensive philosophies with what McCarthy is comfortable with. He’s as confident now as ever before, the game slowing down. He’s playing loose, free, trusting what he’s seeing and letting it fly. J.J. McCarthy’s win over Texans opens door to intriguing Giant possibilities | New York Daily News J.J. McCarthy’s winning performance in Houston opened the door to the possibility that the Giants may have found something in the former Minnesota Vikings first-round pick. Now McCarthy’s play against the division rival Philadelphia Eagles and Washington Commanders after the Giants’ Week 8 bye will clarify exactly what that is. Continuing to play efficiently and cleanly will be a challenge for McCarthy, because the Eagles and Commanders now have film on exactly what this Giants offense looks like with him at QB. The Houston Texans didn’t have much of that scheme to review outside of Dart’s Week 1 win over the Dallas Cowboys. Having someone like Coach Harbaugh, who instills confidence in you 24/7…… https://t.co/iYtNMnJ3uC pic.twitter.com/AXRTmkjI4T — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) October 26, 2026 Challenges accepted: Giants don ’ t ‘ run ’ from problems | Giants.com “Our guys, man, that was a players’ win in every way,” Harbaugh said. “Blocking, tackling, special teams, covering kicks, pass game, operating, getting stops when we needed stops, fighting back from adversity. But just playing one play at a time, as well as you can, regardless of the last play with no thought for the next play, as hard as you can. This was completely the opposite from the post-game scene three weeks ago when the New York Giants cornerback left MetLife Stadium in a frenzy when his walk-off Pick 6 of Jacoby Brissett sealed the Oct. 4 victory over the Cardinals.
